questions.question: An operational due diligence analyst reviews the latest audited financial statements of four hedge funds. Each received an unqualified audit opinion. Which finding is consistent with the fund’s stated strategy and needs no follow-up with the manager?

options.text: A long/short equity fund that reports low and falling leverage shows interest expense that is high and has risen each year.
A buy-and-hold value fund reports large realised gains every year and only small unrealised gains.
A global macro fund reports interest income on the cash and short-term government bonds it holds.
A credit fund that lost money for the year paid its manager an incentive fee for that year.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Read the statements against the strategy**

GARP: “Equity funds should look very different than global macro funds or fixed-income funds.” A global macro fund “most likely has interest income earned in its income statement”.

⇒ C is consistent with the strategy.

**Step 2 – Test the other three**

A: GARP’s own example of an inconsistency: low, falling leverage cannot coexist with high, rising interest expense. B: a long-term buy-and-hold fund “should not be generating large amounts of realized gains”; it should show sizable unrealised gains or losses. D: “There should never be incentive fees earned in years when the fund lost money.”

⇒ A, B and D each call for questions to the manager, or even the auditor.

**Interpretation**

An unqualified opinion is where the review starts, not where it ends: it says the statements are fairly presented, not that they make sense for the strategy the manager describes.

a.reason: Interest expense contradicts the leverage the manager represents; recalculate leverage from the balance sheet.

b.reason: Large realised gains do not fit a buy-and-hold strategy.

d.reason: An incentive fee in a loss year is a red flag; recalculate the fees against the OM.

questions.question: A pension consultant is evaluating the service providers of a multi-strategy hedge fund that uses an external administrator, two prime brokers and an independent valuation agent. Which approach is most consistent with the reading?

options.text: Rely on the offering memorandum’s description of each provider’s role, since contacting providers directly would breach the fund’s confidentiality.
Obtain the providers’ internal control letters and audited financial statements, and interview key contacts about their roles in execution, valuation and safeguarding assets.
Evaluate only the prime brokers, since an administrator and a valuation agent do not hold any of the fund’s assets.
Accept the providers without review if they are large, well-known firms, since their size ensures their independence from the manager.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – What the reading asks for**

Investors should expect the fund to make all key contacts at its service providers available, obtain the providers’ internal control letters and audited financial statements as an independent check on them, and interview them about their role in executing trades, providing technology, performing valuations or verification and safeguarding assets.

⇒ B is the full procedure.

**Step 2 – Why every provider is in scope**

Administrators and valuation agents produce the NAV and verify positions; a failure or a lack of independence there is how a reported value can be wrong even when the assets sit at a prime broker.

**Interpretation**

This is the check that would have exposed Madoff: BMIS kept execution, custody and administration in-house, so there was no independent provider to call (Workbook A24.4, in IM-14 b).

**LO:** IM-12 e: Explain how due diligence can be performed on a hedge fund’s operational environment. • **Reference:** Mirabile, Hedge Fund Investing 2e, Ch.12 (GARP 2025 Ch.10), 10.8 (Service Provider Evaluation); SchweserNotes 2026 Book 5, Reading 94, LO 94.e

IM-13 • Private Capital Investing: Distress Symptoms and Remedies • Vardeez: UNTIERED

**Source:** Written new for the Risk Management and Investment Management P1–P3 workbook (question IM-12 e.7), built from GARP Ch.10.

a.reason: Relies on the fund’s own description; the fund is expected to make the contacts available.

c.reason: Too narrow: valuation and verification providers are part of the evaluation.

d.reason: Size is not evidence of independence or competence; the feeder funds’ large auditors relied on BMIS’s tiny auditor without checking its work.

questions.question: A credit analyst at a regional bank reviews a borrower’s latest annual report while preparing its annual credit review. Which observation is most consistent with an early warning signal of financial distress?

options.text: Revenue dipped in the first quarter, in line with the firm’s usual seasonal pattern.
The tax charge appears low relative to the earnings the firm reports.
Almost all of the year’s earnings were generated by the firm’s core operations.
The firm kept the same auditor and the same fiscal year-end as in prior years.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Recall the early-warning questions**

The reading’s accounting questions include: are earnings generated from core operations, and does the tax charge appear low relative to reported earnings?

⇒ A tax charge that looks low against reported earnings suggests the earnings may be overstated: an early warning signal.

**Step 2 – Check the other observations**

A dip that follows the usual seasonal pattern is the kind of temporary fluctuation the analyst must separate from a permanent deterioration. Earnings from core operations, and an unchanged auditor and fiscal year-end, are the healthy answers to the reading’s questions.

**Interpretation**

The tax line is hard to inflate along with profits: when reported earnings rise but the tax charge does not, ask what kind of earnings they are.

**LO:** IM-13 a: Explain different reasons why firms may experience financial distress and identify potential indicators of distress. • **Reference:** Ippolito, Private Capital Investing (2020), Ch.20; SchweserNotes 2026 Book 5, Reading 95, LO 95.a

**Source:** Written new for the Risk Management and Investment Management P1–P3 workbook (question IM-13 a.2), built from SchweserNotes 2026 Reading 95.

a.reason: A seasonal dip is a temporary fluctuation, not by itself a distress signal.

c.reason: Earnings from core operations are the reassuring answer to the first question.

d.reason: Changes of auditor or fiscal year-end are warning signs; keeping them is not.

questions.question: A distressed-debt analyst is preparing a training note on why firms default. Which statement about performing well below expectations as a cause of financial distress is correct?

options.text: It is the most common cause of distress, and in a recession the key challenge is to judge whether the downturn itself or management’s decisions drive the deterioration.
It is a rare cause of distress, because recessions can be forecast and their effect on revenue hedged in advance.
It covers products that lose demand as preferences shift, which the reading classifies as a crisis of confidence.
In a recession, the deterioration should always be attributed to the business cycle rather than to management’s strategy.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Recall the reading’s statement**

“Performing well below expectations. This is the most common cause of financial distress.” Its two triggers are economic downturns and uncompetitive products or services.

**Step 2 – The diagnostic challenge**

For downturns, “the key challenge is determining whether the downturn itself is driving the deterioration, or whether management decisions and strategies are the underlying cause”.

⇒ A states both points.

**Interpretation**

The diagnosis matters for the remedy: a cyclical problem may need time and liquidity; a management problem needs a new plan, and extra capital can simply give weak management more time to destroy value (IM-13 b).

**LO:** IM-13 a: Explain different reasons why firms may experience financial distress and identify potential indicators of distress. • **Reference:** Ippolito, Private Capital Investing (2020), Ch.20; SchweserNotes 2026 Book 5, Reading 95, LO 95.a

**Source:** Written new for the Risk Management and Investment Management P1–P3 workbook (question IM-13 a.3), built from SchweserNotes 2026 Reading 95.

b.reason: Polarity flip: it is the most common cause, and the business cycle “is unavoidable”.

c.reason: Sibling swap: obsolete products are the second trigger of performing below expectations; a crisis of confidence is usually fraud.

d.reason: Absolute claim: the reading asks the analyst to separate the cycle from management’s decisions, not to assume the answer.

questions.question: A distressed-debt analyst groups four troubled borrowers by the main cause of their distress. Which grouping is correct?

options.text: A roll-up of 40 regional dental practices whose expected economies of scale never materialised: performing well below expectations.
A chemicals maker facing a class action over groundwater contamination that its insurance may not cover: unexpected liabilities.
A retailer whose sales collapsed after its customers moved online: crisis of confidence.
A logistics firm whose former CFO is found to have inflated revenue for five years: unrealistic business plan.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Recall the five families**

Leverage and business performance; unexpected liabilities (tort, contract); performing well below expectations (downturns, uncompetitive products); crisis of confidence (often fraud); unrealistic business plans (LBOs, roll-ups, too many entrants).

**Step 2 – Place each borrower**

Class action for environmental harm: a tort liability, under unexpected liabilities, often underestimated by management and possibly uninsured. Roll-up whose economies of scale never came: unrealistic business plan. Retailer losing customers to online rivals: uncompetitive products, under performing below expectations. CFO fraud: crisis of confidence.

⇒ Only B is grouped correctly.

**Interpretation**

Markets typically “assume the worst” about a tort claim and discount the firm’s securities before the award is known.

**LO:** IM-13 a: Explain different reasons why firms may experience financial distress and identify potential indicators of distress. • **Reference:** Ippolito, Private Capital Investing (2020), Ch.20; SchweserNotes 2026 Book 5, Reading 95, LO 95.a

**Source:** Written new for the Risk Management and Investment Management P1–P3 workbook (question IM-13 a.5), built from SchweserNotes 2026 Reading 95.

a.reason: Roll-ups are one of the reading’s three unrealistic business plans.

c.reason: Obsolete products are performing below expectations, not a crisis of confidence.

d.reason: Accounting fraud is the classic crisis of confidence (Enron), not an unrealistic plan.

questions.question: Shortly after a manufacturer discloses that its former CFO falsified three years of revenue, a credit analyst at an insurer that holds the firm’s bonds is asked what to assess first. Which approach is most consistent with the reading?

options.text: Treat only the three restated years as unreliable, since information from outside the fraud period is unaffected.
Assess how far the fraud contaminates all previously reported information, and whether it could trigger a liquidity crisis through cash balances, credit lines and loan acceleration.
Focus on whether the firm’s products remain competitive, since a crisis of confidence is mainly a problem of customer demand.
Wait for the next audited statements before acting, since market prices overreact to fraud news and then recover.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Reliability of historical information**

“Once financial fraud is uncovered, all previously reported financial information becomes suspect.” The analyst assesses the informational contagion and whether there is a practical cutoff point for reliable data.

**Step 2 – Liquidity and the likelihood of bankruptcy**

The analyst asks whether the fraud could trigger liquidity problems: cash balances, the availability of credit lines and the risk of loan acceleration.

⇒ B covers the two areas of focus the reading names.

**Interpretation**

A crisis of confidence turns a reporting problem into a funding problem: lenders who no longer trust the numbers can pull lines or accelerate loans.

**LO:** IM-13 a: Explain different reasons why firms may experience financial distress and identify potential indicators of distress. • **Reference:** Ippolito, Private Capital Investing (2020), Ch.20; SchweserNotes 2026 Book 5, Reading 95, LO 95.a

IM-13 • Private Capital Investing: Distress Symptoms and Remedies • Vardeez: UNTIERED

**Source:** Written new for the Risk Management and Investment Management P1–P3 workbook (question IM-13 a.6), built from SchweserNotes 2026 Reading 95.

a.reason: Too narrow: the contagion can reach information outside the restated years; that is why a cutoff point must be found.

c.reason: Sibling swap: competitiveness belongs to performing below expectations.

d.reason: Waiting ignores the immediate liquidity question, which is the more urgent of the two.

questions.question: A distressed-debt analyst notes that a retailer’s senior bonds now trade at 45 per 100 of face value, down from 92 six months ago. Which interpretation of the debt trading level is most consistent with the reading?

options.text: The lower trading level signals that the market expects more severe distress, and it informs the analyst about which restructuring solutions are realistic.
The lower trading level signals that the market expects milder distress, because cheaper bonds make open market repurchases more attractive.
The trading level is informative only for bank loans, because bond prices mainly reflect changes in interest rates.
The trading level measures the bonds’ coupon relative to market yields and says nothing about the restructuring options.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – What the trading level is**

The debt trading level is the current market price of the debt relative to its full repayment value.

**Step 2 – What it tells the analyst**

It “serves as an indicator of the market’s expectations about distress severity and potential restructuring options”. A fall from 92 to 45 means the market expects far less to be repaid.

⇒ A: deeper expected distress, and a guide to the realistic solutions.

**Interpretation**

The price is the market’s verdict on the stage of distress. Near full value, the problem looks like liquidity; far below it, the market is pricing in a restructuring of the claim itself.

**LO:** IM-13 b: Describe methods firms can use to remedy a financial distress situation at different stages of distress and explain the potential implications and challenges to using each method. • **Reference:** Ippolito, Private Capital Investing (2020), Ch.20 (after Moyer, 2005); SchweserNotes 2026 Book 5, Reading 95, LO 95.b

**Source:** Written new for the Risk Management and Investment Management P1–P3 workbook (question IM-13 b.1), built from SchweserNotes 2026 Reading 95.

b.reason: Polarity flip: a lower price signals more severe expected distress. Cheaper bonds can make a discounted buyback attractive, but only for a firm with cash to spare.

c.reason: The reading applies the trading level to a firm’s actively traded debt; a fall from 92 to 45 is a credit signal, not a rate move.

d.reason: The trading level is a price relative to repayment value, and the reading links it directly to the restructuring options.

questions.question: A distressed industrial firm with almost no cash wants to cut its bond debt. It offers bondholders new secured notes in exchange for their existing unsecured bonds, and warns that bondholders who do not take part may end up worse off than those who do. Which method is the firm using?

options.text: A noncoercive exchange offer.
A cash tender offer.
A coercive exchange offer.
A direct purchase from bondholders.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Identify the family**

The firm lacks cash and offers new securities for its distressed debt: an exchange offer, not a cash tender or a direct purchase.

**Step 2 – Coercive or noncoercive**

Exchange offers “may be coercive, meaning participants are warned that nonparticipants may be disadvantaged”; noncoercive offers encourage participation by highlighting the opportunity’s attractiveness.

⇒ The warning makes it a coercive exchange offer.

**Interpretation**

Coercion is the firm’s answer to the holdout problem: if staying out looks worse than taking part, fewer creditors hold out (IM-13 c).

**LO:** IM-13 b: Describe methods firms can use to remedy a financial distress situation at different stages of distress and explain the potential implications and challenges to using each method. • **Reference:** Ippolito, Private Capital Investing (2020), Ch.20; SchweserNotes 2026 Book 5, Reading 95, LO 95.b

**Source:** Written new for the Risk Management and Investment Management P1–P3 workbook (question IM-13 b.4), built from SchweserNotes 2026 Reading 95.

a.reason: A noncoercive offer persuades with attractive terms, not with a warning.

b.reason: A tender offer pays cash; this firm has almost none.

d.reason: A direct purchase is a negotiated deal with individual holders, usually for cash.

questions.question: A restructuring adviser briefs the board of a distressed company on the implications of different ways to raise capital and reduce leverage. Which of the following statements is correct?

options.text: A private equity sponsor holding more than 50% of the equity is generally positive for creditors, because the sponsor realises value only after the debt claims are satisfied.
Assets generally fetch better prices after a bankruptcy filing, so a distressed firm should delay asset sales until it has filed.
Secured financing is usually the easiest source of cash for a distressed firm, because its most valuable assets are rarely pledged.
An equity injection from new outside investors can usually be arranged faster than one from the firm’s incumbent investors.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – The equity sponsor**

“A private owner with more than a 50% stake is generally positive for distressed investors. A majority equity holder realizes value only after debt claims are satisfied, which aligns incentives.”

⇒ A is correct.

**Step 2 – Test B, C and D**

Asset sales: a favourable price is “generally easier to obtain before a bankruptcy filing”. Secured financing: “often limited”, since the most valuable assets were pledged in earlier restructurings. Equity: incumbent capital “can typically be arranged quickly”, while new investors take longer because of due diligence.

⇒ B, C and D each reverse the reading.

**Interpretation**

Each method’s implication follows from timing and incentives: sell early, expect the collateral to be gone, and look to existing owners first for fast equity.

**LO:** IM-13 b: Describe methods firms can use to remedy a financial distress situation at different stages of distress and explain the potential implications and challenges to using each method. • **Reference:** Ippolito, Private Capital Investing (2020), Ch.20; SchweserNotes 2026 Book 5, Reading 95, LO 95.b

**Source:** Written new for the Risk Management and Investment Management P1–P3 workbook (question IM-13 b.5), built from SchweserNotes 2026 Reading 95.

b.reason: Polarity flip on timing: sell before filing.

c.reason: Polarity flip: the best assets are usually already pledged.

d.reason: Reversed: incumbents are faster; newcomers need time for due diligence.

questions.question: The head of risk at a global asset manager tells the board that the firm’s market-driven scenario (MDS) process is designed to meet James Surowiecki’s three criteria for good collective decisions. Which of the following correctly matches a feature of the MDS process with the criterion it satisfies?

options.text: Requiring every expert to adopt the firm’s house economic view before proposing shocks satisfies the criterion that opinions be independent.
A centralized process run by the risk management department to aggregate the ideas into a collective view satisfies the criterion of an objective aggregation mechanism.
Passing the policy shocks through a covariance matrix satisfies the criterion that each individual possess specialized knowledge not available to others.
Letting the experts settle the scenario among themselves, without the risk function, satisfies the criterion of an objective aggregation mechanism.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – The three criteria**

(1) Each individual has specialized knowledge not available to others; (2) opinions are independent and not influenced by groupthink; (3) there is an objective mechanism for aggregating private views into a collective assessment.

**Step 2 – Match the MDS features**

The diverse group of professionals supplies (1). The firm’s risk management department “develops a centralized process to aggregate these ideas into a collective view”: that is (3).

⇒ B.

**Interpretation**

The mapping explains why the aggregation sits with risk management rather than with any one investment team: an aggregator that has no stake in a particular view is what makes the mechanism objective.

**LO:** IM-15 a: Describe and evaluate the market-driven scenario (MDS) approach used to develop scenarios for stress testing investment portfolios. • **Reference:** SchweserNotes 2026 Book 5, Reading 97, LO 97.a (Surowiecki, The Wisdom of Crowds)

**Source:** Written new for the Risk Management and Investment Management P1–P3 workbook (question IM-15 a.2), built from SchweserNotes 2026 Reading 97.

a.reason: Polarity flip: imposing a house view is the groupthink that the independence criterion rules out.

c.reason: Sibling swap: the covariance matrix is a statistical tool that implies the nonpolicy shocks; specialized knowledge comes from the diverse experts.

d.reason: Removing the central risk function removes the objective aggregator; a consensus reached among the experts themselves invites groupthink.

questions.question: At an investment committee meeting, the CIO of a balanced fund proposes replacing the fund’s 99% VaR limit with the loss from the firm’s Soft Brexit market-driven scenario, which he describes as “our new measure of tail loss”. Which of the following responses is most consistent with the purpose of the MDS approach?

options.text: The proposal is appropriate, because the MDS approach is designed to quantify the tail loss of a portfolio at a stated confidence level.
The proposal is appropriate, because a scenario’s P&L can be converted into an exact probability of loss without any further assumptions.
The proposal misreads the approach: MDS does not quantify tail losses or set targets; it integrates views in a structured way and prompts managers to reassess their convictions.
The proposal misreads the approach: MDS scenarios are built only from historical episodes, so they cannot inform any forward-looking decision.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – What the approach is for**

“The goal of the MDS approach is not to quantify tail losses or force risk managers to target specific outcomes. Instead, it is a tool for integrating insights from different perspectives in a structured way.”

**Step 2 – What it gives instead**

By quantifying returns under scenarios of varying plausibility, it encourages managers to reassess their strategic convictions and increases awareness of alternative outcomes.

⇒ The CIO’s proposal misreads the approach: C.

**Interpretation**

A scenario loss is the outcome of one coherent story, with no confidence level attached. It complements a VaR limit; it does not replace it.

**LO:** IM-15 a: Describe and evaluate the market-driven scenario (MDS) approach used to develop scenarios for stress testing investment portfolios. • **Reference:** SchweserNotes 2026 Book 5, Reading 97, LO 97.a and LO 97.c (closing paragraph of the Brexit example)

IM-17 • Illiquid Assets • Vardeez: VERY IMPORTANT

**Source:** Written new for the Risk Management and Investment Management P1–P3 workbook (question IM-15 a.6), built from SchweserNotes 2026 Reading 97.

a.reason: Purpose error: quantifying tail losses at a confidence level is what the reading says MDS is not for.

b.reason: Absolute claim: scenario z-scores give only relative probabilities; an absolute probability needs further assumptions (IM-15 b).

d.reason: Right verdict, wrong reason: MDS scenarios are forward-looking, not built only from historical episodes.

questions.loText: Explain the process of unsmoothing returns and the effects of unsmoothing.
questions.question: The head of real estate at a Canadian pension plan unsmooths the quarterly returns of the plan’s appraisal-based property index before the annual asset allocation review. The reported series has a first-order autocorrelation of 0.70, and the properties are reappraised once a year. Which of the following statements about the unsmoothed series is correct?

options.text: Its average quarterly return will be well below the reported average, because unsmoothing restores the losses that the appraisers failed to record.
Its average quarterly return will be close to the reported average, because smoothing spreads each shock over several quarters without removing it.
A first-order AR(1) filter is suﬀicient for this index, because the annual reappraisal cycle affects the level of the index but not the lag structure of its returns.
Its volatility will be lower than the reported volatility, because the filter removes the noise that appraisal errors add to the reported returns.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – What smoothing does to the level**

Each true shock is spread over several quarters but still counted in full, so the index ends where the true index ends. Summing the filter gives $\sum r_{t} = \sum r^{*}_{t} + \frac{\phi}{1-\phi}(r^{*}_{T} - r^{*}_{0})$, a single end term.

⇒ The average return is essentially unchanged: Ang’s first property.

**Step 2 – What it does to dispersion**

The filter adds noise back, so volatility rises: with $\phi= 0.70$ a pure AR(1) filter would scale it by $\sqrt{1.7/0.3} = 2.38$.

**Step 3 – What the reappraisal cycle does**

Annual reappraisals put a fourth-order lag into quarterly returns. A first-order filter misses it; Ang’s third property is that unsmoothing is an art, best done with an ARMA model and knowledge of how the market is valued.

**Interpretation**

Unsmoothing changes the path, not the destination. Individual bad quarters become much worse, which is easy to mistake for a lower mean.

**LO:** IM-17 d: Explain the process of unsmoothing returns and the effects of unsmoothing. • **Reference:** Ang, Asset Management (2014), Ch.13, Unsmoothing (three properties), as reported in Vardeez IM-17 d and Workbook D9; SchweserNotes 2026 Book 5, Reading 99, LO 99.d

**Source:** Written new for the Risk Management and Investment Management P1–P3 workbook (question IM-17 d.4), built from SchweserNotes 2026 Reading 99.

a.reason: Confuses deeper individual quarters with a lower mean: unsmoothing affects risk estimates, not expected returns.

c.reason: Annual reappraisal creates a fourth-order lag in quarterly data; one lag is not enough.

d.reason: Polarity flip: unsmoothing adds noise back and raises volatility.

questions.subject: Investment Risk
questions.loText: Explain the process of unsmoothing returns and the effects of unsmoothing.
questions.question:
A risk manager at a Dutch insurer presents the following statistics for a private real estate index to the investment committee. Over the same period the quarterly volatility of US equities was about 7.5%.

|  | Reported | Unsmoothed |
|---|---|---|
| First-order autocorrelation | 0.78 | close to 0 |
| Quarterly volatility | 2.25% | 6.26% |
| Correlation with the S&P 500 | 9.2% | 15.8% |
| Worst quarter (December 2008) | −8.3% | −36.3% |

Which of the following conclusions should the risk manager draw?

options.text: Real estate’s expected return was overstated by about 28 percentage points, so the index mean must be lowered before it enters the optimiser.
Real estate’s Sharpe ratio is lower on unsmoothed data, and an optimiser fed the unsmoothed statistics will allocate less to real estate.
Because the unsmoothed correlation is still below 20%, smoothing biased the volatility estimate but not the correlation estimate.
Because reported volatility is less than a third of equity volatility, real estate is a low-risk diversifier whose allocation can be raised.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Read the table**

Unsmoothing multiplies quarterly volatility by 6.26/2.25 = 2.8, to a level close to equities (7.5%), raises the correlation with the S&P 500 from 9.2% to 15.8%, and turns a −8.3% quarter into −36.3%.

**Step 2 – Effect on the Sharpe ratio**

The mean is unchanged by unsmoothing, so the excess return stays the same while volatility is 2.8 times larger.

⇒ The Sharpe ratio falls to about a third of its reported value.

**Step 3 – Effect on the allocation**

Higher volatility and higher correlation with equities both reduce the optimal mean-variance weight.

⇒ The optimiser allocates less to real estate on unsmoothed data.

**Interpretation**

Reported appraisal data make real estate look like a near-riskless diversifier. The committee should put unsmoothed statistics into the optimiser.

**LO:** IM-17 d: Explain the process of unsmoothing returns and the effects of unsmoothing. • **Reference:** Ang, Asset Management (2014), Ch.13, Unsmoothing (NCREIF example); SchweserNotes 2026 Book 5, Reading 99, LO 99.c and 99.d

**Source:** Written new for the Risk Management and Investment Management P1–P3 workbook (question IM-17 d.5), built from SchweserNotes 2026 Reading 99.

a.reason: The −36.3% is one quarter’s unsmoothed return, not a bias in the mean; the expected return is unchanged by unsmoothing. The 28 points is 36.3−8.3, a gap in one quarter’s return.

c.reason: The correlation rose from 9.2% to 15.8%: smoothing biases correlations downward too.

d.reason: The 2.25% is the smoothed figure. Unsmoothed, real estate volatility (6.26%) is close to that of equities.

questions.subject: Investment Risk
questions.loText: Explain the process of unsmoothing returns and the effects of unsmoothing.
questions.question: A member of the investment committee of a Canadian university endowment is reviewing a consultant’s report that relies on two data sets: an appraisal-based institutional real estate index whose quarterly returns show a first-order autocorrelation of 0.75, and a commercial database of venture capital returns to which reporting is voluntary. Which of the following statements is correct to include in the committee’s response to the consultant?

options.text: Unsmoothing the real estate index with an AR(1) filter will raise its estimated volatility, correlation and beta with equities, but will leave its estimated expected return essentially unchanged.
Survivorship bias in the venture capital database makes reported returns understate true returns, because funds that drop out of the database tend to be those with above-average returns.
Selection bias in the venture capital database, which arises because values are recorded mainly when they are high, is corrected by applying the same Geltner-Ross-Zisler unsmoothing filter.
The downward bias in the real estate index’s volatility is a small-sample problem that will disappear once the consultant uses a suﬀiciently long history of reported quarterly returns.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Read the autocorrelation**

A first-order autocorrelation of 0.75 signals appraisal smoothing. Infrequent trading makes “estimates of risk, volatilities, correlations, and betas” too low; unsmoothing adds noise back to recover the true returns.

**Step 2 – Apply Ang’s first property**

“Unsmoothing affects only risk estimates and not expected returns”, because smoothing spreads shocks over several periods but still counts all of them, so the first and last prices are unchanged.

⇒ A is correct. For NCREIF, volatility rose from 2.25% to 6.26% a quarter and the correlation with the S&P 500 from 9.2% to 15.8%.

**Interpretation**

The committee should ask for unsmoothed risk estimates before the real estate allocation enters a mean-variance optimiser; raw appraisal data make the asset look like a near-riskless diversifier. With $\phi= 0.75$ a pure AR(1) filter would scale the reported volatility by $\sqrt{1.75/0.25} = 2.65$.

**LO:** IM-17 c: Assess the impact of biases on reported returns for illiquid assets. IM-17 d: Explain the process of unsmoothing returns and the effects of unsmoothing. • **Reference:** Ang, Asset Management, Ch.13 (LTR source text Ch.19), 19.4

**Source:** Tier workbook, Tier D, section D9, Illiquid Assets (question D9.1). Printed in the Risk Management and Investment Management P1–P3 workbook as question IM-17 d.6.

b.reason: Polarity flip: survivorship bias “results from the tendency of poorly performing funds to stop reporting”, so reported returns overstate true returns.

c.reason: Sibling swap: unsmoothing corrects infrequent trading. Selection bias is addressed with Heckman (1979) selection models, which let the threshold above which returns are observed vary over time.

d.reason: Scope error: Ang states that the infrequent-observation bias “is not a ‘small sample’ problem, which goes away when our sample becomes very large; it is a ‘population’ problem”.

questions.source: High quality paper IM-8 a Q1
questions.question: A junior risk analyst at a Singapore pension fund is preparing an onboarding slide for newly hired analysts that explains how the fund’s external equity long/short manager builds and manages its portfolio. Which of the following statements is most accurate?

options.text: Because the long and short books are matched to hedge market risk, the manager’s factor exposures beyond beta are removed automatically, so factor models add little.
If two long positions offer the same expected revaluation, the one expected to converge to the manager’s forecast value sooner is the more valuable position.
Holding-period discipline matters most on the long side, since that is where adverse price moves trigger costly margin calls or a forced exit at a large loss.
The manager’s alpha comes mainly from forecasting the direction of the broad equity market, with individual positions chosen chiefly to express that view.

questions.solution:
Junior analyst’s onboarding slide on how an equity long/short manager builds and manages positions.

**Concept and theory**

An equity long/short strategy is built on fundamental company analysis that weighs the risks and opportunities coming from a firm’s industry, geography and the wider macroeconomic environment. The manager buys securities it judges underpriced and sells short related securities it judges overpriced. Two goals sit side by side: exploit mispricings (the alpha) and hedge overall market risk (the short book offsets much of the long book’s beta). When security selection is good, alpha is earned on both sides of the book.

Two further building blocks matter:

- **Investment horizon.** For every position the manager sets the period over which it expects the price to converge to its forecast value. A position that delivers its expected revaluation sooner is worth more, because the same gain is earned over less time and capital is freed for the next idea.
- **Residual factor exposures.** Hedging beta does not remove every common exposure. Managers use advanced factor models to mitigate the factor exposures that remain beyond beta. The GARP Fung and Hsieh chapter adds that long/short equity funds empirically keep some directional market exposure and a long small-cap, short large-cap tilt, which is exactly the kind of residual exposure a factor model is meant to manage.

| Feature | What the source says |
|---|---|
| Return engine | Security selection (alpha) on longs and shorts |
| Market risk | Reduced by the short book, not eliminated |
| Residual factors | Managed with advanced factor models |
| Horizon | Set per position; faster convergence is more valuable |
| Most horizon-sensitive side | Shorts (margin calls, short squeeze) |

**Applying it to this question**

The slide must describe how the manager builds and manages positions. Test each statement against the source: (A) claims residual factor exposures vanish automatically; (B) concerns the horizon and speed of convergence; (C) concerns which side of the book is most sensitive to the holding period; (D) concerns where alpha comes from. Only B matches the source without alteration.

**Fragile fact.** Horizon matters most for the short side; faster convergence makes a position more valuable; factor models handle exposures beyond beta.

**Reference**

LO 90.a: Describe and compare different types of equity-based and macro hedge fund strategies and explain their return and risk profiles. Schweser Reading 90, Module 90.1, “Equity Long/Short Strategy”. GARP text in the project has no matching section for this Stowell and Stowell reading; content from Schweser, a condensed source whose wording may compress the original framing. Supplementary GARP passage (Chapter 9 Hedge Funds, Fung and Hsieh, long/short equity discussion, garp\_rmim.txt lines 14648 to 14687): directional exposure and small-cap tilt; consistent with Schweser, no conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-8 a, where it is Q1 of 13.

a.reason: **Absolute-claim trap.** The source says the primary goal is to reduce market risk, and that managers also use advanced factor models to mitigate remaining factor exposures beyond beta. Matching books does not remove those exposures automatically. The statement would be correct only for a hypothetical book hedged on every factor, which is not what the strategy promises.

b.reason: Schweser states that managers set an investment horizon for each position, the period over which valuation is expected to converge to the forecast, and that “positions that realize their expected revaluation more quickly are considered more valuable.” With identical expected revaluation, the faster-converging long is therefore the more valuable position.

c.reason: **Role misassignment.** The holding period is described as especially important for short positions, because rising prices can trigger costly margin calls or a short squeeze that forces closure at a large loss. Assigning that sensitivity to the long side moves the risk to the wrong actor. It would be correct if the stem asked about the short book.

d.reason: **Sibling swap.** Forecasting the direction of broad markets and expressing it in positions is the global macro engine. Long/short equity earns alpha from security selection while hedging market direction. The statement would fit a global macro manager.

questions.question:
An internal auditor at a Canadian life insurer is reviewing how the administrator of an equity long/short fund classified four items in the fund’s annual return attribution.

| Item | Description | Classified as |
|---|---|---|
| I | Interest earned on the cash proceeds of short sales, net of broker and securities-lender fees | Source of return |
| II | Dividends on the shares the fund has borrowed and sold short | Source of return |
| III | Interest earned on the liquidity buffer posted at the start of the strategy to cover daily mark-to-market adjustments | Cost |
| IV | Fees paid to borrow shares for the short positions | Cost |

Which of the items are classified correctly?

options.text: I, II and IV only
I, III and IV only
IV only
I and IV only

questions.solution:
Auditor checks how four items in a long/short fund’s return attribution were classified.

**Concept and theory**

A long/short fund’s economics are more than its stock-picking alpha, because the short book creates cash flows of its own. When the fund sells borrowed shares, it receives cash. That cash, held with the broker, earns interest, and the fund keeps that interest after the broker’s and securities lender’s fees: this is the **interest rebate**. At the start of the strategy the fund also posts a **liquidity** **buffer** to cover daily mark-to-market adjustments, and that buffer earns interest too.

Against these, the fund bears costs created by borrowing and by leverage: financing charges on margin loans, fees paid to borrow shares, any **dividends owed on borrowed shares** (the short seller must compensate the lender for dividends paid while the shares are on loan), and transaction costs.

| Sources of return | Costs |
|---|---|
| Alpha on long positions | Financing charges on margin loans |
| Alpha on short positions | Fees to borrow shares for shorts |
| Interest rebate (net of broker and lender fees) | Dividends owed on borrowed shares |
| Interest on the liquidity buffer | Transaction costs |

**Applying it to this question**

- I, interest on short proceeds net of fees, classified as a source: **correct** (interest rebate).
- II, dividends on borrowed shares, classified as a source: **incorrect**; the fund owes these to the lender, so they are a cost.
- III, interest on the liquidity buffer, classified as a cost: **incorrect**; it is a source of return.
- IV, fees to borrow shares, classified as a cost: **correct**.

Correctly classified: I and IV only.

**Fragile fact.** Dividends on borrowed shares flow out of the fund; liquidity-buffer interest flows in; the rebate is income after fees.

**Reference**

LO 90.a: Describe and compare different types of equity-based and macro hedge fund strategies and explain their return and risk profiles. Schweser Reading 90, Module 90.1, “Equity Long/Short Strategy” (sources of return and costs); Key Concepts LO 90.a. GARP text in the project has no matching section for this Stowell and Stowell reading; content from Schweser, a condensed source whose wording may compress the original framing.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-8 a, where it is Q2 of 13.

a.reason: **Polarity flip.** Accepting II means treating dividends on the shorted shares as received. The short seller pays them to the lender, so the direction is reversed. Dividends would be a source only for shares the fund owns, for example in a long position.

b.reason: **Sibling swap.** Accepting III treats the liquidity buffer’s interest like its sibling, the financing charge on margin loans. The buffer is cash the fund posts and earns interest on; the margin loan is money the fund borrows and pays interest on. B would be right if item III described margin loan financing.

c.reason: **Scope or condition error.** Rejecting I because the rebate is “net of fees” confuses the condition attached to the item with its sign. The netting reduces the rebate but it remains income. C would be right only if the fees exceeded the interest so the net figure were a charge.

d.reason: Schweser lists the interest rebate “net of broker and securities-lender fees” as a source of return and “fees paid to borrow shares for short positions” as a cost. Items I and IV match; II and III are reversed.

questions.question:
A treasury analyst at a Japanese life insurer that is invested in an equity long/short fund is estimating the fund’s return for the year, before management and performance fees, as a percentage of beginning capital. The long and short books were beta-matched, and the alpha figures already exclude all market and factor contributions.

| Item | JPY million |
|---|---|
| Beginning capital | 10,000 |
| Alpha on long positions | 640 |
| Alpha on short positions | 330 |
| Interest on short-sale cash proceeds, before fees | 150 |
| Broker and securities-lender fees charged against that interest | 35 |
| Interest earned on the liquidity buffer | 55 |
| Financing charges on margin loans | 90 |
| Dividends on borrowed shares | 70 |
| Transaction costs | 45 |
| Broad equity index return for the year | 11.0% |

What is the fund’s return for the year before management and performance fees?
questions.solution:
Treasury analyst computes a JPY long/short fund’s pre-fee annual return from alpha, short-side income and costs.

**Concept and theory**

The return of an equity long/short fund (before management and performance fees) is the sum of its sources of return less its costs, divided by capital. With beta-matched books and alpha stated net of market and factor effects, the market return contributes nothing further.

R $= \frac{\alpha_{\text{L}} + \alpha_{\text{S}} + (\text{I}_{\text{short}} - \text{F}_{\text{lend}}) + \text{I}_{\text{buffer}} - \text{C}_{\text{margin}} - \text{D}_{\text{borrowed}} - \text{C}_{\text{trans}}}{\text{K}}$

where $\alpha_{\text{L}}$, $\alpha_{\text{S}}$ are alpha on long and short positions; $\text{I}_{\text{short}}$ is interest on short-sale proceeds before fees; $\text{F}_{\text{lend}}$ is broker and securities-lender fees (so $\text{I}_{\text{short}} - \text{F}_{\text{lend}}$ is the interest rebate); $\text{I}_{\text{buffer}}$ is interest on the liquidity buffer; $\text{C}_{\text{margin}}$ is margin financing; $\text{D}_{\text{borrowed}}$ is dividends owed on borrowed shares; $\text{C}_{\text{trans}}$ is transaction costs; K is beginning capital.

**Applying it to this question**

All figures in JPY million.

Total alpha = 640 + 330 = 970

Interest rebate = 150 − 35 = 115

Total sources = 970 + 115 + 55 = 1,140

Total costs = 90 + 70 + 45 = 205

Net result = 1,140 − 205 = 935

R = 935/10,000 = 9.35%

The broad index return of 11.0% is irrelevant: the books are beta-matched and alpha already excludes market and factor contributions. The fund earned 9.35% on capital, of which about 9.70 percentage points came from stock selection, with the short-side income and costs netting to a small drag.

**Fragile fact.** The rebate is income net of fees; dividends on borrowed shares are a cost; with beta-matched books the index return is a distractor.

**Reference**

LO 90.a: Describe and compare different types of equity-based and macro hedge fund strategies and explain their return and risk profiles. Schweser Reading 90, Module 90.1, “Equity Long/Short Strategy” (sources of return and costs). GARP text in the project has no matching section for this Stowell and Stowell reading; content from Schweser, a condensed source whose wording may compress the original framing.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-8 a, where it is Q3 of 13.

a.reason: It applies exactly the Schweser classification: alpha on both books, the interest rebate net of broker and lender fees, and buffer interest as sources; margin financing, dividends owed on borrowed shares and transaction costs as costs.

b.reason: Treating dividends on borrowed shares as income instead of a cost: 935 + 2 × 70 = 1,075, giving 10.75%. It would be right only if the fund held those shares long rather than owing their dividends to the lender.

c.reason: Using the gross short-sale interest and dropping the broker and lender fees: 935 + 35 = 970, giving 9.70% (coincidentally equal to the alpha figure). It would be right if the stem gave the interest already net of fees.

d.reason: Stopping at total sources, 1,140, before deducting the 205 of costs. It would be right if the question asked for gross income before costs.

questions.question:
The CRO of an Australian multi-strategy firm is reviewing the equity long/short sleeve, which has fund capital of AUD 800 million and a gross short book of AUD 400 million. The five largest short positions are shown below.

| Position | Size (AUD m) | % of fund capital | Expected holding period (months) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Short 1 | 36 | 4.50 | 9 |
| Short 2 | 30 | 3.75 | 3 |
| Short 3 | 22 | 2.75 | 4 |
| Short 4 | 18 | 2.25 | 2 |
| Short 5 | 14 | 1.75 | 6 |

Which recommendation is most consistent with the management of short-position risk described for equity long/short strategies?

options.text: Extend the expected holding period of each short, since giving an overvaluation more time to correct lowers the position’s exposure to margin calls.
Concentrate the short book in Shorts 1 and 2, since concentrated positions are how hedge funds extract value from their highest-conviction mispricings.
Cap each short at about 2% to 3% of fund capital, which requires cutting Short 1 to no more than about AUD 24 million and also cutting Short 2.
Cap each short at about 2% to 3% of the gross short book, which requires cutting Short 1 to no more than about AUD 12 million.

questions.solution:
CRO reviews an AUD long/short sleeve’s largest short positions and picks the right risk control.

**Concept and theory**

Short positions carry a distinctive risk shape. A long position’s worst case is a fall to zero; a short position loses as prices rise, and rising prices bring margin calls, and in crowded names a **short** **squeeze** that forces the position to be closed at a substantial loss. For this reason the source stresses that the holding period is especially important for shorts: the longer a short is held while waiting for the overvaluation to correct, the longer it is exposed to these events.

The defence the source describes is diversification of the short book: firms spread their shorts so that **no single short accounts for more than 2% to 3% of the fund’s capital**. The base is fund capital, the measure of what the fund can lose before its own survival is threatened, not the size of the short book.

**Applying it to this question**

Limit at 3% of fund capital: 0.03 × 800 = 24 (AUD million); at 2%: 0.02 × 800 = 16.

- Short 1: 36, 4.50% of capital: above the band; cut to at most about 24.
- Short 2: 30, 3.75%: above the band; cut.
- Short 3: 22, 2.75%: inside the band.
- Shorts 4 and 5: 2.25% and 1.75%: at or below the band.

The expected holding periods are context only; they do not change the size limit.

**Fragile fact.** Base = fund capital; band = 2% to 3% per short; longer holding period means more squeeze and margin-call exposure.

**Reference**

LO 90.a: Describe and compare different types of equity-based and macro hedge fund strategies and explain their return and risk profiles. Schweser Reading 90, Module 90.1, “Equity Long/Short Strategy”. GARP text in the project has no matching section for this Stowell and Stowell reading; content from Schweser, a condensed source whose wording may compress the original framing.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-8 a, where it is Q4 of 13.

a.reason: **Polarity flip.** A longer holding period raises, not lowers, exposure to margin calls and squeezes, because the position stays open longer while prices may rise. A would be correct only if the risk being managed were the chance that the mispricing has not yet corrected, ignoring financing and squeeze risk.

b.reason: **Sibling swap.** Concentration on individual names is a feature the source attributes to the nonhedged (long-only) hedge fund approach. On the short side the prescription is the opposite: diversify. B would describe a nonhedged equity manager’s long book.

c.reason: Schweser states that firms diversify the securities they short so that no single short position accounts for more than 2% to 3% of the fund’s capital. Applying 3% of AUD 800 million gives AUD 24 million, so Short 1 must fall to about AUD 24 million and Short 2 must also be reduced.

d.reason: **Wrong input twin.** The percentage band is right but applied to the wrong base: 0.03 × 400 = 12. The source ties the limit to fund capital. D would be correct if the policy were defined on gross short book value.

questions.question: A risk consultant is presenting to the investment committee of a London family office that is considering a GBP 150 million allocation to a dedicated short (short-biased) hedge fund. Which of the following statements in the consultant’s presentation is least accurate?

options.text: The opportunity set exists partly because mutual funds concentrate on positive-alpha stocks and tend to underweight, rather than short, stocks with negative alpha.
The manager’s edge typically lies in spotting signs of overvaluation such as aggressive accounting, potential legal issues and management efforts to obscure bad news.
Positions may have to be closed through margin calls, short squeezes or risk-limit driven covering even when the manager’s view on valuation is unchanged.
Because equity prices tend to drift lower over long periods, a short-biased fund without specialised insight should still expect a modest positive return.

questions.solution:
Consultant’s presentation on a GBP allocation to a dedicated short fund; find the least accurate statement.

**Concept and theory**

A dedicated short (short-biased) strategy specialises in identifying overpriced securities and selling them short. Why does such a niche exist? Mutual funds are built to find positive-alpha stocks. They typically do not short; at most they underweight stocks with negative alpha. Overvalued securities therefore receive little attention, which leaves room for specialists who develop expertise in reading the signs of overvaluation: aggressive accounting, potential legal issues, and management attempts to obscure negative information. The GARP Fung and Hsieh chapter adds that detailed company research is the core alpha driver and that a focus on firms with weak cash flow generation is common; such funds take more short positions than long ones and so hold net short exposure.

The risk profile is harsh. Positions can be forced shut by margin calls, short squeezes and forced covering driven by risk-management constraints, regardless of whether the valuation thesis is still right. And there is a structural headwind: **market prices tend to rise over time**, so short positions carry a bias toward negative returns. Without specialised insight, a short seller is likely to lose money while taking significant risk. GARP’s regression of the dedicated short bias index on the S&P index gives a slope of −0.81, confirming strong negative correlation with equities.

**Applying it to this question**

The qualifier is least accurate, so three statements match the source and one corrupts it. A (mutual funds underweight rather than short), B (accounting, legal and disclosure red flags) and C (margin calls, squeezes, risk-limit covering) each restate the source. D states the direction of the long-run market drift backwards and draws the wrong conclusion from it.

**Fragile fact.** Markets drift up, so shorts face a negative return bias; mutual funds underweight, they do not short.

**Reference**

LO 90.a: Describe and compare different types of equity-based and macro hedge fund strategies and explain their return and risk profiles. Schweser Reading 90, Module 90.1, “Dedicated Short (Short-Biased) Strategy”. GARP text in the project has no matching section for this Stowell and Stowell reading; content from Schweser, a condensed source whose wording may compress the original framing. Supplementary GARP passage (Chapter 9, “Niche Strategies: Dedicated Short Bias, Emerging Market and Equity Market Neutral”, lines 14692 to 14755): GARP describes funds as net short with some longs, Schweser simply as selling overvalued securities short; a difference of emphasis, not a conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-8 a, where it is Q5 of 13.

a.reason: **Accurate.** This is the source’s explanation of the opportunity: mutual funds focus on positive alpha, typically do not short, and may underweight negative-alpha stocks, so overvalued names are under-researched. A candidate who picks A as the false statement has usually misassigned the role, believing mutual funds actively short negative-alpha stocks.

b.reason: **Accurate.** The source lists aggressive accounting, potential legal issues and attempts to obscure negative information as the signs specialists learn to detect. Choosing it would mean mistaking the strategy for a top-down one.

c.reason: **Accurate.** Margin calls, short squeezes and forced covering driven by risk-management constraints are exactly the significant risks named. The point that these can force exits whatever the thesis is the essence of the risk. Choosing C would come from thinking forced covering happens only when the manager changes view, a scope error.

d.reason: Schweser: market prices tend to rise over time, creating an inherent headwind and a bias toward negative returns on short positions, so without specialised expertise a short-selling fund is likely to lose money. D claims a downward drift and an expected positive return without skill, the reverse on both counts.

questions.question:
A senior risk analyst at a Brazilian pension fund is reviewing two dedicated short managers over a year in which the broad Brazilian equity index rose 18%.

| Manager | Return (%) | Short book (% of capital) | Assets (BRL m) |
|---|---|---|---|
| X | −11 | 95 | 420 |
| Y | 4 | 90 | 310 |

Which interpretation is most consistent with the return and risk profile of a dedicated short strategy?

options.text: Y’s gain shows the strategy carries a natural positive drift, so earning it required no particular skill in identifying overvalued firms.
X’s loss is consistent with the headwind rising prices create for short sellers, while Y’s gain against that headwind is more consistent with specialist skill.
X’s loss shows it was run incorrectly, because a well-run dedicated short fund should earn returns that broadly track a rising equity market.
Y’s gain shows its main risk has passed, because margin calls and short squeezes are triggered mainly when share prices are falling.

questions.solution:
Interpreting two BRL dedicated short managers’ returns in a year when the market rose 18%.

**Concept and theory**

To read a dedicated short manager’s track record, first ask what the strategy should do with no skill at all. Because market prices tend to rise over time, a book of short positions has a structural headwind: absent insight, it is biased toward negative returns, and the source says such a fund is likely to lose money while bearing significant risk. Rising prices are also the trigger for the strategy’s main risks: margin calls, short squeezes and forced covering. GARP’s data reinforce the shape: the dedicated short bias index has a slope of −0.81 on the S&P index, so in a strong rally the strategy is expected to lose.

The skill that can overcome the headwind is the specialist’s ability to find genuinely overvalued firms, through signs such as aggressive accounting, legal issues and obscured negative information.

| Market condition | Expected effect on a dedicated short book |
|---|---|
| Rising prices | Losses on shorts; margin calls, squeezes, forced covering |
| Long-run drift (up) | Headwind; bias to negative returns without skill |
| Skilled stock selection | Shorts in overvalued firms can fall even as the market rises |

**Applying it to this question**

The market rose 18%. Manager X lost 11%, which is what the headwind predicts for a book that is about 95% short. Manager Y gained 4% while about 90% short in the same rally: its shorts must have fallen or risen far less than the market, which is more consistent with skill in identifying overvalued firms. Assets under management and the exact short percentages are not decisive.

**Fragile fact.** For shorts, the danger direction is up: rising prices cause losses, margin calls and squeezes.

**Reference**

LO 90.a: Describe and compare different types of equity-based and macro hedge fund strategies and explain their return and risk profiles. Schweser Reading 90, Module 90.1, “Dedicated Short (Short-Biased) Strategy”. GARP text in the project has no matching section for this Stowell and Stowell reading; content from Schweser, a condensed source whose wording may compress the original framing. Supplementary GARP passage (Chapter 9, “Niche Strategies”, lines 14751 to 14755): negative correlation with equities; consistent with Schweser.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-8 a, where it is Q6 of 13.

a.reason: **Polarity flip.** The natural drift of a short book is negative because markets tend to rise. A gain earned against an 18% rally is the opposite of “no skill required”. A would be correct only in a world where prices drift down over time.

b.reason: It applies both source facts: rising prices create a headwind for short sellers (explaining X), and only specialised expertise lets a short seller avoid losing money in such conditions (explaining Y).

c.reason: **Sibling swap.** Tracking a rising market is the profile of a nonhedged, long-only equity fund with full market exposure. A dedicated short fund is expected to suffer in a rally; X’s loss is not, by itself, evidence of poor management. C would describe a nonhedged equity manager.

d.reason: **Polarity flip.** Margin calls and short squeezes are triggered by rising prices, not falling ones. In a year of rising prices Y’s main risk was fully live. D would be correct for a leveraged long book, where falling prices trigger margin calls.

questions.question:
A portfolio manager at a Frankfurt hedge fund running a nonhedged equity strategy believes a mid-cap industrial stock trading at EUR 50.00 is modestly undervalued and will rise about 12% over six months. She implements a bull call spread using the EUR 50 and EUR 56 strike six-month calls. Each call pays max$(\text{S}_{\text{T}} -$ K, 0) at expiry; ignore financing costs and fees.

| Strike (EUR) | Call premium (EUR) |
|---|---|
| 50 | 3.20 |
| 56 | 0.90 |
| 60 | 0.40 |

If the stock ends at exactly EUR 56.00 at expiry, what is the return on the net premium paid for the spread?
questions.solution:
EUR nonhedged equity manager uses a 50/56 bull call spread; return on net premium if the stock ends at EUR 56.

**Concept and theory**

A nonhedged equity strategy is long only and based on fundamental analysis of individual firms or industries. Unlike a mutual fund, which may find a small expected gain not worth detailed analysis, a hedge fund can concentrate on one stock, assess its upside and downside, and use leverage to amplify even a small mispricing. One tool the source names is the **bull call spread**: buy a call with a lower strike and sell a call with a higher strike. The sold call cheapens the position by giving up gains above the higher strike, which costs little if the expected rise is modest (the source cites 10% to 15%). The payoff at expiry, for strikes $\text{K}_{1} < \text{K}_{2}$ with premiums $\text{c}_{1} \text{and c}_{2}$:

Payoff $= \text{max}(\text{S}_{\text{T}} - \text{K}_{1}$, 0$) - \text{max}(\text{S}_{\text{T}} - \text{K}_{2}$, 0), Net premium $= \text{c}_{1} - \text{c}_{2}$

Return on net premium $= \frac{\text{Payoff} - (\text{c}_{1} - \text{c}_{2})}{\text{c}_{1} - \text{c}_{2}}$

**Applying it to this question**

$\text{K}_{1} =$ 50, $\text{K}_{2} =$ 56, $\text{c}_{1} =$ 3.20, $\text{c}_{2} =$ 0.90, $\text{S}_{\text{T}} =$ 56.

Net premium = 3.20 − 0.90 = 2.30

Long 50 call payoff $= \text{max}($56 − 50, 0) = 6.00

Short 56 call payoff $= - \text{max}($56 − 56, 0) = 0.00

Spread payoff = 6.00

Profit = 6.00 − 2.30 = 3.70

Return on net premium = 3.70/2.30 = 160.9%

A 12% rise in the stock becomes a 160.9% return on the capital at risk in the spread: the leverage that lets a hedge fund profit from a modest mispricing. The EUR 60 call is irrelevant, as the spread uses the 50 and 56 strikes.

**Fragile fact.** Bull call spread = buy low strike, sell high strike; return is on the net premium after subtracting it.

**Reference**

LO 90.a: Describe and compare different types of equity-based and macro hedge fund strategies and explain their return and risk profiles. Schweser Reading 90, Module 90.1, “Nonhedged Equity Strategy”. GARP text in the project has no matching section for this Stowell and Stowell reading; content from Schweser, a condensed source whose wording may compress the original framing. The call payoff function is stated in the stem; no outside-source content is needed.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-8 a, where it is Q7 of 13.

a.reason: It uses the source’s leg structure (buy the lower strike, sell the higher strike) and deducts the net premium paid before dividing by it.

b.reason: Dividing the payoff by the net premium without subtracting the cost: 6.00/2.30 = 260.9%. This is payoff per unit of premium, not return. It would be the answer if the question asked for the payoff multiple of the premium.

c.reason: −160.9% **(sign error).** Reversing the legs (sell the 50 call, buy the 56 call) receives a net credit of 2.30 and loses 6.00 at $\text{S}_{\text{T}} =$ 56: (2.30 − 6.00)/2.30 = −160.9%. That is a bear call spread; it would be correct only for a manager expecting the stock to fall.

d.reason: Using only the long 50 call: (6.00 − 3.20)/3.20 = 87.5%. It ignores the premium received on the written 56 call. It would be correct for an outright long call rather than a spread.

questions.question: A member of the board risk committee of a Singapore general insurer asks the investment team to explain how a nonhedged equity hedge fund differs from the long-only equity mutual funds the insurer already holds. Which of the following statements best describes the difference?

options.text: The nonhedged fund offsets its market exposure with short positions in related securities, whereas the mutual fund keeps full market exposure.
The nonhedged fund relies mainly on broad diversification to manage risk, whereas the mutual fund concentrates on a few high-conviction stocks.
The nonhedged fund can concentrate on individual stocks, weigh both upside and downside, and use leverage to make even a small mispricing worth pursuing.
The nonhedged fund’s use of leverage and options ensures that it outperforms a mutual fund holding the same stocks over any holding period.

questions.solution:
Board member asks how a nonhedged equity hedge fund differs from a long-only mutual fund.

**Concept and theory**

Both a nonhedged equity hedge fund and a traditional equity mutual fund are long only and rely on fundamental stock picking. The difference lies in what each is built to do with that analysis.

| Dimension | Mutual fund | Nonhedged equity hedge fund |
|---|---|---|
| Emphasis | Expected returns | Upside and downside of each stock |
| Risk management | Portfolio diversification | Concentrated, researched positions |
| Small mispricings | May not justify detailed analysis | Worth pursuing, amplified with leverage |
| Tools | Long stock | Long stock, leverage, derivatives (e.g., bull call spread) |
| Market exposure | Full | Full (no hedge) |

Because the hedge fund does not short, it retains full market exposure, which separates it from long/short equity.

**Applying it to this question**

The board member wants the distinguishing feature. The answer must keep both funds long only and fully exposed to the market, place diversification with the mutual fund and concentration and leverage with the hedge fund, and avoid any guarantee.

**Fragile fact.** Nonhedged = long only with full market exposure; diversification belongs to the mutual fund, concentration and leverage to the hedge fund.

**Reference**

LO 90.a: Describe and compare different types of equity-based and macro hedge fund strategies and explain their return and risk profiles. Schweser Reading 90, Module 90.1, “Nonhedged Equity Strategy”; Key Concepts LO 90.a. GARP text in the project has no matching section for this Stowell and Stowell reading; content from Schweser, a condensed source whose wording may compress the original framing.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-8 a, where it is Q8 of 13.

a.reason: **Sibling swap.** Offsetting market exposure with shorts in related securities is the equity long/short strategy. The nonhedged fund is long only and retains full market exposure. A would be right for a long/short equity fund.

b.reason: **Role misassignment.** The attributes are reversed between the actors: the mutual fund relies on diversification; the hedge fund concentrates. B would be right with the two fund types swapped.

c.reason: Schweser: hedge funds can concentrate on individual stocks and evaluate both upside and downside potential, and because they often use significant leverage they can amplify even small mispricings whose expected return may be too small to justify a mutual fund’s detailed analysis.

d.reason: **Absolute-claim trap.** Leverage amplifies small mispricings in both directions; nothing guarantees outperformance over any period. D would need “can enhance” in place of “ensures”.

questions.question: An investment consultant at a Shanghai insurer is drafting a due diligence report, in CNY terms, on a global macro hedge fund and must choose one statement about the strategy to include. Which of the following statements is most accurate?

options.text: Like a mutual fund, the fund is confined to its mandated investment area, but within that area it may apply leverage and derivatives freely.
The manager may switch capital from long equity index futures in one region to currency and interest rate positions elsewhere after reassessing capital flows and policy.
The fund tends to favour less liquid instruments, because illiquidity premia are what compensate it for taking such large leveraged positions.
The fund’s returns come mainly from bottom-up research into individual firms, such as detecting aggressive accounting and hidden legal problems.

questions.solution:
Consultant chooses an accurate statement about a global macro fund for a CNY due diligence report.

**Concept and theory**

A global macro fund makes large, leveraged bets on anticipated price movements across broad equity and fixed-income markets, interest rates, foreign exchange and commodities, often through options, swaps and futures on a wide range of underlying asset classes and indices. Its defining freedom is **broad discretion**: unlike mutual funds restricted to their mandated areas, global macro managers can allocate across sectors, regions and asset classes. The inputs are top-down: economic forecasts, international capital flows, interest rate trends, political developments, relations between countries and governments, and economic policies. The source adds that these funds tend to trade **more liquid** instruments, which suits large positions that must be resized as views change.

GARP’s Fung and Hsieh chapter describes global macro managers as highly dynamic traders taking leveraged directional bets on exchange rates, interest rates, commodities and stock indices, and as “a highly active asset allocator betting on a range of risk factors over time”; its due diligence chapter notes they carry more inflation, rate and currency exposure than most single-strategy funds.

**Applying it to this question**

The statement must capture discretion across asset classes, top-down inputs and liquid derivative instruments. B shows a cross-region, cross-asset reallocation (equity index futures to currency and rate positions) triggered by capital flows and policy, both named inputs.

**Fragile fact.** Global macro trades more liquid instruments and has broad discretion; mutual funds are the ones bound by mandates.

**Reference**

LO 90.a: Describe and compare different types of equity-based and macro hedge fund strategies and explain their return and risk profiles. Schweser Reading 90, Module 90.1, “Global Macro Strategy”. GARP text in the project has no matching section for this Stowell and Stowell reading; content from Schweser, a condensed source whose wording may compress the original framing. Supplementary GARP passages: Chapter 9 Hedge Funds, Global Macro discussion (lines 14197 to 14298) and Chapter 10, “Risk Management Process” (lines 16455 to 16462); consistent with Schweser. GARP adds that approaches may be systematic trend-following or discretionary; Schweser does not cover this, so it is not tested.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-8 a, where it is Q9 of 13.

a.reason: **Scope or condition error.** The confinement to a mandated area is what the source says distinguishes mutual funds from global macro funds. A would be right for a mutual fund, or for a single-asset-class hedge fund.

b.reason: It reflects three source facts: global macro funds can allocate capital across regions and asset classes, they use derivatives on broad indices, and capital flows and economic policies are among the factors they consider.

c.reason: **Polarity flip.** The source says global macro funds tend to trade in more liquid instruments. C would be right if “less” were “more” and the rationale changed to the need to resize large positions.

d.reason: **Sibling swap.** Bottom-up research into accounting red flags and legal problems is the dedicated short specialist’s skill. D would describe a dedicated short manager.

questions.question:
The CRO of a US university endowment is comparing a global macro fund with an emerging markets fund before a USD 75 million allocation and has written four statements.

I. Both strategies may take positions in fixed-income instruments.

II. The global macro manager has broad discretion across regions and asset classes, whereas the emerging markets manager’s universe is the securities of developing countries.

III. The emerging markets manager needs deep insight into the specific markets it invests in, in addition to fundamental valuation skill.

IV. Global macro funds tend to trade less liquid instruments than emerging markets funds, so liquidity constraints are a smaller concern for emerging markets funds.

Which of the statements are correct?

options.text: I, II, III and IV
II and III only
I and III only
I, II and III only

questions.solution:
CRO compares global macro and emerging markets strategies before a USD allocation; which statements are correct?

**Concept and theory**

Both strategies are grouped under macro strategies, but they differ in reach and in risk.

| Dimension | Global macro | Emerging markets |
|---|---|---|
| Universe | Equity and fixed-income markets, rates, FX, commodities, globally | Corporate securities and sovereign debt of developing countries |
| Discretion | Broad: any sector, region or asset class | Bounded by the developing-country universe |
| Edge | Anticipating international macro trends | Fundamental valuation plus deep local insight |
| Instruments | Often derivatives; tend to be more liquid | Local securities; liquidity constraints |
| Risk and return | Large, leveraged, directional bets | Higher returns with heightened political, liquidity and local economic risks |

**Applying it to this question**

- I: global macro trades fixed-income markets; emerging markets funds hold sovereign debt and corporate securities. **Correct.**
- II: broad discretion for global macro versus a developing-country universe. **Correct.**
- III: the source requires both fundamental valuation skill and deep insight into the specific markets. **Correct.**
- IV: global macro funds tend to trade more liquid instruments, and liquidity constraints are a named emerging markets risk. **Incorrect.**

**Fragile fact.** Liquidity runs in favour of global macro and against emerging markets.

**Reference**

LO 90.a: Describe and compare different types of equity-based and macro hedge fund strategies and explain their return and risk profiles. Schweser Reading 90, Module 90.1, “Global Macro Strategy” and “Emerging Markets Strategy”; Key Concepts LO 90.a. GARP text in the project has no matching section for this Stowell and Stowell reading; content from Schweser, a condensed source whose wording may compress the original framing.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-8 a, where it is Q10 of 13.

a.reason: **Polarity flip.** Accepting IV reverses which strategy trades more liquid instruments. A would be correct only if global macro funds favoured illiquid instruments and emerging markets funds faced no liquidity constraints.

b.reason: **Scope or condition error.** Rejecting I under-reads one universe, for example assuming emerging markets funds hold only equities or that global macro avoids bonds. Both strategies explicitly include fixed income. B would be right if one strategy were restricted to equities.

c.reason: **Scope or condition error.** Rejecting II imposes a mutual-fund style mandate on global macro. Broad discretion is its defining feature. C would be right only if global macro were mandate-bound.

d.reason: I, II and III each restate the Schweser descriptions of the two strategies; IV reverses the liquidity comparison, so the correct set is I, II and III only.
