questions.question:
An investment committee member at a U.S. charitable foundation that is exempt from income tax is reviewing a proposed allocation to an onshore credit hedge fund that finances part of its portfolio with direct borrowing. The committee pack shows:

| Item | Value |
|---|---|
| Proposed allocation | USD 40 million |
| Fund borrowing relative to fund equity | 1.8x |
| Management fee | 1.5% |
| Lock-up period | 12 months |

Which of the following statements best describes the portfolio-level tax risk the foundation faces and how it could be mitigated?

options.text: UBTI risk: debt-financed income from the fund may become taxable for the otherwise tax-exempt foundation, and investing through an offshore hedge fund can help mitigate it.
UBTI risk: debt-financed income from the fund may become taxable for the otherwise tax-exempt foundation, and investing through an onshore rather than an offshore hedge fund can help mitigate it.
UBTI risk: debt-financed income from the fund may become taxable, but only for investors that are already taxable, so the foundation’s tax-exempt status removes the concern.
UBTI risk: all income the fund earns, whether or not it is debt financed, may become taxable for the foundation, so no choice of fund vehicle can mitigate it.

questions.solution:
A tax-exempt U.S. foundation considers an onshore credit fund that borrows; which statement best describes the portfolio-level tax risk and its mitigation?

**Concept and theory**

UBTI, unrelated business taxable income, is the one tax-based item on the portfolio-level list. The idea: an investor such as a charitable foundation or pension plan is normally exempt from tax on its investment income. When a hedge fund uses borrowed money to generate income, that debt-financed income can become taxable for the investor even though the investor is otherwise tax exempt. Schweser’s statement has three parts, each a separate testable condition:

| Element | Schweser statement |
|---|---|
| Trigger | Debt-financed income |
| Who is affected | Investors who are otherwise tax exempt |
| Mitigation | Investing through an offshore hedge fund |

It is a portfolio-level risk because it arises from the interaction of the investor’s tax status with the fund’s financing, not from the manager’s skill or conduct.

**Applying it to this question**

The foundation is tax exempt (the affected investor type). The fund finances part of its portfolio with direct borrowing (the trigger: debt-financed income). The fund is onshore, so the stated mitigation, an offshore fund, is not yet being used. The allocation size, the 1.5% fee, the 12-month lock-up, and even the exact 1.8x borrowing ratio are not needed to identify the risk; the only fact that matters from the table is that borrowing exists.

**Fragile fact.** Actor and direction: UBTI hurts tax-exempt investors, it is triggered by debt-financed income, and the mitigant is offshore, not onshore.

**Reference**

LO 91.a: Describe different risks faced by investors in hedge funds. Schweser, Book 5, Reading 91, Module 91.1, “Risks in Hedge Fund Investing”, paragraph 1 (UBTI sentence). GARP text in the project has no matching section (the project’s GARP book has no chapter for this reading); content from Schweser, a condensed source whose wording may compress GARP’s framing. Boundary: the offshore feeder in a master-feeder structure belongs to LO 91.d and was not tested.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-9 a, where it is Q2 of 14.

a.reason: A reproduces all three elements: debt-financed income, an otherwise tax-exempt investor, and offshore investing as the mitigant. This is Schweser’s sentence: “UBTI can arise when debt-financed income becomes taxable for investors who are otherwise tax exempt; investing through an offshore hedge fund can help mitigate this risk.”

b.reason: **Polarity flip on the mitigant.** It reverses offshore to onshore. The foundation’s proposed fund is already onshore, and onshore is where the exposure sits. B would be correct only for a stem in which the source said onshore vehicles shield tax-exempt investors, which it does not.

c.reason: **Role misassignment.** It attributes the risk to investors that are already taxable. Schweser says UBTI arises for investors who are otherwise tax exempt; C reverses the actor and so concludes that the very investor at risk is safe. C would be correct if the question asked who is not the target of UBTI concern.

d.reason: **Scope error plus absolute claim.** It drops the “debt-financed” condition (all income becomes taxable) and then claims no vehicle can help. Both overreach: only debt-financed income is caught, and the source names offshore investing as a mitigant. D would be correct if the source said UBTI applied to all fund income and listed no mitigant.

questions.question:
A risk consultant at a Singapore family office is reviewing a hedge fund peer index that the office uses to set return expectations for a SGD 150 million allocation. The index provider’s methodology note states:

- The index is built only from funds that currently report to the provider’s database.
- Funds that were terminated after poor results are removed from the index history.
- The index covers 12 strategies and is licensed to the family office free of charge.

Which of the following best describes the risk embedded in this index data, together with its category in the portfolio-level versus investment-level classification of hedge fund risks?

options.text: Style drift, an investment-level risk, because the index membership drifts away from its original composition over time.
Survivorship bias, an investment-level risk, because the bias arises from how each fund in the index is managed.
Strategy failure, a portfolio-level risk, because the removed funds were terminated after their strategies failed.
Survivorship bias, a portfolio-level risk, because poorly performing funds that were terminated are no longer observed in the data.

questions.solution:
A Singapore family office’s peer index drops terminated poor performers; which risk is embedded and how is it classified?

**Concept and theory**

Survivorship bias is a portfolio-level risk in Schweser’s framework. GARP’s hedge fund chapter explains the mechanism: commercial hedge fund databases depend on managers choosing to report, and “poor performing funds that have been terminated cannot be readily observed.” If the losers vanish from the record, any average, index, or benchmark built from the surviving funds looks better than the experience of investors who actually held the full set of funds. GARP adds that funds in difficulty often stop reporting, so a database “may only capture part of the downward spiral of a dying fund.” Because the problem lives in the data an investor uses to set expectations and judge managers across the whole allocation, it is classed at the portfolio level, alongside benchmarking issues and UBTI.

**Applying it to this question**

The methodology note contains two decisive facts: only currently reporting funds are included, and terminated poor performers are removed from history. Together these describe the defining feature of survivorship bias. The 12 strategies and the free license are irrelevant inputs. The classification step then asks which level it sits at: Schweser lists survivorship bias as portfolio-level.

**Fragile fact.** Survivorship bias is portfolio-level; the bias makes observed hedge fund performance look better, because the terminated poor performers drop out.

**Reference**

LO 91.a: Describe different risks faced by investors in hedge funds. Schweser, Book 5, Reading 91, Module 91.1, “Risks in Hedge Fund Investing”, paragraph 1. GARP depth: GARP Chapter 9 “Hedge Funds”, Section 9.2 “Empirical Evidence of Hedge Fund Performance”, footnotes 19 and 20 (project text lines 12974 to 12985). That chapter is the older Fung and Hsieh reading, not a dedicated chapter for this LO; it is used only to explain the mechanism. No conflict with Schweser.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-9 a, where it is Q3 of 14.

a.reason: **Sibling swap.** Style drift is an investment-level risk about a single fund departing from its stated strategy; it is not about which funds an index contains. The word “drift” is a lexical lure. A would be correct if the note said that index constituents had moved away from the strategies under which they were classified.

b.reason: **Level misassignment.** It names the right risk but places it at the investment level, with a reason (how each fund is managed) that describes investment-level risks generally. B would be correct only if Schweser listed survivorship bias among investment-level risks, which it does not.

c.reason: **Sibling swap plus level error.** The removed funds may well have suffered strategy failure, but the risk embedded in the index data is their omission, not their failure; and strategy failure is investment-level, not portfolio-level. C would describe the risk faced by an investor who had actually held one of the terminated funds, if it were also labeled investment-level.

d.reason: D names the right risk, places it at the right level, and gives GARP’s mechanism (terminated poor performers are no longer observed). Schweser: “Portfolio-level risks include benchmarking issues, survivorship bias, and unrelated business taxable income.”

questions.question:
An internal auditor at a Japanese life insurer is reviewing the due diligence file on a JPY 30 billion multi-strategy hedge fund held in the insurer’s alternatives portfolio. The file records four findings:

| Finding | Description |
|---|---|
| 1 | The founder makes every allocation decision, and the fund has no designated successor. |
| 2 | Marketed as a merger arbitrage fund, it now runs a large directional currency book. |
| 3 | All of the fund’s OTC derivatives are traded with a single dealer. |
| 4 | In a market-wide sell-off, the fund’s three sleeves, which historically showed near-zero correlation, all lost money together. |

Which of the following mappings of the findings to investment-level risks is most accurate?

options.text: 1: key person risk; 2: style drift; 3: counterparty risk; 4: strategy failure
1: key person risk; 2: style drift; 3: counterparty risk; 4: correlation spikes
1: key person risk; 2: style drift; 3: correlation spikes; 4: counterparty risk
1: conflicts of interest; 2: style drift; 3: counterparty risk; 4: correlation spikes

questions.solution:
An auditor at a Japanese insurer maps four due diligence findings on a multi-strategy fund to investment-level risks.

**Concept and theory**

Investment-level risks are the ways a particular fund can disappoint because of how it is run and how it behaves. Schweser lists seven: counterparty risk, conflicts of interest, key person risk (“key person dependence” in the Key Concepts), strategy failure, style drift, regulatory changes, and correlation spikes (“during periods of market stress”). Each attaches to a different object:

| Risk | What it attaches to |
|---|---|
| Key person risk | Dependence on one individual |
| Style drift | Departure from the stated strategy (the strategy shifts that Schweser’s transparency section says investors worry about) |
| Counterparty risk | The firms the fund trades with |
| Correlation spikes | Normally independent positions moving together in stress |
| Strategy failure | The stated strategy itself not working |
| Conflicts of interest | Manager interests diverging from investors’ |

**Applying it to this question**

Finding 1: one founder makes every decision with no successor, which is dependence on a key person. Finding 2: a merger arbitrage fund running a directional currency book has shifted away from its stated strategy, which is style drift (all four options agree, so it is not the discriminator). Finding 3: all OTC derivatives with one dealer is concentration of counterparty exposure. Finding 4: sleeves with near-zero historical correlation losing together in a market-wide sell-off is the defining picture of a correlation spike in stress. The fund size in yen is irrelevant.

**Fragile fact.** Correlation spikes are an investment-level risk tied to periods of market stress; counterparty risk is about whom the fund trades with. Do not let “market-wide” push you to the portfolio level.

**Reference**

LO 91.a: Describe different risks faced by investors in hedge funds. Schweser, Book 5, Reading 91, Module 91.1, “Risks in Hedge Fund Investing”, paragraph 2, and Key Concepts LO 91.a. Figure 91.1 is not reproduced in the project text, so descriptions are drawn from the risk names and the Key Concepts wording. GARP has no matching chapter; GARP Chapter 10 (due diligence) mentions counterparty risk on OTC derivatives and style drift only in passing (project text lines 16612 and 16646). Content basis is Schweser, a condensed source.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-9 a, where it is Q4 of 14.

a.reason: It calls finding 4 strategy failure. The fact pattern stresses that historically uncorrelated sleeves fell together in a market-wide stress, which is about co-movement, not about one strategy not working. A would be correct if finding 4 said the merger arbitrage sleeve lost money because deal spreads never converged while markets were calm.

b.reason: B maps each finding to the risk whose defining object it describes: key person, style drift, counterparty, correlation spikes. All four are on Schweser’s investment-level list.

c.reason: It reverses the two labels. A single dealer is a counterparty concentration, not a correlation event; simultaneous losses across sleeves are a correlation event, not a counterparty problem. C would be correct only if finding 3 described sleeves moving together and finding 4 described a dealer default.

d.reason: It labels founder dependence as conflicts of interest. A conflict concerns the manager’s interests diverging from investors’; dependence on one person with no successor is key person risk. D would be correct if finding 1 described the founder’s personal interests diverging from those of the fund’s investors.

questions.question:
The chief compliance officer of a Brazilian pension fund is preparing a board report on its BRL 500 million hedge fund program. The report must classify four concerns into the five incremental risks that are particularly pronounced in hedge funds:

I. The manager’s 20% performance fee rewards gains and may push the manager to take more risk than the pension fund would choose.

II. The manager will not disclose positions because rivals would crowd the trade, so the pension fund cannot check strategy alignment.

III. The fund’s largest short position rose sharply as other short sellers rushed to buy shares to close their positions.

IV. The manager operates with significantly less regulatory oversight than the open-end mutual funds the pension fund also uses.

Which classification is most accurate?

options.text: I: risk tolerance; II: transparency; III: short selling; IV: regulation
I: leverage; II: transparency; III: short selling; IV: regulation
I: risk tolerance; II: regulation; III: short selling; IV: transparency
I: risk tolerance; II: transparency; III: leverage; IV: regulation

questions.solution:
A Brazilian pension fund CCO classifies four concerns into the five incremental hedge fund risks.

**Concept and theory**

The second Schweser framework names five incremental risks that are particularly pronounced in hedge funds compared with open-end mutual funds:

| Risk | Core idea in Schweser |
|---|---|
| Leverage | On- or off-balance-sheet; amplifies gains and losses; raises sensitivity to liquidity shocks |
| Regulation | Significantly less oversight than open-end mutual funds; investors must do their own due diligence |
| Short selling | Theoretically unlimited downside; short squeezes |
| Transparency | Secrecy to avoid crowded trades; hard to monitor risk and strategy alignment |
| Risk tolerance | Higher than mutual fund managers; compensation incentivizes more risk; derivatives complexity |

Each concern should be mapped by its cause, not by the tool the manager might use.

**Applying it to this question**

I: the performance fee motivates extra risk taking, which is the risk tolerance item (“compensation structures often incentivize them to take on additional risk”). II: refusal to disclose because rivals would crowd the trade, leaving the investor unable to check strategy alignment, is transparency. III: a heavily shorted position rising sharply as short sellers rush to buy back is a short squeeze, under short selling. IV: significantly less oversight than open-end mutual funds is the regulation item. The BRL program size is irrelevant.

**Fragile fact.** Classify by cause: incentive-driven risk taking is risk tolerance (not leverage); competitive secrecy is transparency (not regulation).

**Reference**

LO 91.a: Describe different risks faced by investors in hedge funds. Schweser, Book 5, Reading 91, Module 91.1, “Risks in Hedge Fund Investing”, paragraph 3 and subsections Leverage, Regulation, Short Selling, Transparency, Risk Tolerance. GARP text in the project has no matching section (the project’s GARP book has no chapter for this reading); content from Schweser, a condensed source whose wording may compress GARP’s framing.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-9 a, where it is Q5 of 14.

a.reason: A maps all four concerns to the incremental risk whose defining statement in Schweser matches the concern.

b.reason: **Sibling swap on I.** It labels the compensation concern as leverage. Leverage may be one way a manager acts on a higher risk appetite, but the concern described is the incentive itself, which Schweser places under risk tolerance. B would be correct if concern I said the fund borrows heavily and its losses are magnified accordingly.

c.reason: **Sibling swap between II and IV.** It swaps transparency and regulation. Concern II is about the manager’s choice to keep positions secret for competitive reasons; concern IV is about the oversight regime. C would be correct only if II described regulatory oversight and IV described manager secrecy.

d.reason: **Sibling swap on III.** It labels the short squeeze as leverage. The described mechanism (shorts forced to buy back, pushing the price up) is the short selling risk; nothing in III mentions borrowing to amplify exposure. D would be correct if III said the fund’s losses were magnified by borrowed money on a long position.

questions.question:
A risk consultant advising a Canadian public pension plan is drafting a slide on leverage risk in the plan’s CAD 2 billion hedge fund portfolio. The draft contains four statements:

I. Hedge fund leverage can be on-balance-sheet, through direct borrowing, or off-balance-sheet, for example through derivatives.

II. Because most hedge fund leverage is collateralized, leverage does not increase a fund’s sensitivity to liquidity shocks.

III. Leverage amplifies losses when returns are negative just as it amplifies gains when returns are positive.

IV. Most hedge fund leverage takes the form of uncollateralized borrowing; collateralized borrowing is rare.

Which of the statements are correct?

options.text: I and II only
III and IV only
I and III only
I, II, and III only

questions.solution:
A consultant to a Canadian pension plan drafts four statements on hedge fund leverage; which are correct?

**Concept and theory**

Leverage is the first of the five incremental risks. Schweser’s account has four separate claims:

| Claim | Schweser |
|---|---|
| Forms | On-balance-sheet (direct borrowing) or off-balance-sheet (for example, derivatives) |
| Symmetry | A powerful ally when returns are positive, a difficult adversary when negative: amplifies losses just as it amplifies gains |
| Liquidity | Can increase a fund’s sensitivity to liquidity shocks |
| Collateral | Most hedge fund leverage is collateralized with cash or assets held by the fund; true uncollateralized borrowing is rare |

Intuition: leverage scales the equity’s exposure to the asset. If a fund holds assets worth several times its equity, a given percentage move in the assets becomes a larger percentage move in equity, in both directions. Schweser states the liquidity and collateral facts side by side: leverage can increase sensitivity to liquidity shocks, and most leverage is collateralized. The second fact does not cancel the first.

**Applying it to this question**

I states the two forms correctly: true. II claims collateralization removes the liquidity-shock sensitivity: false, Schweser says leverage can increase that sensitivity, and collateralization does not reverse it. III states the symmetry: true. IV reverses the collateral fact: false. The CAD 2 billion figure is irrelevant.

**Fragile fact.** Direction: most hedge fund leverage is collateralized; uncollateralized borrowing is the rare case. Collateral does not stop leverage from raising liquidity-shock sensitivity.

**Reference**

LO 91.a: Describe different risks faced by investors in hedge funds. Schweser, Book 5, Reading 91, Module 91.1, “Risks in Hedge Fund Investing”, subsection Leverage. Figure 91.2 (leverage by strategy, 2020 OFR data) is an image not reproduced in the project text, so no strategy-level figures were tested. GARP text in the project has no matching section (the project’s GARP book has no chapter for this reading); content from Schweser, a condensed source whose wording may compress GARP’s framing. Boundary: forced deleveraging arithmetic (Figure 91.3) belongs to LO 91.b.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-9 a, where it is Q6 of 14.

a.reason: **Accepts II: false inference from a true premise.** The premise “most hedge fund leverage is collateralized” is true, but the conclusion that this removes liquidity-shock sensitivity contradicts Schweser. A would be correct if II read “leverage can increase a fund’s sensitivity to liquidity shocks” and III were false.

b.reason: **Accepts IV: polarity flip.** IV reverses “most leverage is collateralized; uncollateralized borrowing is rare.” B also rejects the true statement I. B would be correct only in a world where uncollateralized borrowing were the norm and derivatives were not a form of leverage.

c.reason: Only I and III match Schweser. II and IV each contradict a specific Schweser sentence.

d.reason: **Accepts II.** It gets I and III right but adds the false statement II, the same collateral-implies-safety error as A. D would be correct if II had said leverage can increase liquidity-shock sensitivity.

questions.question:
A portfolio manager on the fund of hedge funds desk of a U.K. insurer is reviewing a GBP 600 million macro fund. The fund’s disclosure states:

- No bank borrowing and no repo financing.
- Market exposure is taken through futures and total return swaps, with gross notional of 4 times NAV.
- All margin and collateral are posted in cash held by the fund.
- Fees are a 2% management fee and a 20% performance fee.

A junior analyst drafts four conclusions. Which conclusion is most accurate?

options.text: The fund is effectively unlevered, because it has no direct borrowing on its balance sheet.
The fund uses off-balance-sheet leverage through derivatives, which amplifies losses as well as gains and can raise its sensitivity to liquidity shocks.
The fund uses on-balance-sheet leverage, because the cash it posts as collateral is recorded as direct borrowing by the fund.
The fund’s leverage carries no liquidity risk, because all of its derivative positions are collateralized with cash held by the fund.

questions.solution:
A U.K. insurer’s fund of funds PM reviews a macro fund with no borrowing but futures and total return swaps at 4 times NAV; which conclusion is most accurate?

**Concept and theory**

Leverage need not appear as a loan on the balance sheet. Schweser distinguishes on-balance-sheet leverage (direct borrowing) from off-balance-sheet leverage (for example, derivatives). A futures contract or a total return swap gives the fund economic exposure to an asset far larger than the cash it posts, so the fund’s equity bears the gains and losses on the full notional. Schweser attaches the same consequences to leverage in either form: amplified gains and losses, and potentially greater sensitivity to liquidity shocks.

|  | On-balance-sheet | Off-balance-sheet |
|---|---|---|
| Instrument | Direct borrowing | Derivatives (futures, swaps) |
| Shows as a liability? | Yes, a loan | Not as a loan |
| Amplifies P&L? | Yes | Yes |

**Applying it to this question**

The deciding facts are “no bank borrowing and no repo” together with “futures and total return swaps with gross notional of 4 times NAV”. The first rules out on-balance-sheet leverage; the second establishes off-balance-sheet leverage. Cash collateral is a feature of most hedge fund leverage and does not neutralize it. The 2/20 fee line and the GBP 600 million size are irrelevant.

LO 91.a: Describe different risks faced by investors in hedge funds. Schweser, Book 5, Reading 91, Module 91.1, “Risks in Hedge Fund Investing”, subsection Leverage. GARP text in the project has no matching section (the project’s GARP book has no chapter for this reading); content from Schweser, a condensed source whose wording may compress GARP’s framing. options.text: Hedge funds operate with significantly less regulatory oversight than open-end mutual funds, so potential investors must conduct their own due diligence.
The Global Financial Crisis showed that hedge funds are regulated indirectly through their highly regulated counterparties, particularly banks.
Before the Dodd-Frank Act, the private adviser exemption in the Advisers Act exempted a manager from registration if it advised fewer than 15 clients.
Since the Dodd-Frank Act, an adviser managing at least \$150 million must register with the SEC, keep records available to the SEC, and accept a chief compliance officer appointed by the SEC.

questions.solution:
A Canadian insurer’s risk committee member checks four statements on U.S. hedge fund regulatory risk; which is NOT correct?

**Concept and theory**

Regulation is an incremental risk for hedge fund investors because hedge funds operate with significantly less regulatory oversight than open-end mutual funds, so the investor cannot rely on a regulator to have checked the fund and must conduct its own due diligence. Schweser’s U.S. account has four elements:

| Element | Schweser |
|---|---|
| Baseline | Significantly less oversight than open-end mutual funds; investors must do their own due diligence |
| Old exemption | Private adviser exemption (Advisers Act): exempt if advising fewer than 15 clients |
| GFC lesson | Hedge funds are indirectly regulated through highly regulated counterparties, particularly banks |
| Dodd-Frank (2010) | Advisers managing at least \$150 million must register with the SEC, maintain extensive records, make them available to the SEC, appoint a CCO, and undergo periodic SEC examinations |

Each Dodd-Frank duty has an actor: the adviser registers, keeps records, appoints its CCO, and submits to examinations; the SEC receives registration, sees records, and examines.

**Applying it to this question**

A, B, and C restate the first three elements. D lists the Dodd-Frank duties but changes the actor for the CCO: the SEC does not appoint a compliance officer inside the adviser; the adviser must appoint one. Since the question asks which statement is NOT correct, D is the answer. The CAD 75 million amount is irrelevant.

**Fragile fact.** Actor: under Dodd-Frank the adviser appoints the CCO; the SEC registers, receives records, and examines. Threshold: at least \$150 million.

**Reference**

LO 91.a: Describe different risks faced by investors in hedge funds. Schweser, Book 5, Reading 91, Module 91.1, “Risks in Hedge Fund Investing”, subsection Regulation, paragraph 1. GARP text in the project has no matching section (the project’s GARP book has no chapter for this reading); content from Schweser, a condensed source whose wording may compress GARP’s framing. Schweser wording note: the LO 91.a section says the private adviser exemption applied to managers advising “fewer than 15 clients”; the LO 91.c section says “fewer than 15 funds”. Both give the same 15 threshold; the 91.a wording is used here. The elimination of the exemption by Title IV and Form PF belong to LO 91.c and were not tested.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-9 a, where it is Q8 of 14.

a.reason: **True statement.** It restates Schweser’s opening sentence on regulation. It would be the answer only if the stem asked for the statement that conflicts with the idea of investor due diligence, for example if A said oversight was comparable to mutual funds.

b.reason: **True statement.** It restates the GFC lesson that hedge funds are indirectly regulated via their counterparties, especially banks. It would be the answer only if it had claimed that banks directly license hedge funds.

c.reason: **True statement.** It restates the private adviser exemption as worded in the LO 91.a section (“fewer than 15 clients”). It would be the answer only if the number or the act were changed, for example “fewer than 150 clients” or “the Investment Company Act”.

d.reason: Schweser: Dodd-Frank “required all hedge fund advisers managing at least \$150 million in assets to register with the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC), maintain extensive records, make those records available to the SEC, appoint a chief compliance officer (CCO), and undergo periodic SEC examinations.” The subject of “appoint” is the adviser. D’s version is a role misassignment, so D is the incorrect statement.

questions.question: A senior risk analyst at a Tokyo-based fund of hedge funds is training newly hired analysts using a recent episode. An underlying fund was short a heavily shorted stock whose price rose from JPY 2,000 to JPY 5,000 within three trading days as short sellers bought shares to close their positions. The fund had posted collateral when it borrowed the shares. Which of the following statements about this episode is most accurate?

options.text: It was a short squeeze, and since the stock’s price cannot fall below zero, the short seller’s potential loss was bounded.
It was a short squeeze, in which forced buying to close short positions can accelerate the price rise, and the short seller’s potential loss is theoretically unlimited.
It was a short squeeze, which occurs when the price of a heavily shorted stock falls rapidly, forcing short sellers to post additional collateral.
It was a short squeeze, and the short seller’s maximum loss was the collateral first posted, since a short seller is never required to add collateral.

questions.solution:
A Tokyo fund of funds trainer uses a short squeeze (JPY 2,000 to JPY 5,000) to test short-selling risk.

**Concept and theory**

Short selling is the third incremental risk. Mechanics in Schweser: the fund borrows shares, posts collateral, adds collateral as required, and eventually repays the borrowed shares when it closes the position. The payoff asymmetry is the key idea:

| Position | Worst case | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Long | Limited downside | Financial assets cannot have negative values |
| Short | Theoretically unlimited downside | A stock’s price has no upper bound |

A short squeeze occurs when the price of a heavily shorted stock rises rapidly, forcing short sellers to buy shares to close their positions; that forced buying can further accelerate the price increase (Schweser cites GameStop in 2021). The squeeze is self-reinforcing: each short seller who covers adds buying pressure that hurts the remaining shorts.

**Applying it to this question**

The facts are a heavily shorted stock, a rapid rise (JPY 2,000 to JPY 5,000, a 150% increase), and short sellers buying to close. That is a short squeeze. The loss per share to a short seller who entered at JPY 2,000 and covered at JPY 5,000 is JPY 3,000, already larger than the original sale proceeds, which illustrates the unbounded downside. Collateral was posted at the start, but Schweser notes additional collateral is added as required.

**Fragile fact.** Direction: a short squeeze is a rapid rise in a heavily shorted stock; the short’s downside is unbounded, the long’s is bounded by zero.

**Reference**

LO 91.a: Describe different risks faced by investors in hedge funds. Schweser, Book 5, Reading 91, Module 91.1, “Risks in Hedge Fund Investing”, subsection Short Selling. GARP text in the project has no matching section (the project’s GARP book has no chapter for this reading); content from Schweser, a condensed source whose wording may compress GARP’s framing.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-9 a, where it is Q9 of 14.

a.reason: **Sibling swap: long-position property applied to a short.** The zero floor on prices bounds the loss of a long position. For a short, the loss comes from price rises, which have no ceiling. A would be correct if the stem described a fund that was long the stock and the question asked about its maximum loss.

b.reason: B states both halves of the Schweser text: forced buying “can further accelerate the stock’s price increase”, and “short positions have theoretically unlimited downside risk because a stock’s price has no upper bound.”

c.reason: **Polarity flip.** A short squeeze is triggered by a rapid price rise, not a fall; a falling price benefits short sellers. C would be correct only if the stem described a heavily owned stock crashing and longs being forced out, which is not a short squeeze.

d.reason: **Condition error plus absolute claim.** Schweser’s mechanics include “adding additional collateral as required”, so the short seller can be required to add collateral, and the loss is not capped at the initial posting. D would be correct only if the source said collateral is fixed at inception and caps the loss.

Under the EU’s AIFMD, funds face mandatory registration and leverage limits, plus detailed reporting, disclosure, and marketing rules for both EU-based and non-EU-based funds; ESMA both interprets and enforces the provisions across member states.
In Singapore, hedge funds with more than \$250 million in assets must register with the MAS and provide quarterly audited reports and annual unaudited reports to investors and the MAS.
In Hong Kong, the SFO requires a hedge fund to hold a single license covering all hedge fund activities, regardless of the specific business activities in which it engages.

questions.solution:
An Australian manager’s regulatory consultant compares EU, Singapore, and Hong Kong hedge fund rules; which statement is most accurate?

**Concept and theory**

Within the regulation incremental risk, Schweser stresses that hedge fund rules vary significantly across international markets, so an investor’s (or manager’s) exposure depends on jurisdiction. The three regimes in this question:

| Regime | Schweser |
|---|---|
| EU (AIFMD, | First comprehensive regulation of hedge funds and private equity funds. |
| 2010) | Mandatory registration, limits on leverage, detailed reporting, disclosure, and marketing rules for both EU-based and non-EU-based funds. ESMA (created 2011) interprets the provisions; enforcement remains with individual member states. |
| Singapore (2010) | Funds with more than \$250 million in assets register with the MAS; regulated funds give quarterly unaudited and annual audited reports to investors and the MAS, and must obtain a capital markets services license. |
| Hong Kong (SFO) | Defines hedge fund activities (dealing in securities, leveraged FX trading, futures). Funds need a license corresponding to the specific business activities they engage in. Recommended reporting and disclosure practices; limits on marketing. |

**Applying it to this question**

Each option contains one fact that can be checked against the table. A splits the EU roles correctly (ESMA interprets, member states enforce). B gives ESMA enforcement power. C swaps which Singapore reports are audited. D replaces activity-specific licensing with a single license. The AUD denomination is irrelevant.

**Fragile fact.** Actors: ESMA interprets AIFMD, member states enforce it. Singapore: quarterly unaudited, annual audited; threshold more than \$250 million.

**Reference**

LO 91.a: Describe different risks faced by investors in hedge funds. Schweser, Book 5, Reading 91, Module 91.1, “Risks in Hedge Fund Investing”, subsection Regulation, paragraphs 2 to 4. GARP text in the project has no matching section (the project’s GARP book has no chapter for this reading); content from Schweser, a condensed source whose wording may compress GARP’s framing. Boundary: the EU’s 100 million euro reporting threshold, the EU passport, and country-specific rules (Portugal, France, Germany) are in the LO 91.c section and were not tested.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-9 a, where it is Q10 of 14.

a.reason: Schweser: AIFMD “requires mandatory registration and imposes limits on leverage; it also sets detailed reporting, disclosure, and marketing rules for both EU-based and non-EU-based funds”, and ESMA “was created to interpret AIFMD provisions, although enforcement remains the responsibility of individual member states.” A matches both clauses.

b.reason: **Role misassignment.** It gives ESMA the enforcement role, which Schweser assigns to individual member states. B would be correct if the source said ESMA both interprets and enforces AIFMD.

c.reason: **Polarity flip on audited versus unaudited.** Schweser says quarterly unaudited and annual audited reports. C reverses the two. C would be correct only if the source said quarterly audited and annual unaudited reports.

d.reason: **Scope error.** Schweser says funds “must obtain a license that corresponds to the specific business activities they engage in.” D overextends this to one license covering everything. D would be correct if the SFO granted a single, activity-independent hedge fund license.

questions.question: A risk analyst at a Dutch pension fund is reviewing a EUR 250 million allocation to a relative value arbitrage fund. The manager refuses position-level disclosure, explaining that if its trades became known, other funds would pile in. Redemptions are quarterly and subject to a 10% investor-level gate. The analyst worries that the manager may quietly shift strategy. Which of the following statements best describes the transparency risk in this allocation?

options.text: The secrecy is best described as regulatory risk, since the reduced disclosure stems from the fund’s lighter oversight than that of open-end mutual funds.
The secrecy makes risk monitoring harder, but the gate eases the problem because it allows a concerned investor to exit promptly if the strategy shifts.
The secrecy reflects the fear that a crowded trade erases the profit opportunity; it hampers monitoring of risk and strategy alignment, and the gate can restrict exit.
The secrecy matters only because the fund has a gate, since an investor able to redeem at any time would face no difficulty monitoring the fund’s risks.

questions.solution:
A Dutch pension analyst reviews a secretive arbitrage fund with a quarterly 10% gate; which statement best describes the transparency risk?

**Concept and theory**

Transparency is the fourth incremental risk. The causal chain in Schweser runs as follows. Many hedge funds try to arbitrage perceived market inefficiencies. If a trade becomes crowded with too many participants, the profit opportunity can quickly disappear. So hedge funds are often highly secretive about their strategies. That secrecy makes it harder for investors to monitor risks and to evaluate strategy alignment. On top of this, exit gates and other liquidity limits can restrict investors who are concerned about strategy shifts. GARP’s investment management chapter makes the same point: many hedge funds refuse to reveal their positions for fear of others taking advantage of the information, which makes it difficult for clients to measure the risk of the investment both at the hedge fund level and within their broader portfolio.

Inefficiency → fear of crowding → secrecy → hard to monitor risk and strategy alignment → gates restrict the exit

**Applying it to this question**

The manager’s stated reason (others would pile in) is the crowding motive. The analyst’s worry (a quiet strategy shift she cannot see) is the monitoring and strategy-alignment problem. The quarterly 10% gate is the liquidity limit that can stop her from leaving if she becomes concerned. The EUR 250 million size is irrelevant.

**Fragile fact.** Cause of secrecy is crowding (a competitive motive), not regulation; gates make the problem worse, not better.

**Reference**

LO 91.a: Describe different risks faced by investors in hedge funds. Schweser, Book 5, Reading 91, Module 91.1, “Risks in Hedge Fund Investing”, subsection Transparency. GARP corroboration: GARP Chapter 6 “VaR and Risk Budgeting in Investment Management”, Section 6.1 “VaR Applications to Investment Management”, paragraph on hedge funds’ lack of transparency (project text lines 7351 to 7356). That chapter is a different reading; it is consistent with Schweser and used only for depth.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-9 a, where it is Q11 of 14.

a.reason: **Sibling swap.** It relabels the secrecy as regulatory risk. Regulation is a separate incremental risk about oversight; Schweser attributes the secrecy to the manager’s competitive motive (crowding). A would be correct if the stem said the fund avoided disclosure because it was exempt from registration and reporting.

b.reason: **Polarity flip on the gate.** A gate restricts redemptions; it does not let investors exit promptly. Schweser says gates “can restrict investors who are concerned about strategy shifts.” B would be correct only if the fund offered daily liquidity with no gate.

c.reason: C contains each link of Schweser’s chain: crowded trades erase the opportunity, secrecy hampers monitoring of risks and strategy alignment, and gates can restrict investors concerned about strategy shifts.

d.reason: **Scope error.** It makes the gate a necessary condition for the transparency problem. Secrecy hampers monitoring regardless of liquidity terms; the gate only adds an exit problem on top. D would be correct if the source said monitoring is difficult only when redemptions are restricted.

| Q | U.S. adviser | 150 | 14 | 1.2 |

P: 140 ≥ 150? No ⇒ no SEC registration

Q: 150 ≥ 150? Yes ⇒ registers with the SEC

R: 250 > 250? No ⇒ no MAS registration

S: 260 > 250? Yes ⇒ registers with the MAS

Result: Q and S. The client counts (12, 14, 40, 9) and leverage figures are deliberately irrelevant inputs.

**Concept and theory**

China is Schweser’s example of a distinctive and restrictive regime, and it illustrates how regulation can directly constrain a strategy’s feasibility:

| Element | Schweser |
|---|---|
| Fund types | Government supported or private; the private segment is at an early stage |
| Primary regulator | China Securities Regulatory Commission (CSRC) |
| Leverage | Prohibited for Chinese hedge funds |
| Short selling | Restricted to 50 securities in the CSI 300 Index |

| Insurers | The China Insurance Regulatory Commission (CIRC) has encouraged insurers to use their own capital to set up asset managers running hedge-fund-like strategies |

The two agencies play opposite roles: the CSRC restricts hedge funds, while the CIRC encourages insurer-owned vehicles.

**Applying it to this question**

The CRO is an insurer, so the CIRC’s encouragement of insurer-established asset managers is relevant to the second route. Any option must also get the CSRC’s restrictions right. A does both. The CNY 5 billion size is irrelevant.

**Fragile fact.** CSRC restricts (no leverage, 50 CSI 300 shorts, no client-share lending, about 10% a year to short); CIRC encourages insurers. China prohibits leverage; the EU limits it.

LO 91.a: Describe different risks faced by investors in hedge funds. Schweser, Book 5, Reading 91, Module 91.1, “Risks in Hedge Fund Investing”, subsection Regulation, paragraph 5. Schweser’s own Module Quiz 91.1, Question 1 on Chinese short-selling restrictions is tagged to LO 91.a, which confirms the international regimes are in scope here. c.reason: **Role misassignment.** It swaps the two agencies: the CIRC becomes the restrictor and the CSRC the encourager of insurer vehicles. C would be correct only if the CIRC were the primary hedge fund regulator and the CSRC supervised insurers.

questions.question: A member of the investment committee of a Singapore insurer is reviewing a draft paragraph on manager risk tolerance for a SGD 200 million hedge fund mandate. Which of the following statements in the draft is most accurate?

options.text: Hedge fund managers’ risk tolerance is generally similar to that of open-end mutual fund managers; they differ mainly in their access to newer, more innovative strategies.
Hedge fund managers’ frequent use of derivatives can help mitigate risk, but it introduces complexities that make assessing the fund’s risk more difficult.

questions.solution:
A Singapore insurer’s committee member reviews a draft on hedge fund manager risk tolerance; which statement is most accurate?

**Concept and theory**

Risk tolerance is the fifth incremental risk. Schweser makes four claims:

| Claim | Schweser |
|---|---|
| Level | Hedge fund managers generally have a higher risk tolerance than most open-end mutual fund managers |
| Cause | Their compensation structures often incentivize them to take on additional risk |
| Opportunity set | Access to a wider range of opportunities, including newer and more innovative strategies |
| Derivatives | Frequently used; they can help mitigate risk but also introduce complexities that make risk assessment more difficult |

The intuition behind the compensation point: when pay rises with gains, the manager is rewarded for taking more risk, so the manager’s preferred level of risk can exceed the investor’s. Derivatives cut both ways: they can hedge, but they make the fund’s true exposures harder for an outsider to assess.

**Applying it to this question**

Check each option’s two clauses. A contradicts the level claim. B restates the derivatives claim with both halves. C states the cause correctly but then misplaces risk tolerance in the wrong framework. D attributes the cause to regulation rather than compensation. The SGD 200 million mandate size is irrelevant.

**Fragile fact.** Derivatives in hedge funds are two-sided: they can mitigate risk and make it harder to assess. Risk tolerance belongs to the five incremental risks, not to the portfolio-level list.

**Reference**

LO 91.a: Describe different risks faced by investors in hedge funds. Schweser, Book 5, Reading 91, Module 91.1, “Risks in Hedge Fund Investing”, subsection Risk Tolerance. GARP text in the project has no matching section (the project’s GARP book has no chapter for this reading); content from Schweser, a condensed source whose wording may compress GARP’s framing.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-9 a, where it is Q14 of 14.

a.reason: **Polarity flip.** Schweser says hedge fund managers generally have a higher risk tolerance than most open-end mutual fund managers, not a similar one. The second clause (access to newer strategies) is true, which makes the option tempting. A would be correct if the source said risk tolerance was similar.

b.reason: Schweser: managers “frequently use derivatives, which can help mitigate risk but also introduce complexities that make risk assessment more difficult.” B states both halves.

c.reason: **Sibling swap across frameworks.** Risk tolerance is one of the five incremental risks, not one of the portfolio-level risks (benchmarking issues, survivorship bias, UBTI). The first clause is true. C would be correct if it said risk tolerance is one of the five incremental risks particularly pronounced in hedge funds.

d.reason: **Sibling swap of cause.** Schweser ties the higher risk appetite to compensation structures, not to regulatory leverage limits; regulation is a separate incremental risk. D would be correct only if the source attributed manager risk tolerance mainly to looser regulation.

Systemic risk is the threat of disruption to the broader financial system or economy, as opposed to the loss suffered by one fund or one investor. The reading identifies two key ways in which hedge funds contribute to it.

|---|---|
| 1. Strategy failure and forced unwinding | A fund whose strategy fails may be forced to unwind positions at fire-sale prices. Selling far below fundamental value depresses prices for every other holder of those assets, which is contagion. |
| 2. Losses to lenders and counterparties | Hedge funds borrow from, and trade with, financial institutions (mainly banks). A failing fund can impose large losses on the institutions that lend to it or act as its counterparties, carrying the damage into the regulated core of the system. |

II. The Bank of England also concluded that hedge funds, by facilitating risk transfer, necessarily increase systemic risk.

III. The Bank of England’s view is not universal; critics argue that hedge fund leverage and complex, nonlinear strategies can increase systemic risk.

The 2006 failure of Amaranth Advisors raised questions about whether hedge funds pose systemic risk. The reading presents two sides.

| Actor | Position |
|---|---|

| Critics | The Bank of England view is not universal; hedge fund leverage and complex, nonlinear strategies can increase systemic risk. |

options.text: Lenders relaxed collateral requirements, allowing hedge funds to add leverage and bid asset prices into a bubble that burst once lending standards were tightened again.
Hedge funds rotated out of risky assets after a fundamental reassessment, so price declines were confined to the asset classes whose fundamentals had deteriorated.

Lenders forced hedge funds to post additional collateral, which funds raised by unwinding positions; the fire sales spread losses to otherwise uncorrelated asset classes, amplified by leverage and computer-driven selling.

The reading states that it is clear the relationship between hedge funds and their bank counterparties can create systemic risk, and that the GFC showed how. The chain is:

1. Lenders (banks, prime brokers) force hedge funds to post additional collateral.
2. Funds raise the collateral by unwinding positions.
3. The resulting fire sales spread contagion and produce significant losses in asset classes that were otherwise uncorrelated, because forced sellers sell whatever they hold, not what is fundamentally overvalued.
4. The effects are amplified by leverage and by computer-driven selling.
5. Selling pressure is increased further by margin calls from counterparties, investor redemptions and declining risk appetite; funds of hedge funds add a cascade of redemptions.

questions.question:
A treasury analyst at a German bank’s prime brokerage unit is stress testing a hedge fund client. Leverage is measured, as in the reading, as the loan divided by the fund’s equity. The fund’s current position is shown below.

| Item | Value |
|---|---|
| Market value of bond portfolio | EUR 240.0 million |
| Margin (equity as a share of the position) | 20% |
| Financing spread charged by the bank | 85 bps |
| Target leverage (loan / equity) | 4.0x |

The bond portfolio falls 5% in value and the loan balance is unchanged. The fund restores its target leverage solely by selling bonds at market prices and using the proceeds to repay the loan. The forced sale is closest to:

options.text: EUR 12.0 million
EUR 48.0 million
EUR 60.0 million
EUR 144.0 million

questions.solution:
German prime broker: forced sale needed to restore 4.0x loan/equity leverage after a 5% fall.

**Concept and theory**

The reading illustrates contagion risk from forced selling under leverage (Figure 91.3). Leverage is measured as loan divided by equity, so a 25% margin (equity 25, loan 75) corresponds to 3.0x. The mechanism:

- When the asset price falls, the whole loss hits equity, while the loan amount does not change; leverage therefore rises.
- To restore the target, the fund sells assets and repays the loan. A sale at market price exchanges assets for cash and does not change equity.
- Hence the loan must shrink to target × new equity, and the sale equals the reduction in the loan.

With V = position value, L = loan, E $= \text{V} -$ L = equity, k = target loan/equity, and d = price decline:

$\text{E}_{1} = \text{V}($1 $- \text{d}) -$ L, $\text{L}^{*} = \text{k E}_{1}$, Sale $= \text{L} - \text{L}^{*}$.

Because L = kE before the shock, this simplifies to Sale $= \text{k} \times($loss in value): every unit of equity lost requires k units of debt to be repaid.

**Applying it to this question**

$\text{E}_{0} =$ 20% × 240.0 = 48.0 (EUR m)

L = 240.0 − 48.0 = 192.0; $\text{L/E}_{0} =$ 192.0/48.0 = 4.0x

$\text{V}_{1} =$ 240.0 × (1 − 0.05) = 228.0; loss = 12.0

$\text{E}_{1} =$ 228.0 − 192.0 = 36.0; $\text{L/E}_{1} =$ 192.0/36.0 = 5.33x

$\text{L}^{*} =$ 4.0 × 36.0 = 144.0

Sale = 192.0 − 144.0 = 48.0

Check: remaining bonds 228.0 − 48.0 = 180.0 = 144.0 loan + 36.0 equity; 144.0/36.0 = 4.0x

Meaning: a 5% price fall (EUR 12 million) forces EUR 48 million of selling, four times the loss, with no fundamental reason to sell. This is the amplification that turns a fund’s loss into market-wide selling pressure. The 85 bps financing spread is irrelevant.

**Fragile fact.** Convention: in the reading, 25% margin means 3.0x (loan/equity), not 4.0x; and a sale at market leaves equity unchanged, so Sale $= \text{k}\times$ loss.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** “LO 91.b: Explain how the activities of hedge funds and exposure to hedge funds can increase systemic risk.”

**Schweser:** Reading 91, Module 91.1, “Impact of Hedge Funds on Systemic Risk”, subsection “Systemic Risk From Hedge Fund Activities” and Figure 91.3 (Contagion Risk From Forced Hedge Fund Selling Under Leverage).

**GARP:** GARP text in the project has no matching section; content from Schweser, a condensed source whose wording may compress the original reading’s framing.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-9 b, where it is Q6 of 12.

a.reason: **Intermediate result: the price loss.** EUR 12.0 million = 240.0 × 5%, the loss in value. Selling only the amount lost ignores that each euro of lost equity supports four euros of debt. A would be correct for a fund whose target loan/equity is 1.0x (50% margin), where Sale = 1.0× loss.

b.reason: B is the reduction in the loan needed to bring loan/equity back to 4.0x given equity of EUR 36 million, exactly as in the reading’s Scenario C, where the loan falls from 75 to 45 against unchanged equity of 15.

Under the reading’s convention the multiple is the loan/equity ratio. C would be correct if target loan/equity were 5.0x.

Which of the following statements about this episode is most accurate?

Three principles follow:

1. Leverage rises after a price fall because the loan does not change while equity absorbs the whole loss.
2. The sale does not change equity; it shrinks the balance sheet (assets and loan fall together).

$\text{V}_{1} =$ 160 × 0.85 = 136; loss = 24

$\text{E}_{1} =$ 136 − 120 = 16; $\text{L/E}_{1} =$ 120/16 = 7.5x

$\text{L}^{*} =$ 3.0 × 16 = 48; Sale = 120 − 48 = 72

After sale: stock 64 = 48 loan + 16 equity

Now audit the statements: A says the sale is 24 (it is 72); B says the sale rebuilds equity (equity stays at 16); C says leverage rises to 7.5x as equity falls from 40 to 16 (true); D says sales track fundamentals (the reading says the opposite).

b.reason: **Scope or condition error on what the sale changes.** Selling at market and repaying the loan reduces assets and loan by the same amount; equity is unchanged at GBP 16 million, just as equity stays at USD 15 in the reading’s Scenario C. questions.reading: IM-9: Risk, Regulation and Organizational Structure
questions.source: High quality paper IM-9 b Q8
questions.question:
The chief risk officer of a US bank is reviewing the bank’s exposures to its hedge fund clients after several of them suffered large losses. The bank’s CET1 ratio is 13.2%. Three exposures are listed below.

| No. | Exposure | USD m |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Annual fees from trading, clearing, custody and securities lending for 40 hedge fund clients, which would fall if several clients failed | 310 |
| 2 | Margin loans secured by client securities whose value could decline faster than anticipated | 6,200 |
| 3 | Credit default swaps and other OTC derivatives with hedge fund clients | 1,450 |

Using the reading’s three primary types of risk that banks face when they engage with hedge funds, which of the following correctly classifies exposures 1, 2 and 3, respectively?

options.text: Revenue risk; credit risk; counterparty risk
Revenue risk; counterparty risk; credit risk
Credit risk; credit risk; counterparty risk
Market risk; credit risk; counterparty risk

questions.solution:
US bank CRO: classify fee income, margin loans and OTC derivatives exposures to hedge funds.

**Concept and theory**

The second half of the LO concerns exposure to hedge funds. Banks face three primary types of risk when they engage with hedge funds:

| Risk | Source | Loss event |
|---|---|---|
| Revenue risk | Fee and service income: trading, clearing, custody, securities lending, financing, reporting | Failure of multiple hedge funds materially reduces this revenue stream |
| Credit risk | Margin loans secured by collateral | Collateral value declines faster than anticipated, leaving the bank undersecured |
| Counterparty risk | Derivatives with hedge funds: CDSs and other OTC contracts | Hedge fund fails to perform on the derivative |

These are the channels through which a hedge fund failure becomes a banking problem, and therefore potentially a systemic one.

**Applying it to this question**

Exposure 1 is fee income from trading, clearing, custody and securities lending, lost if clients fail: revenue risk. Exposure 2 is a secured margin loan whose collateral may fall faster than anticipated: credit risk. Exposure 3 is CDS and other OTC derivatives: counterparty risk. The CET1 ratio and the USD amounts are irrelevant to classification.

**Fragile fact.** Pairing: margin loans map to credit risk; CDS and OTC derivatives map to counterparty risk; fees map to revenue risk.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** “LO 91.b: Explain how the activities of hedge funds and exposure to hedge funds can increase systemic risk.”

**Schweser:** Reading 91, Module 91.1, “Impact of Hedge Funds on Systemic Risk”, subsection “Systemic Risk From Bank Exposure to Hedge Funds”.

**GARP:** GARP text in the project has no matching section; content from Schweser, a condensed source whose wording may compress the original reading’s framing.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-9 b, where it is Q8 of 12.

a.reason: A assigns each exposure to the reading’s own category, in order: revenue risk, credit risk, counterparty risk.

b.reason: **Sibling swap: credit and counterparty.** B swaps the two lending-related categories. In the reading, margin loans create credit risk and derivatives create counterparty risk. B would be correct only under a labeling convention the reading does not use.

c.reason: **Sibling swap: revenue as credit.** C labels lost fee income as credit risk. A fall in fees is not a loss on a loan; it is the bank’s revenue risk. C would be correct only if exposure 1 were unpaid fees owed by a defaulted client.

d.reason: **Scope error: category outside the reading’s three.** D labels lost fee income as market risk, a category the reading does not list among the three primary risks banks face with hedge funds. D would be correct only for a stem about the bank’s own trading positions.

questions.question: An internal auditor at a Canadian bank is validating a draft board report on the bank’s CAD-denominated exposures to hedge funds and their link to systemic risk. Which of the following statements in the draft report is least accurate?

options.text: Revenue risk: the bank earns fee and service income from hedge funds, and the failure of multiple hedge funds could materially reduce this revenue stream.
Credit risk: margin loans are secured by collateral, but its value can decline more quickly than anticipated, potentially leaving the bank undersecured.
Counterparty risk: this arises on the bank’s margin loans to hedge funds, whereas credit default swaps and other OTC contracts give rise to credit risk.
Systemic link: a hedge fund failure can increase systemic risk by imposing large losses on the institutions that lend to it or act as its counterparties.

questions.solution:
Canadian bank auditor: least accurate statement in a board report on hedge fund exposures.

**Concept and theory**

Banks are exposed to hedge funds through three risks (revenue, credit, counterparty). The second channel by which hedge fund activities create systemic risk is that hedge funds can impose large losses on the institutions that lend to them or act as their counterparties. The two lending-type risks differ by instrument:

| Risk | Instrument | Why the bank can lose |
|---|---|---|
| Credit risk | Margin loans | Collateral can lose value faster than expected, leaving the loan undersecured |
| Counterparty risk | CDSs and other OTC derivatives | The hedge fund may fail to perform on the contract |

The collateral point is subtle: margin loans are secured, so the risk is not that there is no collateral, but that collateral values fall faster than anticipated, typically in exactly the fire-sale conditions described elsewhere in the LO.

**Applying it to this question**

Check each line of the draft against the source. A (revenue risk) matches. B (credit risk, undersecured) matches. D (systemic link) matches the second channel. C attaches margin loans to counterparty risk and derivatives to credit risk, which is the reverse of the reading.

**Fragile fact.** Instrument pairing: margin loan to credit risk; CDS and OTC contracts to counterparty risk. Do not swap them.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** “LO 91.b: Explain how the activities of hedge funds and exposure to hedge funds can increase systemic risk.”

**Schweser:** Reading 91, Module 91.1, “Impact of Hedge Funds on Systemic Risk”, subsection “Systemic Risk From Bank Exposure to Hedge Funds” and “Systemic Risk From Hedge Fund Activities”.

**GARP:** GARP text in the project has no matching section; content from Schweser, a condensed source whose wording may compress the original reading’s framing.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-9 b, where it is Q9 of 12.

a.reason: **Accurate; choosing it is a qualifier misread.** The reading says banks earn significant fee and service income from hedge funds and that the failure of multiple hedge funds could materially reduce it. A would be the answer only if it had misdescribed revenue risk, for example by calling lost fee income a credit loss.

b.reason: **Accurate; choosing it confuses “secured” with “riskless”.** A candidate who believes collateral eliminates credit risk would wrongly flag B. The reading explicitly says collateral can decline faster than anticipated, potentially leaving the bank undersecured. B would be the answer only if it had claimed credit risk is eliminated by collateral.

c.reason: The reading states that credit risk arises on margin loans, secured by collateral whose value can fall faster than anticipated, and that counterparty risk arises through derivatives such as CDSs and other OTC contracts. C swaps the two instruments.

d.reason: **Accurate; choosing it confuses investor-level risk with systemic risk.** D restates the reading’s second channel of systemic risk. A candidate who thinks hedge fund risk stays with the fund’s own investors (LO 91.a thinking) might flag it. D would be the answer only if it had said losses fall solely on the fund’s investors.

questions.question: A member of the board risk committee of a European bank asks the bank’s CRO to summarize the 2021 default of Archegos Capital, as described in the reading, before the committee reviews the bank’s prime brokerage limits. Which of the following summaries is most accurate?

options.text: Archegos was a family office whose total return swaps created exposures resembling hedge fund leverage; banks lost about USD 10 billion in total, and banks then required hedge funds to reduce leverage.

Archegos was a family office whose total return swaps created exposures resembling hedge fund leverage; banks lost about USD 5 billion in total, and banks then required hedge funds to reduce leverage.

Archegos was a hedge fund whose credit default swaps created exposures typical of hedge fund leverage; banks lost about USD 10 billion in total, and banks then required hedge funds to reduce leverage.

Archegos was a family office whose total return swaps created exposures resembling hedge fund leverage; banks lost about USD 10 billion in total, and banks then relaxed leverage limits to retain fee income.

questions.solution:
Board risk committee: most accurate summary of the Archegos Capital default (2021).

**Concept and theory**

Archegos shows that the systemic risk of hedge fund-style leverage does not depend on the legal label of the borrower. The reading’s account has four elements:

| Element | Reading |
|---|---|
| Entity type | A family office, not a hedge fund |
| Instrument | Total return swaps, creating exposures that closely resembled hedge fund leverage |
| Losses | Credit Suisse about USD 5 billion; other banks collectively about USD 5 billion more (so roughly USD 10 billion in total) |
| Response | A clear warning to the banking system; banks required hedge funds to reduce leverage, recognizing the potential systemic risk to the sector |

Outside-source background (not in Schweser or the project’s GARP text, and not tested here): a total return swap generally lets the client receive the economic return of a reference asset held by the bank in exchange for a financing payment and margin, so the exposure is leveraged without a loan appearing on the client’s balance sheet. The reading itself says only that Archegos’s total return swaps created exposures closely resembling hedge fund leverage.

**Applying it to this question**

All four options share a common template, and each differs in one element. Check each element against the table: entity (family office), instrument (total return swaps), total losses (about 5 + 5 = USD 10 billion), response (banks required hedge funds to reduce leverage). Only A is correct on all four.

**Fragile fact.** Number and label: about USD 5 billion at Credit Suisse plus about USD 5 billion elsewhere; Archegos was a family office using total return swaps.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** “LO 91.b: Explain how the activities of hedge funds and exposure to hedge funds can increase systemic risk.”

**Schweser:** Reading 91, Module 91.1, “Impact of Hedge Funds on Systemic Risk”, subsection “Systemic Risk From Bank Exposure to Hedge Funds” (Archegos paragraph).

**GARP:** GARP text in the project has no matching section; content from Schweser, a condensed source whose wording may compress the original reading’s framing.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-9 b, where it is Q10 of 12.

a.reason: A matches every element: family office, total return swaps resembling hedge fund leverage, roughly USD 10 billion of bank losses (Credit Suisse about USD 5 billion plus about USD 5 billion at other banks), and banks then requiring hedge funds to reduce leverage.

b.reason: **Dropped term.** USD 5 billion is Credit Suisse’s loss alone; it drops the additional USD 5 billion lost by other banks. B would be correct if the stem asked for Credit Suisse’s loss only.

c.reason: **Sibling swap: entity and instrument.** C calls Archegos a hedge fund and replaces total return swaps with credit default swaps, which the reading mentions only as an example of the derivatives that create bank counterparty risk generally. C would be correct for a hypothetical hedge fund whose losses arose from CDS positions.

d.reason: **Polarity flip on the response.** The reading says the failure prompted banks to require hedge funds to reduce leverage. D reverses this into relaxing limits. Correct only if banks had prioritized revenue over risk, which the reading does not say.

questions.question:
A risk consultant is advising a financial stability committee in Hong Kong on proposals to contain the systemic risk associated with hedge funds. The committee is considering the following four proposals.

I. Banks adopt more conservative lending practices toward hedge funds.

II. Hedge funds operate with lower leverage and greater diversification within their portfolios.

III. Regulators impose the strictest feasible limits on hedge fund and private equity activity, to minimize their footprint in markets.

IV. Regulators apply reasonable regulation to hedge funds.

Which of the proposals are consistent with the reading’s approaches to mitigating the impact of hedge funds on systemic risk?

options.text: I and II only
I, II, III and IV
II and IV only
I, II and IV only

questions.solution:
Hong Kong financial stability committee: which proposals match the reading’s three mitigation approaches.

**Concept and theory**

The reading lists three main approaches to mitigating the impact of hedge funds on systemic risk. Each targets one link in the chain described in the LO.

| Approach | Link it addresses |
|---|---|
| 1. More conservative lending practices by banks | Limits the losses hedge funds can impose on lenders (credit and counterparty channels) and the leverage available to them |
| 2. Lower leverage and greater diversification within hedge fund portfolios | Reduces forced selling after shocks and the chance that one strategy failure triggers a fire-sale unwind |
| 3. Reasonable regulation | Constrains excesses without draining market liquidity |

The qualifier “reasonable” matters: the reading warns that excessively strict regulation of hedge funds and private equity firms could have unintended negative effects by reducing the liquidity these investors provide.

**Applying it to this question**

I matches approach 1, II matches approach 2, IV matches approach 3. III is the excessive regulation the reading warns against. The consistent set is I, II and IV.

**Fragile fact.** Qualifier: the third approach is reasonable regulation; strict regulation is the trap.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** “LO 91.b: Explain how the activities of hedge funds and exposure to hedge funds can increase systemic risk.”

**Schweser:** Reading 91, Module 91.1, “Impact of Hedge Funds on Systemic Risk”, subsection “Systemic Risk From Bank Exposure to Hedge Funds” (mitigation paragraph).

**GARP:** GARP text in the project has no matching section; content from Schweser, a condensed source whose wording may compress the original reading’s framing.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-9 b, where it is Q11 of 12.

a.reason: **Scope error: drops reasonable regulation.** Excluding IV treats all regulation as harmful. The reading warns only against excessive regulation and includes reasonable regulation as the third approach. A would be correct if the stem asked for approaches that rely on market participants alone.

b.reason: **Absolute claim: accepts strictest feasible limits.** Including III assumes more regulation is always better. The reading says excessively strict rules can reduce liquidity and have unintended negative effects. B would be correct only if the reading endorsed regulation without limit.

c.reason: **Role misassignment: omits the banks.** Dropping I treats mitigation as the hedge funds’ and regulators’ job only. The reading names banks’ conservative lending as the first approach. C would be correct for a stem asking which proposals act on hedge funds directly.

d.reason: D contains exactly the three approaches named in the reading and excludes the strict-limits proposal, which the reading says could have unintended negative effects on financial markets.

questions.question: A policy analyst at a central bank is drafting a note for the governor, who has proposed sharply tightening the rules on hedge funds and private equity firms to reduce systemic risk. The analyst wants to explain the reading’s caution about this approach. Which of the following best explains that caution?

options.text: Strict rules would mainly cut banks’ fee income from hedge funds, and the reading identifies this revenue risk as the largest channel through which hedge funds create systemic risk.
Strict rules could reduce the liquidity hedge funds provide, since they often act as investors of last resort, taking on risks such as distressed securities that traditional investors avoid.
Strict rules are unnecessary, since the reading concludes that hedge funds reduce systemic risk overall by facilitating risk transfer rather than by concentrating it.
Strict rules would push traditional investors into acting as investors of last resort, taking on risks such as distressed securities that hedge funds would otherwise avoid.

questions.solution:
Central bank note to the governor: why sharply tightening hedge fund rules could backfire.

**Concept and theory**

Hedge funds are not only a source of systemic risk; they also supply liquidity. The reading notes that hedge funds often act as investors of last resort, taking on risks such as distressed securities that traditional investors are unwilling to assume. If excessively strict regulation drives hedge funds and private equity firms out of these markets, the liquidity they provide disappears, which can have unintended negative effects on financial markets and, per the key concepts, may unintentionally heighten systemic risk.

| Regulatory stance | Effect in the reading |
|---|---|
| Reasonable regulation | One of three mitigation approaches |
| Excessively strict regulation | Reduces the liquidity hedge funds and private equity provide; unintended negative effects; may heighten systemic risk |

**Applying it to this question**

The governor’s proposal is sharp tightening, which is excessive rather than reasonable regulation. The deciding fact is the liquidity argument and who plays the role of investor of last resort: hedge funds, not traditional investors.

**Fragile fact.** Actor: hedge funds are the investors of last resort; traditional investors are the ones unwilling to hold distressed securities.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** “LO 91.b: Explain how the activities of hedge funds and exposure to hedge funds can increase systemic risk.”

**Schweser:** Reading 91, Module 91.1, “Impact of Hedge Funds on Systemic Risk”, subsection “Systemic Risk From Bank Exposure to Hedge Funds” (mitigation paragraph) and Key Concepts LO 91.b.

**GARP:** GARP text in the project has no matching section; content from Schweser, a condensed source whose wording may compress the original reading’s framing.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-9 b, where it is Q12 of 12.

a.reason: **Sibling swap and unsupported ranking.** Revenue risk is one of the three bank exposures, but the reading does not rank it as the largest channel, and the caution about strict regulation concerns liquidity, not bank fee income. A would be correct only if the reading had made the fee-income argument.

b.reason: B reproduces the reading’s reasoning: excessively strict regulation could reduce the liquidity hedge funds provide, because they often act as investors of last resort, taking on risks such as distressed securities that traditional investors are unwilling to assume.

c.reason: **Absolute claim and misattribution.** The risk-transfer argument is the Bank of England’s view after Amaranth, and the reading notes it is not universal; it also states that the hedge fund and bank relationship clearly can create systemic risk. Claiming the reading concludes hedge funds reduce systemic risk overall overstates one side of a debate. Correct only if the stem asked for the Bank of England’s position.

d.reason: **Role misassignment.** D swaps the actors: in the reading, hedge funds take on distressed securities that traditional investors are unwilling to assume. Correct only if traditional investors were the natural buyers of distressed assets.
