questions.question:
A compliance officer at a U.S. hedge fund manager is reviewing the launch plan for four new funds, each of which is to avoid registration under the Investment Company Act of 1940 (the ’40 Act) by relying on Section 3(c)(1) or Section 3(c)(7). The planned investor bases are below.

| Fund | Investors | Investor type | Target AUM (USD m) |
|---|---|---|---|
| North | 85 | Accredited, not all qualified purchasers | 240 |
| South | 140 | All qualified purchasers | 1150 |
| East | 620 | All qualified purchasers | 3400 |
| West | 100 | Accredited, not all qualified purchasers | 410 |

Which of the following statements is most accurate?

options.text: Fund North must register under the ’40 Act, because a fund that admits investors who are not qualified purchasers cannot rely on any exemption.
Fund West can rely on Section 3(c)(1), because its investor count does not exceed the 100-investor limit of that exemption.
Fund East can avoid ’40 Act registration under Section 3(c)(7), but it must register under the Securities Exchange Act of 1934.
Fund South must register under the Securities Exchange Act of 1934, because Section 3(c)(7) funds with more than 100 investors must do so.

questions.solution:
Compliance officer checks which of four planned funds (85, 140, 620 and 100 investors) can use Section 3(c)(1) or 3(c)(7), and what follows.

**Concept and theory**

The Investment Company Act of 1940 requires every mutual fund to register with the SEC. Registration brings regular reporting and limits on leverage, short selling and performance fees. Those limits would make most hedge fund strategies and fee models unworkable, so hedge funds are structured to fall inside one of two exemptions. The logic of both is the same: if the pool of investors is small or wealthy enough, the full retail-style protection of the ’40 Act is not needed.

|  | Section 3(c)(1) | Section 3(c)(7) |
|---|---|---|
| Condition | Fewer than 100 investors | Limited to qualified purchasers (individuals with more than \$5 million in investment assets) |
| Investor count limit | The count itself is the condition (99 is the maximum) | No investor cap for the ’40 Act exemption |
| Further trigger | None stated | Must register under the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 if it has 500 or more investors |

The two exemptions are different routes: 3(c)(1) restricts how many investors, 3(c)(7) restricts who the investors are. The 500-investor ’34 Act trigger is attached to 3(c)(7) in the source.

**Applying it to this question**

North: 85 investors is fewer than 100, so 3(c)(1) is available whatever the investors’ wealth. South: all qualified purchasers, 140 investors, below 500, so 3(c)(7) applies with no ’34 Act registration. East: all qualified purchasers, so 3(c)(7) removes the ’40 Act requirement, but 620 is at least 500, so ’34 Act registration is triggered. West: 100 investors is not fewer than 100, so 3(c)(1) fails; not all investors are qualified purchasers, so 3(c)(7) fails too. The AUM column is irrelevant: neither exemption has a size test.

**Fragile fact.** 3(c)(1) is a count test (fewer than 100); 3(c)(7) is an investor-quality test (qualified purchasers) whose ’34 Act trigger is 500 or more investors. Do not cross the numbers.

**Reference**

**LO 91.c:** “Summarize different approaches taken by regulators to mitigate risks related to hedge funds.” Schweser Book 5, Reading 91, Module 91.2, section “U.S. Regulatory Framework”. Key Concepts, LO 91.c. GARP: the GARP text in the project has no matching section (the Stowell and Stowell chapter assigned to this reading is not in the file); content from Schweser, a condensed source whose wording may compress the original framing.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-9 c, where it is Q1 of 14.

a.reason: **Absolute claim.** The statement turns the 3(c)(7) condition into a universal rule. Section 3(c)(1) has no investor-quality condition in the source; North qualifies on its count of 85. A would be correct only if North had 100 or more investors, so that the qualified purchaser route was its only option.

b.reason: **Scope or condition error at the boundary.** The condition is “fewer than 100”, not “no more than 100”. West, at exactly 100, fails. B would be correct if West had 99 investors.

c.reason: Schweser states that a fund may be exempt if limited to qualified purchasers, but “funds relying on this exemption must register under the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 (’34 Act) if they have 500 or more investors.” East has 620 qualified purchasers, so both halves of C hold.

d.reason: **Wrong threshold twin.** D borrows the 100 figure from 3(c)(1) and attaches it to the 3(c)(7) ’34 Act trigger, which is 500. South’s 140 investors are well below 500. D would be correct if South had 500 or more investors.

questions.question:
An operations analyst at a fund administrator is screening five prospective individual investors for a U.S. hedge fund that relies exclusively on the Section 3(c)(7) exemption from the Investment Company Act of 1940. Net worth and investment assets are in USD million; income is in USD thousand for each of the two prior years, with whether that level is reasonably expected to continue.

| Investor | Net worth | Investment assets | Income (2 prior years) | Continues? | Age |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| P | 9.0 | 6.2 | 310 / 320 | Yes | 58 |
| Q | 7.5 | 4.8 | 900 / 900 | Yes | 47 |
| R | 5.5 | 5.0 | 180 / 190 | No | 66 |
| S | 6.0 | 5.4 | 120 / 140 | No | 71 |
| T | 2.0 | 1.5 | 400 / 410 | Yes | 39 |

How many of the five investors can the fund admit consistently with the exemption it relies on?
questions.solution:
Fund administrator screens five investors for a fund relying solely on Section 3(c)(7); how many can be admitted?

**Concept and theory**

Two different wealth tests appear in this LO and they guard different gates. The qualified purchaser test belongs to the Section 3(c)(7) exemption from the ’40 Act: an individual must have more than \$5 million in investment assets. The accredited investor test belongs to Regulation D, which governs private placements: an individual needs a net worth of at least \$2.5 million, or annual income of \$250,000 in each of the prior two years with a reasonable expectation of maintaining that level. The accredited test is the lower bar. A fund that relies only on 3(c)(7) must be limited to qualified purchasers, so being accredited is not enough.

|  | Qualified purchaser (3(c)(7)) | Accredited investor (Reg D) |
|---|---|---|
| Measure | Investment assets | Net worth, or income |
| Threshold | More than \$5 million | At least \$2.5 million net worth, or \$250,000 income in each of the prior two years with expectation of continuing |

**Applying it to this question**

Test: investment assets > 5.0 (USD million).

P: 6.2 > 5.0 ⇒ qualified purchaser

Q: 4.8 \< 5.0 ⇒ not (accredited only)

R: 5.0 = 5.0 ⇒ not (“more than” fails)

S: 5.4 > 5.0 ⇒ qualified purchaser

T: 1.5 \< 5.0 ⇒ not (accredited via income only)

Count of eligible investors = 2 (P and S). Net worth, income and age are irrelevant to the 3(c)(7) test. The number means only P and S may enter; admitting any of the others would breach the condition the fund’s exemption rests on.

**Fragile fact.** Qualified purchaser: investment assets, strictly more than \$5 million. Accredited: net worth at least \$2.5 million or \$250,000 income in each of two years. Different measure, different threshold, different rule.

**Reference**

**LO 91.c:** “Summarize different approaches taken by regulators to mitigate risks related to hedge funds.” Schweser Book 5, Reading 91, Module 91.2, section “U.S. Regulatory Framework”. The dollar thresholds are as stated in Schweser. GARP: the GARP text in the project has no matching section (the Stowell and Stowell chapter assigned to this reading is not in the file); content from Schweser, a condensed source whose wording may compress the original framing.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-9 c, where it is Q2 of 14.

a.reason: Schweser defines qualified purchasers as “individuals with more than \$5 million in investment assets”. Only P (6.2) and S (5.4) exceed 5.0.

b.reason: Treating “more than \$5 million” as “at least \$5 million” admits R (exactly 5.0): P, R, S = 3. Correct only if the threshold were “\$5 million or more”.

c.reason: Applying the \$5 million threshold to net worth instead of investment assets admits P (9.0), Q (7.5), R (5.5) and S (6.0) = 4. Correct only if the test were stated on net worth.

d.reason: Applying the Reg D accredited test: P, Q, R, S pass on net worth ≥ 2.5; T passes on income (400 and 410, expected to continue) = 5. This would be the answer if the fund relied on Section 3(c)(1) with fewer than 100 investors and was marketed under Reg D to accredited investors.

questions.question: The chief compliance officer of a U.S. hedge fund manager is presenting to newly hired analysts on how the firm’s next fund will be offered to investors under Regulation D (Reg D). Which of the following statements should she present as accurate?

options.text: The fund may advertise to the general public, provided that every investor ultimately admitted to the fund is accredited.
An individual qualifies as accredited with income of \$250,000 in the most recent year alone, whatever the outlook for the current year.
Rule 506 permits up to 35 accredited investors, alongside an unlimited number of nonaccredited investors.
An individual with a net worth of \$2.5 million qualifies as accredited even if his annual income is well below \$250,000.

questions.solution:
CCO presents to new hires on offering a fund under Regulation D: which statement is accurate?

**Concept and theory**

Hedge funds raise capital through private placements rather than public offerings. Regulation D is the rule set for those placements, and its central idea is that a fund that does not reach out to the general public, and that sells only to investors able to look after themselves, does not need the protections of a public offering. Three elements follow.

- No public advertising: hedge funds market themselves through private placements and “do not advertise to the general public”.
- Accredited investors only, defined (per Schweser) as an individual with a net worth of at least \$2.5 million **or** annual income of \$250,000 in each of the prior two years with a reasonable expectation of maintaining that level.
- Rule 506 relaxes this slightly: it permits up to 35 nonaccredited investors.

The two branches of the accredited definition are alternatives: either one is sufficient.

**Applying it to this question**

The deciding fact is the word “or” in the definition. A net worth of \$2.5 million satisfies the first branch, so income is irrelevant for that investor. Each of the other statements breaks a stated condition.

**Fragile fact.** Rule 506’s 35 is a cap on nonaccredited investors; the accredited definition is “net worth or two-year income”, not both.

**Reference**

**LO 91.c:** “Summarize different approaches taken by regulators to mitigate risks related to hedge funds.” Schweser Book 5, Reading 91, Module 91.2, section “U.S. Regulatory Framework”. (paragraph on Regulation D). Thresholds as stated in Schweser. questions.question:
A risk consultant is validating the 2026 business plan of a U.S. hedge fund manager that wants to keep its regulatory burden low. The plan contains four claims:

I. By keeping the number of funds it advises below 15, the manager can rely on the private adviser exemption and avoid registering with the SEC.

II. By keeping benefit plan investors at 22% of total fund assets, the funds avoid triggering ERISA requirements.

III. The funds could raise benefit plan participation to exactly 25% of total fund assets and still avoid triggering ERISA requirements.

IV. Once registered with the SEC, the manager’s required reports will go to both the SEC and the Financial Stability Oversight Council (FSOC).

Which of the claims are correct?

options.text: I and II only
II and IV only
II and III only
I, II and IV only

questions.solution:
Consultant validates four claims in a U.S. manager’s 2026 plan: private adviser exemption, ERISA 22% and 25%, reporting to SEC and FSOC.

**Concept and theory**

Two separate statutes reach the manager and the fund. The Investment Advisers Act of 1940 governs the manager. It used to contain the private adviser exemption: a manager advising fewer than 15 funds (Schweser’s 91.c wording) did not have to register, and many firms structured themselves to stay below that number. Title IV of the Dodd-Frank Act of 2010 (the Private Fund Investment Advisers Registration Act) eliminated the exemption, so the 15 threshold “is no longer relevant” and hedge fund managers must register with the SEC. Title IV also requires reports to both the SEC and the FSOC.

ERISA governs pension (benefit plan) money. Hedge funds avoid triggering ERISA’s requirements by keeping benefit plan participation to less than 25% of total fund assets.

| Rule | Before Dodd-Frank | Today (per source) |
|---|---|---|
| Private adviser exemption | Fewer than 15 avoids SEC registration | Eliminated by Title IV; register with SEC |
| ERISA | Benefit plans below 25% of assets | Same: below 25% of assets |
| Reporting | Not required | To the SEC and the FSOC |

**Applying it to this question**

I: relies on a pre-2010 rule; false. II: 22% \< 25%; true. III: 25% is not less than 25%; false. IV: Title IV mandates reports to both the SEC and the FSOC; true. Correct set: II and IV.

**Fragile fact.** ERISA: strictly less than 25% of total fund assets. Private adviser exemption: gone since Title IV. The “15” is a historical number only.

**Reference**

**LO 91.c:** “Summarize different approaches taken by regulators to mitigate risks related to hedge funds.” Schweser Book 5, Reading 91, Module 91.2, section “U.S. Regulatory Framework”. GARP note: GARP Chapter 11 (Predicting Fraud by Investment Managers), Form ADV Data, footnote 5, describes the pre-Dodd-Frank exemption (Section 203(b)(3)) as applying to firms with “fewer than 15 U.S. clients”; Schweser’s 91.c section says “fewer than 15 funds” and its 91.a section says “fewer than 15 clients”. This looks like a wording or version difference; the question does not turn on the unit.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-9 c, where it is Q4 of 14.

a.reason: Including I applies a rule that Title IV removed; excluding IV misses a true reporting duty. A would be right for a business plan written before Dodd-Frank (and with IV omitted).

b.reason: Schweser: Title IV “eliminates the private adviser exemption” and “mandates that hedge funds submit reports to both the SEC and the Financial Stability Oversight Council”; and hedge funds avoid ERISA “by limiting benefit plan participation to less than 25% of total fund assets”.

c.reason: III treats “less than 25%” as “25% or less”. At exactly 25% the limit is breached. C would be right if the plan capped participation at, say, 24% and IV were false.

d.reason: Adds the stale claim I to the two true claims. D would be right only under a hypothetical regime that kept the private adviser exemption while also imposing reporting to the SEC and the FSOC; under the actual post-Title IV regime, claim I is false.

questions.question:
A regulatory reporting analyst at a multi-manager platform is planning next year’s Form PF calendar for five affiliated advisers, all registered with the SEC. AUM figures are private fund assets under management; Charlie reports in euros, and the platform uses USD 1.10 per EUR for threshold tests.

| Adviser | Reporting currency | AUM (millions) | Gross leverage (x) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Alpha | USD | 150 | 1.4 |
| Bravo | USD | 1500 | 3.8 |
| Charlie | EUR | 1400 | 2.2 |
| Delta | USD | 2300 | 6.5 |
| Echo | USD | 620 | 1.1 |

Assuming AUM stays at these levels for the year, how many Form PF filings will the five advisers make in total over the year?
questions.solution:
Reporting analyst counts total annual Form PF filings for five advisers with AUM of \$150m, \$1,500m, EUR 1,400m, \$2,300m and \$620m.

**Concept and theory**

Title IV of Dodd-Frank requires hedge funds to report to the SEC and the FSOC so that regulators can monitor AUM, leverage, counterparty exposures and investment strategies. It also introduced Form PF, which requires detailed operational and portfolio information. The source sets two filing frequencies, tied to AUM:

$\text{Filing frequency} = \begin{cases} \text{annual (1 filing per year)} & \text{if \textdollar 150m} \le \text{AUM} \le \text{\textdollar 1.5bn} \\ \text{quarterly (4 filings per year)} & \text{if AUM} > \text{\textdollar 1.5bn} \end{cases}$

“At least \$150 million” includes \$150 million; “more than \$1.5 billion” excludes \$1.5 billion.

**Applying it to this question**

Convert Charlie first: $\text{AUM}_{\text{USD}} =$ 1,400 × 1.10 = 1,540 (USD million).

Alpha: 150 ≥ 150, 150 ̸> 1,500 $\Rightarrow\text{annual} =$ 1

Bravo: 1,500 ̸> 1,500 $\Rightarrow\text{annual} =$ 1

Charlie: 1,540 > 1,500 $\Rightarrow\text{quarterly} =$ 4

Delta: 2,300 > 1,500 $\Rightarrow\text{quarterly} =$ 4

Echo: 620 $\Rightarrow\text{annual} =$ 1

Total = 1 + 1 + 4 + 4 + 1 = 11

The leverage column is irrelevant: frequency depends on AUM only. The result means the platform must plan eleven submissions: two advisers on a quarterly cycle and three on an annual cycle.

**Fragile fact.** Annual at at least \$150 million (inclusive); quarterly at more than \$1.5 billion (exclusive). Convert foreign-currency AUM before testing.

**Reference**

**LO 91.c:** “Summarize different approaches taken by regulators to mitigate risks related to hedge funds.” Schweser Book 5, Reading 91, Module 91.2, section “U.S. Regulatory Framework”. (paragraph on Title IV and Form PF). questions.question: A newly appointed member of the board of a U.S. hedge fund management firm asks the firm’s general counsel to explain what Title IV of the Dodd-Frank Act (the Private Fund Investment Advisers Registration Act) changed. Which of the following statements by the general counsel is most accurate?

options.text: Title IV raised the private adviser exemption threshold from 15 to 100, so most small managers remain exempt from SEC registration.
Title IV requires hedge funds to report to the FSOC, which replaces the SEC as the primary regulator of registered hedge fund advisers.
Title IV’s reporting requirements allow regulators to monitor hedge funds’ AUM, leverage, counterparty exposures and investment strategies.
Title IV requires hedge funds to register under the Investment Company Act of 1940, ending their reliance on Sections 3(c)(1) and 3(c)(7).

General counsel explains to a new board member what Title IV of Dodd-Frank changed.

**Concept and theory**

Dodd-Frank followed the Madoff fraud and the GFC, both of which renewed scrutiny of hedge funds. Its Title IV, the Private Fund Investment Advisers Registration Act, works on the manager, not the fund vehicle:

- it eliminates the private adviser exemption from the Advisers Act, so the former 15 threshold is no longer relevant and hedge fund managers must register with the SEC;
- it requires hedge funds to submit reports to both the SEC and the FSOC, so regulators can monitor AUM, leverage, counterparty exposures and investment strategies;
- it introduces Form PF (annual from \$150 million AUM, quarterly above \$1.5 billion).

The fund-level exemptions from the ’40 Act (3(c)(1), 3(c)(7)) are a separate layer. The source presents them as the current route by which hedge funds avoid ’40 Act limits; Title IV is not described as touching them.

**Applying it to this question**

The board member asked what Title IV changed. The deciding fact is the purpose of Title IV’s reporting: visibility of AUM, leverage, counterparty exposures and strategies. Each wrong statement misstates a threshold, an actor or the layer of regulation.

**Fragile fact.** Title IV acts on the adviser (SEC registration under the Advisers Act) and sends reports to two bodies, the SEC and the FSOC. The fund’s ’40 Act exemptions remain.

**Reference**

**LO 91.c:** “Summarize different approaches taken by regulators to mitigate risks related to hedge funds.” Schweser Book 5, Reading 91, Module 91.2, section “U.S. Regulatory Framework”. Key Concepts, LO 91.c. **Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-9 c, where it is Q6 of 14.

a.reason: **Polarity flip, with a sibling number.** Title IV did not raise the threshold; it eliminated the exemption altogether. The figure 100 is borrowed from Section 3(c)(1). A would describe a hypothetical law that loosened, rather than removed, the exemption.

b.reason: **Role misassignment.** Reports go to both the SEC and the FSOC; managers register with the SEC. Nothing in the source makes the FSOC the primary regulator. B would be right only if the stem described a regime in which the SEC handed supervision to the FSOC.

**Concept and theory**

Schweser describes U.S. regulatory interest in hedge funds as coming “in waves”. The pattern is an attempt at regulation, a retreat toward self-regulation, then a crisis-driven return:

| Year | Event |
|---|---|

| 2006 | A federal court overturns the rule; the SEC has not since mandated registration by its own rule |
| 2007 | President’s Working Group on Financial Markets rejects broad new regulation and encourages voluntary industry guidelines |
| 2008 to 2009 | Madoff fraud and GFC turmoil renew scrutiny |
| 2010 | Dodd-Frank brings hedge funds within its scope (Title IV) |

questions.question: A supervisor at a national securities regulator is reviewing two case files. In Case 1, a hedge fund bought shares of a takeover target two days before the bid was announced, after a tip from an employee of the bidder’s adviser. In Case 2, a fund’s gross leverage rose from 4x to 9x over a quarter, and it was repeatedly late, and on one occasion inaccurate, in posting collateral to two prime brokers. Which of the following best describes how the regulator’s high-level concerns apply to these cases?

options.text: Case 1 raises market integrity, policed with the same rules and enforcement used across financial markets; Case 2 raises financial stability, addressed by limiting leverage and requiring timely, accurate collateral posting.

Case 1 raises investor protection, addressed by restricting participation to sophisticated investors; Case 2 raises financial stability, addressed by limiting leverage and requiring timely, accurate collateral posting.

Case 1 raises market integrity, policed with the same rules and enforcement used across financial markets; Case 2 raises investor protection, addressed by restricting participation to sophisticated investors.

Case 1 raises market integrity, policed under insider trading rules written specifically for hedge funds; Case 2 raises financial stability, addressed by limiting leverage and requiring timely, accurate collateral posting.

Regulator’s two case files: trading on a takeover tip, and a fund at 9x leverage posting collateral late and inaccurately.

**Concept and theory**

At a high level, regulators of hedge funds have three concerns, each with its own tool:

| Concern | Question it asks | Tool (per source) |
|---|---|---|
| Investor protection | Are hedge funds defrauding investors? | Restrict participation to investors presumed sophisticated enough to evaluate hedge fund risks |
| Market integrity | Are hedge funds trading on insider information? | The same rules and enforcement mechanisms applied across financial markets |
| Financial stability | Could hedge funds destabilize markets? | Limit leverage; require timely and accurate posting of collateral |

The design logic: fraud on investors is managed by controlling who invests; insider trading is not special to hedge funds, so general market rules apply; destabilization runs through leverage and collateral, so those are constrained.

**Applying it to this question**

Case 1 is trading ahead of a bid on a tip: insider information, so market integrity, policed by the general market rules. Case 2 combines rising leverage with late and inaccurate collateral: these are exactly the financial stability tools. The leverage figures (4x to 9x) only confirm the channel; no calculation is needed.

questions.question: A junior risk analyst at a Singapore pension fund is preparing an onboarding note for newly hired analysts that explains the legal form of a US hedge fund in which the pension fund holds SGD 180 million. The note must contain one statement about how the partnership is organized and how investors enter and leave it. Which of the following statements is most accurate?

options.text: The fund’s investors are admitted as the general partners, while the hedge fund manager is admitted as a limited partner of the partnership.
The partnership is usually closed-ended, so it does not issue new shares after launch, and investors exit only when the fund is wound up.
The partnership is usually open-ended, so it issues new shares to incoming investors and redeems leavers, subject to lockups and gates in the partnership agreement.
The partnership is usually open-ended, so investors may redeem at any time, and the partnership agreement cannot impose lockups or gates on redemptions.

questions.solution:
Onboarding note for a Singapore pension fund: which statement about the hedge fund partnership’s roles and investor entry and exit is most accurate?

**Concept and theory**

A hedge fund is typically formed as a limited partnership. A partnership has two classes of partner. The general partner (GP) runs the business; in a hedge fund that is the hedge fund manager, who makes the investment decisions and earns the fees. The limited partners (LPs) supply the capital; in a hedge fund those are the investors. Schweser’s key concepts add that the limited partnership structure provides liability protection and is designed to minimize regulatory oversight and taxation.

The second structural feature is that the partnership is usually open-ended. Unlike a vehicle with a fixed pool of capital, an open-ended partnership can keep taking in money and paying it out: it issues new shares to incoming investors and redeems the shares of investors who wish to exit. That flexibility is not unconditional. The partnership agreement can specify lockups and gates. (Schweser names them without defining them; in standard usage a lockup is a period after subscription during which an investor cannot redeem, and a gate limits how much can be redeemed at a redemption date.) So the correct description has three parts: open-ended, issue and redeem, and “subject to” the agreement’s lockups and gates.

| Feature | Typical hedge fund LP | Common confusion |
|---|---|---|
| General partner | Hedge fund manager | Investors |
| Limited partners | Investors | Manager |
| Capital | Open-ended: issue and redeem | Closed-ended: fixed until wind-up |
| Redemption limits | Lockups and gates per agreement | “Any time, no limits” |

**Applying it to this question**

The stem asks for one statement about two things: who is which partner, and how investors enter and leave. Only one option gets both the open-ended feature and its condition right. A and B fail on the first element (roles, then the open-ended feature). D gets the open-ended feature right but drops the condition that redemptions are subject to the partnership agreement’s lockups and gates.

**Fragile fact.** Manager = general partner, investors = limited partners; open-ended means the fund issues and redeems, but always subject to lockups and gates in the partnership agreement.

**Reference**

Where a hedge fund is legally domiciled is a deliberate design choice. Schweser says hedge funds choose their domicile strategically to minimize taxes and reduce regulatory oversight. |---|---|
| Fund | Taxes can be reduced |
| Manager (fees) | Still taxed on fees earned |
| Investor (gains) | Still taxed in home jurisdiction |

**Concept and theory**

A master-feeder structure separates where money is invested from where investors enter. The master fund is where all capital is pooled and all trading activity occurs. It is funded by several feeder vehicles, each designed for a different group of investors. Typically there is one feeder for onshore investors and one for offshore investors; for a US-domiciled fund, the offshore feeder is generally used for non-US investors and for US tax-exempt investors such as pension funds.

Why build it? Schweser gives the motive directly: the structure is used to avoid multiple layers of taxation and to allow tax-exempt investors to participate in a tax-efficient manner. A useful analogy is a single kitchen (the master) serving several dining rooms (the feeders): the cooking happens once, in one place, but each group of guests comes in through the door that suits it.

| Component | Role |
|---|---|
| Master fund | Pools all capital; all trading occurs here |
| Onshore feeder | Entry vehicle for onshore investors |
| Offshore feeder | Non-US investors and US tax-exempt investors |
| Motive | Avoid multiple layers of tax; tax-efficient access for tax-exempts |

questions.question: A senior risk analyst at an Australian investment consultant is drafting a report for a superannuation fund client (AUD 2.4 billion in alternatives) on why US hedge fund managers organize their funds as limited partnerships. The manager under review charges a 2% management fee and a 20% performance fee. Which of the following statements should the analyst include as the most accurate description of the manager’s tax motivation?

options.text: The performance fee, as carried interest, may be taxed at the capital gains rate if the assets that generated the gains were held for at least one year, while the management fee is taxed as ordinary income.
The management fee may be taxed at the capital gains rate if the assets that generated the gains were held for at least one year, while the performance fee is taxed as ordinary income.
The performance fee, as carried interest, is taxed at the capital gains rate whatever the holding period of the assets that generated the gains, while the management fee is taxed as ordinary income.

The performance fee, as carried interest, may be taxed at the capital gains rate if the investors have held their partnership interests for at least one year, while the management fee is taxed as ordinary income.

questions.solution:
Report for a superannuation client: the tax motivation behind the limited partnership for a 2-and-20 manager.

**Concept and theory**

The main tax incentive for the partnership structure sits in how the manager’s two fees are taxed. Under the typical 2-and-20 model the manager charges:

- a **2% management fee** on assets, which is taxed as ordinary income;
- a **20% performance fee** on gains, also known as carried interest, which may be taxed at the lower capital gains rate if the underlying assets that generated the gains were held for at least one year.

This “carried interest loophole” lets performance fees be taxed as capital gains rather than ordinary income; Schweser says this reduces the manager’s tax liability by roughly half. Note the two conditions: it applies to the performance fee only, and the holding-period test is on the underlying assets, not on anyone’s partnership interest.

| Fee | Tax treatment | Condition |
|---|---|---|
| Management fee (2%) | Ordinary income | None |
| Performance fee (20%) | May be capital gains rate | Underlying assets held at least one year |

**Applying it to this question**

All four options assign some fee to capital gains treatment under some condition. Check three things in each: which fee, which tax rate, and whose holding period. Only A has the performance fee, the capital gains rate, and the underlying assets’ holding period of at least one year. The AUD 2.4 billion figure is irrelevant.

**Fragile fact.** Carried interest = the performance fee; the one-year test is on the underlying assets that generated the gains, not on the investors.

**Reference**

LO 91.d (Schweser, verbatim): “Describe a typical organizational structure for a hedge fund and explain motivations for adopting this structure.” Schweser Reading 91, Module 91.2, section “Hedge Fund Organizational Structure”, subsection “Tax Motivations and Regulatory Considerations” (first paragraph) and Key Concepts LO 91.d. GARP: the GARP text in the project has no matching section (the 2025 GARP file does not contain this reading); content from Schweser, a condensed source whose wording may compress GARP’s framing. No GARP vs Schweser conflict could arise.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-9 d, where it is Q5 of 10.

a.reason: Schweser: “Management fees are taxed as ordinary income, while performance fees, also known as carried interest, may be taxed at the lower capital gains rate if the underlying assets that generated the gains were held for at least one year.” A restates this.

b.reason: **Sibling swap.** B moves capital gains treatment to the management fee and ordinary income to the performance fee, reversing the two fees. B would be correct in a stem that asked which statement inverts the treatment of the two fees.

c.reason: **Scope or condition error.** C keeps the right fee and rate but drops the holding-period condition (“whatever the holding period”). The source says the performance fee may be taxed at the capital gains rate if the underlying assets were held for at least one year; gains on positions held for less do not qualify. C would be correct only if every gain came from positions held at least one year.

d.reason: **Role misassignment.** D has the right condition length (one year) but applies it to the wrong actor: the investors’ holding of partnership interests. The test is on the underlying assets the fund held. D would be right only in a stem about the investors’ own capital gains on their interests, which is not what this reading describes.

questions.question:
A risk consultant at a São Paulo advisory firm is reviewing the subscription plan for a US-domiciled hedge fund that uses a master-feeder structure with a Delaware onshore feeder and a Cayman Islands offshore feeder. Four prospective investors are listed below.

|  | Investor | Commitment (BRL million) |
|---|---|---|
| I | US private university endowment (US tax-exempt) | 150 |
| II | Brazilian family office (non-US investor) | 90 |
| III | US-resident taxable individual | 25 |
| IV | US corporate pension plan (US tax-exempt) | 210 |

Which of the investors would typically enter the fund through the offshore feeder?

options.text: II only
I, II, III and IV
I, II and IV only
III only

questions.solution:
São Paulo consultant allocating four prospective investors between onshore and offshore feeders of a US-domiciled master-feeder fund.

**Concept and theory**

In a master-feeder structure the feeders exist because different investor groups need different entry vehicles to participate tax-efficiently; all of them end up in the same master fund, where the trading happens. Schweser states the typical allocation for a US-domiciled hedge fund: one feeder for onshore investors and another for offshore investors, with the offshore feeder generally used for non-US investors and for US tax-exempt investors, such as pension funds. By elimination, the onshore feeder is the vehicle for the remaining group, US taxable investors.

The non-obvious part is that being a US investor does not by itself put you in the onshore feeder. Tax status matters: a US tax-exempt investor goes offshore, because the structure is designed to allow tax-exempt investors to participate in a tax-efficient manner.

| Investor type (US-domiciled fund) | Typical feeder |
|---|---|
| US taxable (individuals, etc.) | Onshore feeder |
| Non-US investors | Offshore feeder |
| US tax-exempt (pension funds, etc.) | Offshore feeder |

**Applying it to this question**

Classify each investor by the two tests (US or non-US; taxable or tax-exempt):

- I, US university endowment: US tax-exempt, so offshore feeder.
- II, Brazilian family office: non-US, so offshore feeder.
- III, US-resident taxable individual: US taxable, so onshore feeder.
- IV, US corporate pension plan: US tax-exempt (the source’s own example is pension funds), so offshore feeder.

Offshore feeder: I, II and IV. The commitment sizes in BRL are irrelevant inputs; feeder choice depends on tax status and residence, not on ticket size.

**Fragile fact.** US-domiciled fund: offshore feeder = non-US investors plus US tax-exempt investors (pensions, endowments); only US taxable investors go onshore.

**Reference**

LO 91.d (Schweser, verbatim): “Describe a typical organizational structure for a hedge fund and explain motivations for adopting this structure.” Schweser Reading 91, Module 91.2, section “Hedge Fund Organizational Structure”, subsection “Organizational and Structural Design” (third paragraph). Classifying a university endowment as US tax-exempt is an application of the source’s category (its example is pension funds). GARP: the GARP text in the project has no matching section (the 2025 GARP file does not contain this reading); content from Schweser, a condensed source whose wording may compress GARP’s framing. No GARP vs Schweser conflict could arise.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-9 d, where it is Q6 of 10.

a.reason: A applies the intuitive rule “offshore means foreign” and drops the second group the source names, US tax-exempt investors. It would be correct only if I and IV were taxable US investors.

b.reason: B assumes every investor benefits from the offshore feeder, ignoring that the structure provides one feeder for onshore investors. A US taxable individual uses the onshore feeder. B would be correct only if investor III were non-US or tax-exempt.

c.reason: Schweser: “For a U.S.-domiciled hedge fund, the offshore feeder is generally used for non-U.S. investors and for U.S. tax-exempt investors, such as pension funds.” I and IV are US tax-exempt and II is non-US, giving I, II and IV only.

d.reason: D reverses the mapping, sending the US taxable investor offshore and everyone else onshore. It would be the correct answer to the opposite question, “which investors would typically enter through the onshore feeder?”

questions.question: A member of the board risk committee of a Chinese asset manager is reviewing a CNY-denominated mandate with a US hedge fund manager. The manager’s tax-planning memo includes four statements about the history of the tax rules on hedge fund fees, and the committee member must identify the one that can be relied on. Which of the following statements is most accurate?

options.text: In 2008 the carried interest loophole was closed, while managers retain the Section 457 option to defer receipt of management fees to a later tax year.
The Section 457 deferral of management fees was eliminated in 2008, and attempts to end carried interest treatment failed in 2008 and 2021, so it remains in place but could change.
Managers may still defer receipt of management fees to a later tax year under Section 457, and attempts to end carried interest treatment failed in 2008 and 2021.
The Section 457 deferral of management fees was eliminated in 2008, and because carried interest treatment survived repeal attempts in 2008 and 2021, it is now permanently secured.

questions.solution:
Board risk committee member checking a US manager’s memo on the history of Section 457 deferral and carried interest reform.

**Concept and theory**

Two separate tax features have helped managers, and they have had different fates.

Deferral of management fees (Section 457). Before 2008, hedge fund managers could defer tax on their management fees: under Internal Revenue Code Section 457 they could choose to postpone receiving these fees until a later tax year and so manage the timing of their tax obligations. This loophole was eliminated in 2008.

Carried interest. The performance fee may be taxed at the capital gains rate (if the underlying assets were held at least one year). Attempts to eliminate this loophole failed, once in 2008 and again in 2021 under the Biden Administration. For now it remains in place, but it could change in the future, which is why managers continue to monitor it closely.

| Feature | 2008 | Status now |
|---|---|---|
| Section 457 deferral of management fees | Eliminated | Not available |
| Carried interest treatment | Repeal attempt failed (again in 2021) | In place, could change |

**Applying it to this question**

Each option makes two claims: one on Section 457 and one on carried interest. The correct option needs Section 457 eliminated in 2008 and carried interest surviving but not guaranteed. Tick each half: A fails both halves (swapped), C fails the Section 457 half, D fails the “could change” half, B passes both. The CNY mandate is context only.

**Fragile fact.** 2008: Section 457 deferral ended, carried interest repeal failed; 2021: carried interest repeal failed again; carried interest stands but is not guaranteed.

**Reference**

LO 91.d (Schweser, verbatim): “Describe a typical organizational structure for a hedge fund and explain motivations for adopting this structure.” Schweser Reading 91, Module 91.2, section “Hedge Fund Organizational Structure”, subsection “Tax Motivations and Regulatory Considerations” (second and third paragraphs). GARP: the GARP text in the project has no matching section (the 2025 GARP file does not contain this reading); content from Schweser, a condensed source whose wording may compress GARP’s framing. No GARP vs Schweser conflict could arise.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-9 d, where it is Q7 of 10.

a.reason: **Sibling swap.** A swaps the fates of the two features: it says carried interest treatment was closed in 2008 and that Section 457 deferral survives. Both facts are attributed to the wrong sibling. A would be correct only in a world where the 2008 reform had targeted carried interest instead of deferral.

b.reason: Schweser: the Section 457 deferral “loophole was eliminated in 2008”; attempts to eliminate the carried interest loophole failed in 2008 and in 2021, and “the carried interest provision remains in place, but it could change in the future.” B matches both halves.

c.reason: **Polarity flip.** C gets the carried interest half right but reverses the Section 457 outcome, saying deferral is still available when it was eliminated in 2008. C would have been accurate before 2008.

d.reason: **Absolute claim.** D gets both histories right but converts “remains in place” into “permanently secured”. The source says it could change in the future and that managers monitor it closely. D would be correct only if the stem asked about the current status without the word “permanently”.

questions.question:
A portfolio manager at a fund of hedge funds is estimating the tax bill of a US manager that runs a hedge fund organized as a limited partnership, using the data below for the past year.

| Item | Value |
|---|---|
| Average assets under management | USD 800 million |
| Management fee | 2% of average AUM |
| Performance fee | 20% of the fund’s gains |
| Gains from positions held at least one year | USD 90 million |
| Gains from positions held less than one year | USD 60 million |
| Fund domicile | Cayman Islands |
| Number of limited partners | 240 |
| Manager’s ordinary income tax rate | 37% |
| Manager’s capital gains tax rate | 20% |

Assuming the fee taxation described for the typical hedge fund partnership applies, the manager’s total tax on the year’s fees is closest to:

options.text: USD 11.92 million
USD 8.04 million
USD 17.02 million
USD 13.96 million

questions.solution:
Fund of funds PM estimating a US manager’s tax on 2-and-20 fees when part of the gains come from positions held less than one year.

**Concept and theory**

The manager’s two fees are taxed differently. The management fee is ordinary income. The performance fee (carried interest) may be taxed at the capital gains rate only if the underlying assets that generated the gains were held for at least one year; the portion of the performance fee that comes from gains on positions held for less than a year does not meet the source’s condition for the capital gains rate, so it is taxed at the ordinary income rate, the only other rate in the stem. With symbols:

$\text{T} = \underbrace{\text{m A t}_{\text{o}}}_{\text{management fee}} + \underbrace{\text{p G}_{\ge 1}\,\text{t}_{\text{cg}}}_{\text{carry, long-held}} + \underbrace{\text{p G}_{<1}\,\text{t}_{\text{o}}}_{\text{carry, short-held}}$

where m is the management fee rate, A average AUM, p the performance fee rate, $\text{G}_{\ge 1}$ and $\text{G}_{<1}$ the gains from positions held at least one year and less than one year, $\text{t}_{\text{o}}$ the ordinary income rate and $\text{t}_{\text{cg}}$ the capital gains rate. The fund’s offshore domicile does not change the manager’s tax: Schweser states that managers still pay taxes on the fees they earn.

**Applying it to this question**

All amounts in USD million.

Management fee = 0.02 × 800 = 16.00

Tax on management fee = 16.00 × 0.37 = 5.92

Performance fee, long-held gains = 0.20 × 90 = 18.00

Tax on long-held carry = 18.00 × 0.20 = 3.60

Performance fee, short-held gains = 0.20 × 60 = 12.00

Tax on short-held carry = 12.00 × 0.37 = 4.44

Total tax T = 5.92 + 3.60 + 4.44 = 13.96

Meaning: the manager pays about USD 13.96 million on USD 46 million of fees, an average rate of about 30.3%. Taxing everything as ordinary income would cost USD 17.02 million, so carried interest treatment saves about USD 3.06 million here, and only on the long-held portion. The Cayman domicile and the 240 limited partners are irrelevant inputs.

**Fragile fact.** Only the slice of the performance fee earned on assets held at least one year gets the capital gains rate; the management fee never does, and the fund’s offshore domicile does not shelter the manager’s fees.

**Reference**

LO 91.d (Schweser, verbatim): “Describe a typical organizational structure for a hedge fund and explain motivations for adopting this structure.” Schweser Reading 91, Module 91.2, section “Hedge Fund Organizational Structure”, subsection “Tax Motivations and Regulatory Considerations” (first paragraph) and “Organizational and Structural Design” (first paragraph, manager still taxed on fees). The tax rates are stem inputs, not source facts. GARP: the GARP text in the project has no matching section (the 2025 GARP file does not contain this reading); content from Schweser, a condensed source whose wording may compress GARP’s framing. No GARP vs Schweser conflict could arise.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-9 d, where it is Q8 of 10.

a.reason: Taxes the whole performance fee at the capital gains rate, ignoring the one-year holding test: 5.92 + 30 × 0.20 = 5.92 + 6.00 = 11.92. It would be correct if all USD 150 million of gains had come from positions held at least one year.

b.reason: Stops after taxing the performance fee: 3.60 + 4.44 = 8.04, leaving out the tax on the management fee. It would answer “what is the tax on the performance fee alone?”

c.reason: Taxes all fees as ordinary income: (16 + 30) × 0.37 = 17.02. It would be correct if the carried interest provision were repealed, or if none of the gains came from positions held at least one year.

d.reason: Applying Schweser’s rule (management fees as ordinary income; performance fees at the capital gains rate only where the underlying assets were held at least one year) gives USD 13.96 million.

questions.question:
A treasury analyst at a German bank that lends to hedge funds is preparing a report for the credit committee (current exposure EUR 1.1 billion) on where hedge funds are domiciled and why. The analyst drafts four statements:

I. Hedge funds choose their domicile strategically to minimize taxes and reduce regulatory oversight.

II. In the United States, Delaware is a common choice of domicile because of its favorable legal environment.

III. The Cayman Islands is the domicile of more than half of offshore hedge funds.

IV. Bermuda is the domicile of a larger share of offshore hedge funds than the British Virgin Islands.

Which of the statements are correct?

options.text: I and II only
I, II and III only
I, III and IV only
II, III and IV only

questions.solution:
German bank credit report: which of four statements on hedge fund domicile motives and offshore domicile shares are correct?

**Concept and theory**

Schweser opens the organizational structure section with domicile. Hedge funds strategically choose their domicile to minimize taxes and reduce regulatory oversight. In the United States, Delaware is a common choice because of its favorable legal environment. Offshore funds are most frequently located in:

| Offshore domicile | Share of offshore funds (%) |
|---|---|
| Cayman Islands | 55 |
| British Virgin Islands | 15 |
| Bermuda | 10 |

The ranking (Cayman, then BVI, then Bermuda) and the fact that Cayman alone is more than half are the facts most likely to be tested. Domicile reduces fund-level tax only; managers and investors are still taxed (see Q2).

**Applying it to this question**

- I: true; both motives (minimize taxes, reduce regulatory oversight) are stated in the source.
- II: true; Delaware, favorable legal environment.
- III: true; 55% is more than half.
- IV: false; Bermuda (10%) hosts a smaller share than the BVI (15%).

Correct set: I, II and III only. The EUR 1.1 billion exposure is irrelevant.

**Fragile fact.** Offshore order: Cayman 55% > BVI 15% > Bermuda 10%; onshore US: Delaware. Motive: minimize taxes and reduce regulatory oversight.

**Reference**

LO 91.d (Schweser, verbatim): “Describe a typical organizational structure for a hedge fund and explain motivations for adopting this structure.” Schweser Reading 91, Module 91.2, section “Hedge Fund Organizational Structure”, subsection “Organizational and Structural Design” (first paragraph). GARP: the GARP text in the project has no matching section (the 2025 GARP file does not contain this reading); content from Schweser, a condensed source whose wording may compress GARP’s framing. No GARP vs Schweser conflict could arise.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-9 d, where it is Q9 of 10.

a.reason: Rejects III, i.e. treats the Cayman share as half or less. The source gives 55%. A would be right if statement III had said “more than two-thirds”.

b.reason: Schweser: “Hedge funds strategically choose their domicile to minimize taxes and reduce regulatory oversight. In the United States, Delaware is a common choice because of its favorable legal environment. Offshore funds are most frequently located in the Cayman Islands (55%), the British Virgin Islands (15%), and Bermuda (10%).” Statements I to III follow; IV contradicts the figures.

c.reason: Accepts IV, which swaps the ranks of the two smaller siblings (Bermuda 10% placed above BVI 15%), and rejects II, the onshore Delaware fact. C would be right only if IV read “the BVI hosts a larger share than Bermuda” and II were false.

d.reason: Rejects I, i.e. treats the tax and oversight motive as wrong, which is the motivation the LO asks you to explain, and accepts the ranking swap in IV. D would be right only if domicile were chosen for reasons other than tax and oversight and Bermuda outranked the BVI.

questions.question: A risk consultant is advising two former bank traders who are launching a USD-denominated hedge fund and who ask why the limited partnership is the typical legal form. Which of the following statements best explains the structure and the motivations for adopting it?

options.text: The manager acts as general partner and investors as limited partners; the form provides liability protection and is designed to minimize regulatory oversight and taxation, notably through carried interest treatment of the performance fee.

The manager acts as general partner and investors as limited partners; the form provides liability protection and is designed to accept fuller regulatory oversight in return for carried interest treatment of the performance fee.

Investors act as general partners and the manager as limited partner; the form provides liability protection and is designed to minimize regulatory oversight and taxation, notably through carried interest treatment of the performance fee.

The manager acts as general partner and investors as limited partners; the form provides liability protection and is designed to minimize regulatory oversight and taxation, notably through capital gains treatment of the management fee.

questions.solution:
Consultant explaining to two founding traders why the limited partnership is the typical legal form and what motivates it.

**Concept and theory**

This question integrates the two halves of the LO: describe the structure and explain the motivations. Structure. The legal entity is typically a limited partnership: the hedge fund manager is the general partner and the investors are the limited partners, organized as an open-ended partnership.

The main tax motive is carried interest: management fees are taxed as ordinary income, while performance fees (carried interest) may be taxed at the lower capital gains rate if the underlying assets that generated the gains were held for at least one year, which roughly halves the manager’s tax liability on that income. Schweser calls this a strong tax incentive for managers to adopt the partnership structure.

| Element | Typical hedge fund limited partnership |
|---|---|
| General partner | Manager |
| Limited partners | Investors |
| Protection | Liability protection |
| Design aim | Minimize regulatory oversight and taxation |
| Main tax lever | Capital gains rate on carried interest (performance fee) |

**Applying it to this question**

Each option has three slots: the partner roles, the design aim (direction on regulatory oversight and taxation), and which fee gets favorable treatment. A correct answer must have manager = GP, “minimize” oversight and tax, and the performance fee as the carried interest lever. Only A fills all three slots correctly; each other option corrupts exactly one slot.

**Fragile fact.** Design direction: the partnership minimizes (not accepts) regulatory oversight and taxation; the tax lever is the performance fee, and the manager is the general partner.

LO 91.d (Schweser, verbatim): “Describe a typical organizational structure for a hedge fund and explain motivations for adopting this structure.” Schweser Reading 91, Module 91.2, section “Hedge Fund Organizational Structure”, subsections “Organizational and Structural Design” (second paragraph) and “Tax Motivations and Regulatory Considerations” (first paragraph), and Key Concepts LO 91.d. GARP: the GARP text in the project has no matching section (the 2025 GARP file does not contain this reading); content from Schweser, a condensed source whose wording may compress GARP’s framing. No GARP vs Schweser conflict could arise.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-9 d, where it is Q10 of 10.

The main text places the manager as general partner and investors as limited partners. A combines these facts.

questions.question: A junior risk analyst at a Canadian public pension plan is preparing an orientation slide for newly hired analysts who will monitor the plan’s CAD 2.4 billion private credit allocation. The slide must define private credit and summarise how the market has mainly operated over the past three decades. Which of the following statements is the most accurate to include on the slide?

options.text: Private credit is corporate credit arranged through bilateral agreements by commercial banks and nonbank lenders alike; it has mainly involved closed-end funds, financed by institutional investors, lending to middle-market companies.
Private credit is nonbank corporate credit arranged through bilateral agreements; it has mainly involved closed-end funds, financed by institutional investors, lending to middle-market companies.
Private credit is nonbank corporate credit arranged through bilateral agreements; it has mainly involved open-ended funds, financed by institutional investors, lending to middle-market companies.

Private credit is nonbank corporate credit arranged through bilateral agreements; it has mainly involved closed-end funds, financed by institutional investors, lending to companies that issue public bonds.

questions.solution:
Pension plan analyst writes an orientation slide defining private credit and its three-decade operating model.

**Concept and theory**

Private credit is defined by who lends and how. The lender is not a commercial bank, and the instrument is not a public security; the loan is a bilateral agreement between a nonbank lender and a company. Schweser’s definition is precise: private credit is “nonbank corporate credit from bilateral agreements, excluding public securities and commercial banks”.

Why does the market exist? Some companies fall into a gap. They need more money than a single commercial bank can reasonably lend, yet they are too small to raise funds in a public offering. For about three decades this gap was filled by one dominant model:

| Element | Typical arrangement (past three decades) |
|---|---|
| Who supplies the money | Institutional investors |
| Vehicle | Closed-end fund, raised and managed by an asset manager |
| Who lends | The asset manager, directly to the borrower |
| Who borrows | Middle-market companies (annual revenue about USD 100 million to USD 1 billion) |

Two exclusions do the work in the definition: commercial bank lending (even if bilateral) is not private credit, and public securities (even if issued by a middle-market company) are not private credit.

**Applying it to this question**

Each option has two clauses: a definition and a description of the operating model. Check each clause against the source. Option B keeps the definition intact (nonbank, bilateral) and the model intact (closed-end, institutional money, middle-market borrowers). Every other option corrupts exactly one element: the lender set (A), the vehicle (C) or the borrower segment (D). The CAD 2.4 billion allocation size is irrelevant context.

**Fragile fact.** The definition excludes two things: public securities and commercial banks. Bilateral is necessary but not sufficient; the lender must be nonbank.

**Reference**

**LO 92.a (Schweser, verbatim):** Describe characteristics of private credit, including its typical investors and borrowers, and compare private credit to other types of loans and fixed-income instruments.

**Schweser:** Reading 92, Module 92.1, Private Credit Characteristics (opening paragraphs under LO 92.a); Key Concepts LO 92.a.

**GARP:** the assigned reading is the IMF Global Financial Stability Report (April 2024), Chapter 2, “The Rise and Risks of Private Credit”. The GARP text in the project has no matching section; content is from Schweser, a condensed source whose wording may compress the original framing. No GARP versus Schweser conflict can therefore be checked.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-10 a, where it is Q1 of 10.

a.reason: **Scope error: overextends the definition.** It brings commercial banks inside the definition. The source explicitly excludes commercial banks; a bilateral loan from a bank is a traditional bank loan, the very alternative private credit is compared with. A would be correct only if the stem asked for a definition of bilateral corporate lending in general.

b.reason: Schweser, Module 92.1: private credit is “nonbank corporate credit from bilateral agreements, excluding public securities and commercial banks”, and for the past three decades it “mainly consisted of asset managers obtaining funding from institutional investors through a closed-end fund structure and then using those funds to lend to middle-market companies”. Option B restates both sentences without alteration.

c.reason: **Sibling swap: open-ended for closed-end.** The vehicle is swapped with its sibling. The investment committee has asked for the one company that best fits the niche that private credit has traditionally served. The analyst has compiled the following data.

| Company | Sector | Revenue (USD m) | Need exceeds what one bank can provide? | Large enough for a public offering? | EBITDA margin (%) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Pelham | IT services | 60 | No | No | 18.5 |
| Quarry | Logistics | 450 | No | No | 9.0 |
| Ravel | Healthcare | 4800 | Yes | Yes | 21.0 |
| Selwyn | Industrials | 720 | Yes | No | 7.5 |

Which company is the best fit for the traditional private credit niche?

options.text: Pelham
Quarry
Ravel
Selwyn

questions.solution:
Singapore asset manager screens four borrowers to find the best fit for the traditional private credit niche.

**Concept and theory**

Private credit “services a niche market” defined by three conditions that must all hold together:

1. Size: mid-sized companies, annual revenue between USD 100 million and USD 1 billion.
2. Too big for one bank: borrowing requirements exceed what most single commercial banks can reasonably provide.
3. Too small for public markets: not sufficiently large to raise funds through a public offering.

The logic is a gap argument. A company whose need fits inside one bank’s appetite will normally borrow from the bank (cheaper, since private credit’s total cost is most likely higher). A company large enough for a public offering can use the public bond market or syndicated loans. The private credit lender earns its place only where neither alternative works.

**Applying it to this question**

Apply the three conditions as a filter, row by row:

| Company | Revenue in band? | Need above one bank? | Too small for public offering? | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Pelham | No (60) | No | Yes | Below the band; a bank can serve it |
| Quarry | Yes (450) | No | Yes | A single bank can serve it |
| Ravel | No (4,800) | Yes | No | Public markets available |
| Selwyn | Yes (720) | Yes | Yes | All three conditions met |

I. The total cost of the private credit loan is likely to be higher than that of the bank loan.

II. The private credit lender is more likely to agree to customised terms, such as deferred interest payments.

III. The private credit loan is likely to carry fewer covenants than the bank loan, because the lender relies on its relationship with the company instead.

IV. Private credit covenants such as limits on dividend distributions and share buybacks exist mainly to protect the company’s shareholders.

Which of the statements are accurate?

options.text: I and II only
I, II, and III only
II only
I, II, and IV only

questions.solution:
Australian treasurer compares a private credit loan with a bank term loan on cost, customisation and covenants.

**Concept and theory**

A private credit loan is negotiated directly between the lender (an asset manager) and the borrower. That directness drives three differences from a traditional bank loan:

| Feature | Private credit | Traditional bank loan |
|---|---|---|
| Total cost (e.g. interest) | Most likely greater | Lower |
| Customisation | Much greater (e.g. deferred interest payments) | Less customised |
| Covenants | Greater use, to protect lenders (limits on dividends, buybacks, asset sales) | Fewer |

The intuition: the borrower pays more, and in exchange gets terms shaped around its business. The lender, taking on a riskier borrower, protects itself with collateral and covenants that stop cash leaving the company (dividends, buybacks) or assets being sold out from under the loan.

- II: customised terms such as deferred interest. Matches the source example. Accurate.

- IV: covenants protect shareholders. The source says covenants protect lenders. Inaccurate.

| Loan | Lender(s) | Borrower | Size (CNY bn) |
|---|---|---|---|
| X | One asset manager, under a bilateral agreement | Mid-sized, private equity-backed software firm; weak earnings | 1.2 |
| Y | A group of 14 lenders, because the amount is too high for one lender | Investment-grade utility with moderate leverage | 18.0 |
| Z | A group of 9 lenders, because the amount and risk are too high for one lender | Highly leveraged retailer, rated noninvestment grade, paying a high interest rate | 6.5 |

Which of the following classifications is the most accurate?

options.text: X: private credit; Y: leveraged loan; Z: broadly syndicated loan
X: bank loan; Y: broadly syndicated loan; Z: leveraged loan
X: private credit; Y: broadly syndicated loan; Z: private credit

| Instrument | Who lends | Defining condition |
|---|---|---|
| Private credit | One nonbank lender (asset manager), bilateral | Nonbank, bilateral, not a public security |
| Traditional bank loan | A commercial bank | Bank lending (excluded from private credit) |
| Broadly syndicated loan | Multiple lenders to one borrower | Amount and/or risk too high for one lender alone |
| Leveraged loan | Multiple lenders (it is a broadly syndicated loan) | Borrower is highly leveraged; likely noninvestment grade with a high interest rate |

Loan X: one asset manager, bilateral, mid-sized PE-backed firm with weak earnings: private credit (nonbank, bilateral, and a typical borrower profile).

Loan Y: 14 lenders, amount too high for one lender, investment-grade borrower with moderate leverage: broadly syndicated loan, not a leveraged loan.

Loan Z: 9 lenders, amount and risk too high for one lender, highly leveraged, noninvestment grade, high rate: a broadly syndicated loan whose precise label is leveraged loan.

Loan sizes in CNY are irrelevant to the classification.

questions.question: A junior risk analyst at a Canadian public pension plan with CAD 40 billion of assets is preparing a slide for newly hired analysts on why private credit grew so strongly in the years after the 2007 to 2009 financial crisis. Which of the following statements is most accurate?

options.text: Growth accelerated mainly because an extended period of rising interest rates after the crisis made floating-rate private loans more attractive to borrowers.
Banks increasingly withdrew from lending to riskier mid-sized companies, while stricter regulation of financial institutions pushed lending activity toward private credit.
Any further tightening of regulatory requirements on financial institutions would be expected to slow the movement of lending activity toward private credit.
Most of the asset class’s growth took place in the years leading up to the crisis, after which growth stalled as post-crisis regulation was tightened.

questions.solution:
Pension-plan analyst preparing a new-hire slide on why private credit grew after the 2007 to 2009 crisis; pick the most accurate statement.

**Concept and theory**

Private credit is nonbank corporate lending made through bilateral agreements, historically by asset managers that raise money from institutions in closed-end funds and lend it to middle-market companies. Its growth profile is a story about who stopped lending and who started. Three forces in the reading explain the post-crisis surge:

| Force | What the reading says |
|---|---|
| Rate environment | An extended period of low interest rates made private credit an increasingly attractive alternative form of financing for borrowers. |
| Bank retreat | Banks increasingly abandoned loans to riskier mid-sized companies, and private credit filled the gap. |
| Regulation | Stricter regulatory requirements for financial institutions pushed activity toward private credit; insurers entered because their charges were less onerous than banks’. If regulation keeps increasing, there could be more movement toward private credit. |

The key logic is regulatory displacement: when regulated lenders find a type of loan expensive to hold, the lending migrates to less regulated lenders rather than disappearing.

**Applying it to this question**

The slide asks for the cause of growth after the crisis. Check each statement for direction (rates low, regulation pushing toward private credit) and timing (after 2007 to 2009, not before). Only one statement gets both the actor (banks withdrawing) and the direction (regulation pushes activity toward private credit) right.

**Fragile fact.** Direction: tighter regulation of financial institutions means more, not less, private credit; the rate backdrop for the growth phase was low rates.

questions.question:
A treasury analyst at a euro-area bank with a EUR 85 billion balance sheet is comparing regional private credit growth for an internal strategy paper. She has collected the following data:

| Region | Private credit share of total corporate credit, June 2023 (%) |
|---|---|
| United States | 7.0 |
| Europe | 1.6 |
| Asia | 0.2 |

Using the approximate annual growth rates for the past five years reported in the reading, and assuming annual compounding, which of the following best describes how cumulative five-year growth in Asian private credit compares with cumulative five-year growth in European private credit?

options.text: Asia exceeds Europe by about 3.0 percentage points.
Asia exceeds Europe by about 15.0 percentage points.
Asia exceeds Europe by about 29.6 percentage points.
Europe exceeds Asia by about 29.6 percentage points.

questions.solution:
Euro-area bank treasury analyst comparing cumulative five-year private credit growth in Asia and Europe, with share data provided.

**Concept and theory**

The reading gives regional growth rates for the past five years: about 20% a year in the United States and in Asia, and an average of about 17% a year in Europe. An annual growth rate compounds: each year’s growth applies to a base that already includes previous growth. Cumulative growth over n years at annual rate g is

$\text{G}_{\text{n}} = ($1 $+ \text{g})^{\text{n}} -$ 1,

where $\text{G}_{\text{n}}$ is cumulative proportional growth over the period, g is the annual growth rate (decimal) and n is the number of years. A small gap in annual rates becomes a much larger gap in cumulative growth because of compounding. The share-of-corporate-credit table in the stem (7%, 1.6%, 0.2%) measures market penetration, a stock, and has no role in a growth-rate calculation.

**Applying it to this question**

Inputs from the reading: $\text{g}_{\text{Asia}} =$ 0.20, $\text{g}_{\text{Europe}} =$ 0.17, n = 5. The table is excess data.

(1 $+ \text{g}_{\text{Asia}})^{5} =$ $\text{1.20}^{5} =$ 2.48832

$\text{G}_{\text{Asia}} =$ 2.48832 − 1 = 1.48832 = 148.8%

(1 $+ \text{g}_{\text{Europe}})^{5} =$ $\text{1.17}^{5} =$ 2.19245

$\text{G}_{\text{Europe}} =$ 2.19245 − 1 = 1.19245 = 119.2%

$\text{G}_{\text{Asia}} - \text{G}_{\text{Europe}} =$ 148.8% − 119.2% = 29.6 percentage points

Meaning: over five years Asian private credit roughly multiplied by 2.5 and European by 2.2; Asia’s cumulative growth exceeds Europe’s by about 30 percentage points, even though the annual gap is only 3 points. Note that Asia’s very low 0.2% share means this fast growth comes from a tiny base.

**Fragile fact.** The roughly 20% rate belongs to the United States and Asia; Europe is the 17% region. Growth rates are not shares.

**Reference**

LO 92.b: Explain the return profile and growth profile of the private credit asset class, and compare the historical returns of private credit to those of other asset classes.

Schweser Book 5, Reading 92, Module 92.1, section “Private Credit Growth” (paragraph 4). Compounding is standard arithmetic applied to the source figures; the rates are “about” values, so the answer is approximate. GARP text in the project has no matching section; content from Schweser, a condensed source whose wording may compress the framing of the assigned reading (IMF, Global Financial Stability Report, April 2024, Chapter 2, “The Rise and Risks of Private Credit”). No GARP versus Schweser conflict can therefore be checked.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-10 b, where it is Q4 of 10.

a.reason: **Unit or time-conversion slip: annual difference reported as cumulative.** 20% − 17% = 3.0 percentage points is the gap in annual rates. A would be correct if the question asked for the difference in annual growth rates.

b.reason: **Dropped term: compounding ignored.** Simple growth gives 5 × 20% = 100% for Asia and 5 × 17% = 85% for Europe, a 15.0 point gap. This drops the growth-on-growth terms. B would be correct if the stem specified simple (non-compounded) growth.

Part of the growth profile is a widening borrower base. Private credit began as financing for the middle market (roughly USD 100 million to USD 1 billion of revenue), companies too big for a single bank but too small for a public offering. **Applying it to this question**

The firm is a large corporate that would normally issue bonds or take syndicated loans, precisely the new type of borrower the reading describes. The question asks for its motive. Private credit’s growth profile is tied to private equity in two ways. First, the growth in private credit “mirrors the growth in private equity”. Second, “a substantial amount of private credit involves the borrower being backed by a private equity firm”. Alongside this, the customer base has broadened. The original and continuing focus is mid-sized borrowers, and lenders have added larger corporates that “normally would have borrowed via syndicated loans or public bond issuances”. These larger firms have public-market access; they choose private credit for tailoring, lower disclosure and lower cost than a bond issue.

**Applying it to this question**

This is a “least accurate” question, so three statements are true and one is corrupted. Check each against the source: A (mirrors PE) true; B (substantial PE backing) true; C (was and remains mid-sized) true; D says the larger corporates lacked access to syndicated loans and bonds, which reverses “normally would have borrowed via” those markets.

**Fragile fact.** Who lacks public-market access: the mid-sized core borrower, not the newer large corporates, who would normally have used syndicated loans or bonds.

b.reason: **Accurate.** Schweser: “a substantial amount of private credit involves the borrower being backed by a private equity firm.” It would become inaccurate if it claimed all, or almost no, private credit borrowers were sponsor-backed.

questions.question:
A portfolio manager at a UK university endowment with GBP 3.2 billion of assets is presenting a review of asset-class performance since 2020 to the investment committee. The endowment’s current allocation is shown below.

| Asset class | Allocation (GBP million) |
|---|---|
| Public equity (S&P 500 index fund) | 1,120 |
| Private equity | 640 |
| Private credit | 480 |
| Real estate | 400 |
| Natural resources | 320 |
| Venture capital | 240 |

Which of the following comparisons of private credit returns since 2020 is most accurate?

options.text: Private equity and real estate have delivered similar returns, with both trailing private credit.
Private credit has trailed the S&P 500 but has significantly outperformed venture capital.
Private credit has performed similarly to natural resources and somewhat better than real estate.
Private credit has performed similarly to real estate and somewhat better than natural resources.

questions.solution:
Endowment portfolio manager presenting asset-class returns since 2020; allocation table is excess data.

**Concept and theory**

The return profile of private credit is best understood as a ranking that changed over time. For the period since 2020 the reading gives a clear ordering relative to six asset classes:

| Asset class | Private credit relative performance since 2020 |
|---|---|
| Private equity | PE significantly outperformed private credit |
| Natural resources | Similar performance |
| Real estate | Private credit somewhat better |
| S&P 500 | Private credit significantly outperformed |
| Venture capital | Private credit significantly outperformed |

The reading gives no causal explanation for this ordering, so learn it as a ranking. The ranking since 2020 is therefore roughly: PE first, then private credit and natural resources together, then real estate, with the S&P 500 and VC well behind private credit.

**Applying it to this question**

The allocation sizes are irrelevant: the question is about relative returns, not weights. Test each comparison against the table. The two adverbs carry the discrimination: “similarly” belongs to natural resources and “somewhat better” to real estate.

**Fragile fact.** Since 2020: similar to natural resources, somewhat better than real estate, significantly better than S&P 500 and VC, significantly worse than PE.

**Reference**

LO 92.b: Explain the return profile and growth profile of the private credit asset class, and compare the historical returns of private credit to those of other asset classes.

No GARP versus Schweser conflict can therefore be checked.

b.reason: **Polarity flip.** Private credit has significantly outperformed the S&P 500 since 2020, not trailed it. The VC half is correct, which makes the trap persuasive. B would be correct only if “trailed” were “significantly outperformed”.

An internal auditor at a US property and casualty insurer is validating a performance commentary on private credit returns from the end of the 2007 to 2009 financial crisis to the present. The commentary contains the following statements:

I. For about 10 years after the financial crisis, private credit outperformed both private equity and real estate.

II. Over that same decade, private equity and real estate delivered similar returns.

III. The reversal around 2020 was driven by a sharp fall in private credit returns rather than by a jump in private equity returns.

IV. Around 2020, private equity returns moved dramatically ahead of private credit returns.

Which of the statements should the auditor accept as accurate?

options.text: I and IV only
I, II and IV only
I, II, III and IV
II, III and IV only

Insurer’s internal auditor validating four statements on private credit returns from the post-crisis decade to the present.

The historical return comparison has two regimes:

| Period | Reading’s description |
|---|---|
| About 10 years after the crisis | Private credit outperformed private equity and real estate; PE and real estate returns were similar. |
| Around 2020 | “A significant change”: private equity returns jumped dramatically ahead of private credit. |
| Since 2020 | PE significantly ahead; private credit similar to natural resources, somewhat better than real estate, significantly better than S&P 500 and VC. |

III assigns the reversal to a fall in private credit, which is inconsistent with the source (PE jumped; private credit stayed ahead of most other classes).
