questions.question:
A securities regulator in Brazil is reviewing a semiliquid evergreen private credit fund that is distributed mainly to retail investors and invests almost entirely in illiquid direct loans to mid-sized companies. The fund’s current terms are shown below.

| Feature | Current term |
|---|---|
| Net assets | BRL 2.4 billion |
| Redemption frequency | Monthly |
| Notice period | 5 business days |
| Settlement | 3 business days after the dealing date |
| Management fee | 1.25% per year |
| Retail share of investors | 68% |

The regulator is considering four proposals:

I. Reduce redemption frequency to quarterly and lengthen both the notice period and the settlement period.

II. Mandate the use of liquidity management techniques and liquidity stress testing, given the fund’s substantial liquidity mismatch.

III. Require disclosures on investment risks and redemption restrictions that are thorough and understandable to the fund’s investors.

IV. Shorten the settlement period so that redeeming investors receive cash sooner, reducing their incentive to redeem early in stressed conditions.

Which proposals are consistent with the reading’s policy recommendations for liquidity risk?

options.text: I and II only
II, III and IV only
I, III and IV only
I, II and III only

questions.solution:
Brazilian securities regulator considers four proposals for a monthly-dealing semiliquid fund of illiquid loans sold to retail investors.

**Concept and theory**

Liquidity mismatch arises when a fund promises investors faster access to cash than its assets can generate. Private loans are illiquid, so any structure that offers redemptions (open-ended or semiliquid funds) creates a mismatch. The reading acknowledges that clear efforts have been made, however open-ended structures and generous redemption policies still pose mismatch risk, especially for funds of illiquid assets. The scenario it wants addressed is many unsophisticated investors trying to withdraw at once in reaction to stressed conditions.

The remedies all act on one lever: limiting the outflow of funds. (The mechanism column is an explanatory gloss, not source text.)

| Remedy | Mechanism |
|---|---|
| Allow only closed-end funds | Removes redemption rights altogether |
| More infrequent redemptions | Fewer exit windows |
| More notice for redemptions | Manager sees outflows coming |
| More time for settlement | Manager has longer to raise cash |
| Mandated liquidity management techniques and stress testing | Where substantial mismatches exist |
| Thorough, understandable disclosures | Educates investors on risks and redemption limits |

**Applying it to this question**

The fund deals monthly, holds illiquid direct loans and is mainly retail: a clear case of substantial liquidity mismatch with unsophisticated investors. Test each proposal against the remedy list.

- I: fewer redemptions, more notice, more settlement time. Matches three remedies.
- II: liquidity management techniques and stress testing where substantial mismatch exists. The condition is met. Matches.
- III: thorough and understandable disclosures on risks and redemption restrictions. Matches.
- IV: shorter settlement. Opposite of “more time for settlements”.

Net assets, the management fee and the retail share as a number are irrelevant inputs; the retail share matters only qualitatively.

**Fragile fact.** Every liquidity remedy slows or blocks outflows: less frequent redemptions, longer notice, longer settlement; never the reverse.

**Reference**

**LO 92.d (Schweser, verbatim):** “Assess potential policy recommendations that could help mitigate the risks associated with private credit.” **Schweser:** Reading 92, Module 92.2, “Policies for Mitigating Private Credit Risks”, subsection “Liquidity Risks”. **GARP:** GARP text in the project has no matching section; content from Schweser, a condensed source whose wording may compress the original reading (IMF, Global Financial Stability Report, April 2024, Chapter 2). No GARP vs Schweser conflict can therefore arise on this point.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-10 d, where it is Q3 of 12.

a.reason: **Scope error, dropped element.** A omits III. Disclosure of investment risks and redemption restrictions is explicitly listed as a liquidity remedy (to educate investors). A would be right only if the question excluded investor disclosure measures.

b.reason: **Polarity flip in IV.** B includes IV and drops I. Shortening settlement reverses the reading’s “more time for settlements”. The intuition that faster payment calms investors is not in the source; the source limits outflows by slowing them. B would be right only if the reading recommended faster settlement.

c.reason: **Polarity flip in IV, dropped element.** C includes IV and drops II, the mandated liquidity management techniques and stress testing that the reading recommends where substantial mismatches exist, a condition this fund meets.

d.reason: I, II and III each restate a remedy the reading lists for liquidity risk; IV contradicts one. D (I, II and III only) is the only option that includes every consistent proposal and excludes IV.

questions.question: A senior credit risk analyst at a UK bank is reviewing the renewal of a GBP 450 million credit facility to a private credit firm. The firm uses the borrowed funds to lend to mid-sized companies and has also extended revolving credit lines to many of those borrowers. Which of the following best describes the related policy recommendation in the reading?

options.text: The private credit firm should demonstrate to the bank that it has strong liquidity management processes, including stress tests of constrained funding sources, write-downs on leveraged assets, and large and abrupt uses of credit by its borrowers.

The bank should demonstrate to its prudential supervisor that it has stress tested the facility for constrained funding sources, write-downs on leveraged assets, and large and abrupt uses of credit by the firm’s borrowers.

The private credit firm should demonstrate to the bank that it has strong liquidity management processes, including stress tests of constrained funding sources, write-downs on leveraged assets, and simultaneous redemption requests from its investors.

The private credit firm should demonstrate to the bank that it has strong liquidity management processes, including stress tests of constrained funding, write-downs and abrupt borrower draws, but only where its leverage already exceeds a regulatory cap.

questions.solution:
UK bank analyst renewing a GBP 450 million facility to a private credit firm that also extends revolving lines to borrowers.

**Concept and theory**

Leverage in private credit is layered: investors, funds and borrowers each borrow, and fund-level reporting can omit or obscure leverage at SPVs and feeder or master funds. One concrete channel the reading highlights is that private credit firms borrow from banks to lend to other borrowers. If those firms face a funding squeeze, write-downs or sudden borrower draws, the bank that funds them is exposed.

The recommendation therefore assigns a clear actor and audience:

- Who acts: the private credit firm.
- To whom: its banks.
- What: it demonstrates strong liquidity management processes.
- How: three stress tests: (1) funding sources become constrained, (2) write-downs on leveraged assets, (3) large and abrupt uses of credit by the firm’s borrowers.

This sits under the leverage heading, even though the wording speaks of liquidity management, because it addresses the bank-to-fund-to-borrower leverage chain.

**Applying it to this question**

The bank lends to the firm and the firm has extended revolving lines to its borrowers, so all three stress scenarios are live: the bank line could shrink, leveraged loans could be written down, and many borrowers could draw at once. The recommendation does not depend on any threshold.

**Fragile fact.** Actor and audience: the private credit firm demonstrates to its banks; the third stress test is borrower draws on credit, not investor redemptions.

**Reference**

**LO 92.d (Schweser, verbatim):** “Assess potential policy recommendations that could help mitigate the risks associated with private credit.” **Schweser:** Reading 92, Module 92.2, “Policies for Mitigating Private Credit Risks”, subsection “Leverage Risks”. **GARP:** GARP text in the project has no matching section; content from Schweser, a condensed source whose wording may compress the original reading (IMF, Global Financial Stability Report, April 2024, Chapter 2). No GARP vs Schweser conflict can therefore arise on this point.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-10 d, where it is Q5 of 12.

a.reason: A has the right actor (the private credit firm), the right audience (the bank), and the right three stress tests, as listed in the reading.

b.reason: **Role misassignment.** B keeps the three stress tests but makes the bank demonstrate them to its own supervisor. The reading requires the private credit firm to demonstrate its processes to its banks. B would be right only in a stem about bank prudential supervision of lending to nonbanks.

c.reason: **Sibling swap.** C replaces “large and abrupt uses of credit by the firm’s borrowers” with simultaneous investor redemptions. Investor redemption pressure belongs to the liquidity risk heading (semiliquid funds and mass withdrawals). C would be right in a stem about an open-ended fund’s redemption stress.

The reading imposes no such threshold on the demonstration; leverage caps are a separate, conditional regulatory tool. D would be right only if the source made the stress testing conditional, which it does not.

questions.question:
A risk consultant is advising a euro area supervisor that wants to assess leverage in the private credit funds it oversees. For one representative fund, the consultant maps where leverage sits and whether it appears in the fund’s regulatory report.

| Layer | Leverage source | EUR m | Reported? |
|---|---|---|---|
| Fund | Subscription credit line | 180 | Yes |
| SPV held by the fund | Asset-backed facility | 420 | No |
| Feeder fund | NAV-based loan | 95 | No |
| Insurer investors | Derivatives and repo | Not known | No |

Which response is most consistent with the reading’s policy recommendations for leverage risk?

options.text: Base oversight on the EUR 180 million reported at fund level, since leverage held outside the fund itself, such as at SPVs or feeder funds, falls outside the scope of the leverage recommendations.
Impose a standing leverage cap on every private credit fund immediately, since the reading recommends caps as the default rule whenever data on leverage are incomplete.

Expand reporting requirements within and across borders and strengthen cooperation between regulators to close the data gaps, and impose leverage caps if leverage is judged high enough to cause negative systemic effects.
Have each national supervisor design its own leverage reporting template independently, since reporting inconsistencies across countries are best resolved within each country’s own sectors.

Consultant to a euro area supervisor maps leverage at fund, SPV, feeder and investor level, most of it unreported.

**Concept and theory**

The reading’s starting point on leverage is a data problem: there is not enough information to determine the extent of leverage in private credit. Within funds, reports may omit or obscure the many interconnected sources of leverage (for example SPVs and feeder or master funds), and data omissions and reporting inconsistencies across countries and sectors prevent a holistic view of total leverage.

The recommendations respond in a sequence:

1. Overcome data deficiencies: more reporting requirements, both within and outside borders, together with enhanced cooperation between regulators.
2. Firms borrowing from banks demonstrate liquidity management through stress tests (see Q5).
3. Leverage caps may need to be imposed by regulators when it is determined that leverage levels are too high and could lead to negative systemic effects.

The caps are conditional and come after the determination; the reporting fix is the general remedy.

Only EUR 180 million of the mapped leverage appears in the fund’s report; EUR 420 million at the SPV and EUR 95 million at the feeder (EUR 515 million, so EUR 695 million of known leverage in total) and an unknown amount at the investors do not. The sums are an irrelevant computation: no threshold is given, and the deciding fact is qualitative. The table illustrates exactly the omission the reading describes, so the right response fixes reporting across borders with regulator cooperation, and keeps caps for when leverage is judged systemically dangerous.

**Fragile fact.** Leverage caps are conditional (“may need to be imposed when it is determined” that leverage is too high and could be systemic); the unconditional fix is more reporting plus regulator cooperation, within and outside borders.

**Reference**

**LO 92.d (Schweser, verbatim):** “Assess potential policy recommendations that could help mitigate the risks associated with private credit.” **Schweser:** Reading 92, Module 92.2, “Policies for Mitigating Private Credit Risks”, subsection “Leverage Risks”. **GARP:** GARP text in the project has no matching section; content from Schweser, a condensed source whose wording may compress the original reading (IMF, Global Financial Stability Report, April 2024, Chapter 2). No GARP vs Schweser conflict can therefore arise on this point.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-10 d, where it is Q6 of 12.

The reading’s whole point is that leverage sits beyond the fund (SPVs, feeder and master funds, investors, borrowers) and that reports may obscure it. A would be right only if the reading’s leverage concern stopped at the fund’s own balance sheet.

The chief risk officer of a Singapore insurer is applying the reading’s valuation recommendation on external valuations to four private credit positions. Internal policy defines a valuation as significant if the position exceeds 5% of the insurer’s private credit net asset value (NAV), and as prone to error if the range of valuation estimates is wider than ±5% of the mark.

| Position | Share of NAV (%) | Estimate range (±% of mark) | Spread (bps) | Currency |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| P1 | 11.5 | 9.0 | 575 | SGD |
| P2 | 0.6 | 12.0 | 650 | SGD |
| P3 | 10.2 | 1.5 | 425 | SGD |
| P4 | 0.4 | 1.0 | 500 | SGD |

Under the reading’s recommendation, for which positions may more frequent external valuations need to be imposed?

P1 and P2 only
P1 and P3 only
P1, P2 and P3 only

Singapore insurer’s CRO decides which of four positions meet the condition for more frequent external valuations.

**Concept and theory**

The reading does not call for more frequent external valuations everywhere; it attaches a condition: “When valuations are significant and/or prone to error, more frequent external valuations may need to be imposed.” The phrase “and/or” is an inclusive OR: either condition is enough.

Why each condition matters on its own:

- Significant: a large position can move the institution’s reported capital or NAV materially even if the estimate is fairly tight.
- Prone to error: a small position with a wide estimate range signals weak methods or data, which an external valuer can test.

Formally, with $\text{S}_{\text{i}}$ = “position i is significant” and $\text{E}_{\text{i}}$ = “position i is prone to error”:

External valuations may be imposed on i $\Leftarrow\Rightarrow\text{S}_{\text{i}} \vee\text{E}_{\text{i}}$.

This targeted rule sits alongside LO 92.c’s warning that more frequent valuation is not always useful; the condition targets external valuation at the positions where size or estimation error makes it matter (this rationale is an interpretation, not a quoted statement).

**Applying it to this question**

Apply the insurer’s thresholds: $\text{S}_{\text{i}}$ if share of NAV > 5%; $\text{E}_{\text{i}}$ if estimate range > ±5%.

| Position | Share (%) | $\text{S}_{\text{i}}$ | Range (±%) | $\text{E}_{\text{i}}$ | $\text{S}_{\text{i}} \vee\text{E}_{\text{i}}$ |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| P1 | 11.5 | Yes | 9.0 | Yes | Yes |
| P2 | 0.6 | No | 12.0 | Yes | Yes |
| P3 | 10.2 | Yes | 1.5 | No | Yes |
| P4 | 0.4 | No | 1.0 | No | No |

P1, P2 and P3 qualify; only P4 fails both tests. The spreads and currency are irrelevant inputs.

**LO 92.d (Schweser, verbatim):** “Assess potential policy recommendations that could help mitigate the risks associated with private credit.” **Schweser:** Reading 92, Module 92.2, “Policies for Mitigating Private Credit Risks”, subsection “Valuation Risks”; also LO 92.d Key Concepts. **GARP:** GARP text in the project has no matching section; content from Schweser, a condensed source whose wording may compress the original reading (IMF, Global Financial Stability Report, April 2024, Chapter 2). No GARP vs Schweser conflict can therefore arise on this point.

questions.question:
A member of a national financial stability committee in Australia notes that insurers and pension funds in neighboring jurisdictions with more lenient rules hold far larger private credit positions than domestic peers, and that the domestic insurance, pension, securities and banking supervisors each see only part of the exposures. She assesses four statements:

I. Regulatory arbitrage means that more private credit risk may be taken where rules are more lax, and it may be contributing to substantial private credit holdings by insurers and pension funds.

II. Where risks are concentrated, harmonizing risk assessment processes across sectors and borders is recommended to reduce or eliminate regulatory arbitrage.

III. Supervisors in different domestic sectors should cooperate to determine what additional information is required, learn more about interconnected risks and reduce contagion risks.

IV. Because regulatory arbitrage spreads private credit risk across many jurisdictions, it reduces the need for cross-border cooperation between regulators where risks are concentrated.

Which statements are consistent with the reading’s discussion of policy recommendations for interconnectedness risk?

options.text: I and II only
II and III only
I, II and III only
I, III and IV only

questions.solution:
Australian financial stability committee member assesses four statements on regulatory arbitrage and cooperation.

**Concept and theory**

Regulatory arbitrage is the search for the most favorable (least onerous) rules. When strictness differs across countries and sectors, more private credit risk is taken where the rules are more lax. Arbitrage can happen locally (between sectors such as insurance and pensions) and internationally (between countries). The reading says it may be contributing to substantial private credit holdings by insurers and pension funds, and that their many interconnections and potential systemic effects should be a warning sign to regulators.

Because arbitrage moves risk toward lax regimes, it concentrates rather than disperses risk. The recommendations:

- Cross-border cooperation between regulators to ensure oversight, especially when risks are more concentrated (the lack of data mirrors the leverage problem).
- Local, cross-sector cooperation: regulators in different sectors determine what additional information is needed, learn more about interconnected risks and reduce contagion.
- Where risks are concentrated, harmonization of risk assessment processes across sectors and borders to reduce or eliminate arbitrage.

**Applying it to this question**

The committee sees exactly the two symptoms the reading flags: larger holdings by insurers and pensions in lenient jurisdictions (arbitrage) and fragmented domestic supervision (need for cross-sector cooperation). Test each statement.

- I: correct definition and the insurer and pension link. Consistent.
- II: harmonization across sectors and borders where risks are concentrated. Consistent.
- III: domestic cross-sector cooperation, its three purposes. Consistent.
- IV: claims arbitrage spreads risk and lowers the need for cooperation. Inconsistent.

**Fragile fact.** Regulatory arbitrage concentrates risk in lax jurisdictions and sectors; the cure is cooperation (cross-border and cross-sector) and harmonized risk assessment.

**Reference**

**LO 92.d (Schweser, verbatim):** “Assess potential policy recommendations that could help mitigate the risks associated with private credit.” **Schweser:** Reading 92, Module 92.2, “Policies for Mitigating Private Credit Risks”, subsection “Interconnectedness Risks”. **GARP:** GARP text in the project has no matching section; content from Schweser, a condensed source whose wording may compress the original reading (IMF, Global Financial Stability Report, April 2024, Chapter 2). No GARP vs Schweser conflict can therefore arise on this point.

questions.question: A conduct supervisor at a European securities regulator is reviewing a private credit manager. One fund run by the manager has bought loans from another of the manager’s own funds at a price set by the manager, and the manager is distributing a semiliquid feeder fund (minimum investment EUR 15,000) to retail clients through bank branches. Which supervisory response is most consistent with the reading’s policy recommendations for conduct risk?

options.text: Identify the conduct risks present, recommend increased disclosure of the conflict of interest, and check that sales practices are fair, suitability is addressed, and retail clients understand the credit and liquidity risks and redemption restrictions.

Accept the price set between the two affiliated funds as fair, since private transactions between funds of the same manager carry a built-in control of market pricing, and focus the review on the feeder fund’s sales practices.

Leave the assessment of sales practices and suitability to the manager’s own compliance function, since the manager is best placed to judge its clients’ interests, and focus the review on the affiliated loan transfer.
Prohibit all retail distribution of the feeder fund, since the reading concludes that conduct risk cannot be mitigated by disclosure or controls once unsophisticated investors are present.

Conduct risk in private credit has two roots in the reading: (1) greater numbers of unsophisticated investors, and (2) conflicts of interest where the private credit fund is involved on both sides of a transaction. Private transactions have no built-in control of market pricing, so a transfer between two funds of one manager may be unfair to one side.

- determine what conduct risks exist;
- recommend increased disclosure when there is a conflict of interest;
- consider investors’ best interests first: are sales practices fair, and is suitability sufficiently addressed;

The approach is identification, disclosure and investor protection controls, not outsourcing to the manager and not an outright ban.

Both roots are present: a fund-to-fund transfer priced by the manager (conflict, no market pricing control) and retail distribution of a semiliquid product (unsophisticated investors facing redemption limits). The response must cover both and must be carried out by the supervisor.

questions.question: The chief risk officer of a Chinese wealth manager is assessing a proposal from the product team to increase the redemption frequency of a CNY 6 billion semiliquid private credit product, invested in illiquid direct loans, from quarterly to monthly, in order to make it more attractive to retail clients. Which assessment is most accurate in light of the reading’s policy recommendations?

options.text: The change lowers liquidity mismatch risk, since investors who can exit more often are less likely to rush for the exit in stress, and leaves conduct risk unchanged.
The change raises liquidity mismatch risk but lowers conduct risk, since more frequent cash settlement at net asset value disciplines the manager’s valuations.
The change raises liquidity mismatch risk, and raises conduct risk only through mis-selling, since frequent redemptions give the manager no incentive to influence valuations.
The change raises liquidity mismatch risk and also conduct risk, since the manager may manipulate valuations to discourage redemptions or tie redemptions to reinvestment with the manager.

**Concept and theory**

Redemption frequency is a lever that pulls two risks in the same direction.

Liquidity. The liquidity remedies call for more infrequent redemptions, more notice and more settlement time, because generous redemption policies in funds of illiquid assets create mismatch risk. More frequent redemptions therefore raise mismatch risk.

Conduct. In the conduct section, the reading gives a specific example: allowing more frequent redemptions could cause managers to (1) manipulate valuations to discourage redemptions, or (2) make redemptions conditional on investing the redeemed money in other investments controlled by the manager. Both are conflicts of interest that hurt investors.

| Effect of more frequent redemptions | Direction | Channel |
|---|---|---|
| Liquidity mismatch risk | Up | More exit windows against illiquid loans |
| Conduct risk | Up | Valuation manipulation; conditional redemptions |

The appeal to retail investors is exactly what makes the trade-off sharp: frequent redemptions attract retail money (unsophisticated investors), which also widens the conduct concern.

**Applying it to this question**

The product holds illiquid direct loans and is aimed at retail clients. Moving from quarterly to monthly raises both risks through the two channels above. The fund size is irrelevant.

**Fragile fact.** More frequent redemptions push both liquidity mismatch risk and conduct risk up; the conduct channel runs through valuations and conditional redemptions.

P1. Funds with substantial private credit holdings adopt bank-like processes to monitor loan performance in structured products and direct lending.

P2. Private credit firms that borrow from banks show their banks stress tests of constrained funding, write-downs on leveraged assets, and abrupt draws on credit by their borrowers. P3. Risk assessment processes are harmonized across sectors and borders to reduce regulatory arbitrage.

P4. Supervisors recommend increased disclosure where a fund is involved on both sides of a transaction.

Which mapping is correct?

options.text: P1: credit; P2: liquidity; P3: interconnectedness; P4: conduct
P1: credit; P2: leverage; P3: interconnectedness; P4: conduct
P1: valuation; P2: leverage; P3: interconnectedness; P4: conduct

| Heading | Principal recommendations |
|---|---|
| Credit | Bank-like monitoring of private credit performance in structured products and direct lending; scrutiny of underwriting and credit risk |

| Conduct | Supervisors identify risks, recommend disclosure of conflicts, put investors first, ensure retail understanding |

- P2: stress tests shown to banks. The wording says “liquidity management processes”, but the reading places it under leverage, because it addresses private credit firms borrowing from banks to lend on. Leverage.
- P3: harmonized risk assessment to reduce regulatory arbitrage. Interconnectedness.
- P4: disclosure where a fund is on both sides of a transaction. Conduct.

questions.question:
A junior risk analyst at a Canadian public pension plan is classifying three new transactions for the plan’s private markets dashboard, using the categories of private market investment described in the reading.

| Deal | Description |
|---|---|
| 1 | A CAD 40 million senior term loan to a privately held logistics company that plans an initial public offering within three years |
| 2 | A privately negotiated purchase of CAD 25 million of newly issued common shares from a TSX-listed mining company whose shares trade in very low volume |
| 3 | A direct purchase of a portfolio of privately held farmland parcels |

Which of the following correctly classifies deals 1, 2 and 3, in that order?

options.text: Private debt; private equity; private real asset
Private equity; private investment in public equity (PIPE); private real asset
Private debt; private investment in public equity (PIPE); private real asset
Private debt; private investment in public equity (PIPE); private equity

questions.solution:
Classify a senior loan to a private firm, a private share placement by a thinly traded listed miner, and a direct farmland purchase.

**Concept and theory**

The reading opens LO 93.a by describing what private markets are for: they help private companies raise capital through a wide range of securities, including equity, convertible debt and traditional debt. Investors then label what they hold by two questions: what instrument is bought (equity, debt or a real asset) and who issues it (a private firm or a publicly traded one).

| Category | What is bought | Issuer |
|---|---|---|
| Private equity (PE) | Equity | A private firm |
| Private debt (PD) | Debt | A private firm |
| Private real asset (PRA) | A privately held real asset | Held privately (no issuer security) |
| Private investment in public equity (PIPE) | Equity, through a private placement | A publicly traded firm with limited trading volume |

Two further facts matter. First, a PE investment may eventually become publicly traded through a listing: this describes a possible future path for an equity stake, not a reason to relabel a loan. Second, PIPEs exist because some listed firms with thin trading volume seek capital through private transactions (private placements) rather than in the open market. The word “private” in PIPE describes the transaction; the issuer is listed.

**Applying it to this question**

Deal 1: the instrument is a senior term loan, so it is debt; the borrower is privately held. Debt investment in a private firm is private debt. The planned IPO is a deliberately irrelevant input: it could matter for a future equity stake, but it does not turn a loan into equity.

Deal 2: the issuer is TSX-listed, so it is publicly traded, and its shares trade in very low volume; the plan buys newly issued shares in a privately negotiated deal. That is a private placement by a thinly traded listed firm, which the reading calls a PIPE. It is not PE, because PE is equity in private firms.

Deal 3: the plan buys the farmland parcels themselves, which are privately held real assets. That is a PRA investment.

Classification: private debt; PIPE; private real asset.

**Fragile fact.** In a PIPE the issuer is publicly traded (with limited trading volume) and only the transaction is private; a possible future listing of a private firm does not change today’s category.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** “LO 93.a: Explain the motivations for investors to invest in private markets.”

**Schweser:** Book 5, Reading 93 (Private Markets Investing), Module 93.1, section “Private Market Investment Motivations”; opening paragraph on PE, PD, PRA and PIPEs; Key Concepts, LO 93.a.

**GARP:** GARP text in the project has no matching section; content from Schweser, a condensed source (Schweser cross-references Demaria et al., Chapter 3, not in the project’s GARP file). No GARP vs Schweser conflict arises.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-11 a, where it is Q1 of 10.

a.reason: **Sibling swap.** A labels deal 2 as private equity. The mistake is focusing on the private negotiation and ignoring that the issuer is listed. PE and PIPE are sibling equity categories separated by the issuer’s status. A would be correct if the mining company were privately held with no listed shares.

b.reason: **Sibling swap.** B labels deal 1 as private equity, swapping the debt category for the equity one. The trigger is the IPO plan, which recalls the fact that a PE investment may eventually list. B would be correct if deal 1 were a subscription for ordinary shares in the private logistics company rather than a senior loan.

c.reason: C matches each deal to the reading’s definitions: debt investments in private firms are private debt; private placements by publicly traded firms with limited trading volume are PIPEs; investments in privately held real assets are PRA investments.

d.reason: **Sibling swap.** D labels deal 3 as private equity, swapping the real asset category for the equity one. The plan bought the parcels directly, not shares in a company. D would be correct if deal 3 were a share subscription in a privately held agribusiness operating company.

questions.question: A senior risk analyst at a Japanese life insurer is drafting a board note on the first of the reading’s six motivation categories, performance and diversification. The board has asked that the note describe this category exactly as the reading frames it. Which of the following statements is most accurate?

options.text: Private market investments have the potential to earn higher returns than public market assets, and they may help hedge traditional asset performance during periods of market uncertainty.
Private market investments earn higher returns than public market assets in every market environment, and they therefore also hedge traditional asset performance during periods of uncertainty.
Private market investments have the potential to earn higher returns than public market assets, but their diversification benefit is expected mainly in calm markets and fades when uncertainty rises.

Private market investments have the potential to earn higher returns than public market assets, and this category’s diversification benefit comes from reaching regions without developed public markets.

questions.solution:
Choose the statement that describes the performance and diversification motivation exactly as the reading frames it.

**Concept and theory**

The reading groups investors’ reasons for entering private markets into six categories. The first, performance and diversification, bundles two separate ideas:

(i) Return potential: private market investments have the potential to generate higher returns than public market assets. The reading frames this as a possibility, never as a promise.

(ii) Diversification: they may provide diversification benefits by hedging traditional asset performance during periods of market uncertainty. The benefit is tied to uncertain periods, which is when a hedge is most valuable.

Several other categories also mention diversification, which is why GARP-style questions set sibling traps here:

| Category | Where its diversification language comes from |
|---|---|
| Performance and diversification | Hedging traditional asset performance during periods of market uncertainty |
| Broader investment universe | Far more private firms than public firms, giving unique diversification across industries, business models and lifecycle stages |
| Potential for absolute returns | Returns less correlated with public market performance |
| Wider geographic reach | Regions with underdeveloped or nonexistent public markets; reduces home country bias |

**Applying it to this question**

The board wants the category described exactly. Two words decide it: “potential” (not a guarantee) and “during periods of market uncertainty” (the timing of the hedge). The option must also take its diversification argument from category 1, not from a sibling category. Only one option has all three features.

**Fragile fact.** Higher returns are a potential; the hedging benefit is stated for periods of market uncertainty; geography belongs to a different category.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** “LO 93.a: Explain the motivations for investors to invest in private markets.”

**Schweser:** Book 5, Reading 93 (Private Markets Investing), Module 93.1, section “Private Market Investment Motivations”; item 1, Performance and diversification; Key Concepts, LO 93.a.

**GARP:** GARP text in the project has no matching section; content from Schweser, a condensed source (Schweser cross-references Demaria et al., Chapter 3, not in the project’s GARP file). No GARP vs Schweser conflict arises.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-11 a, where it is Q2 of 10.

a.reason: A restates the source: private market investments have the potential to generate higher returns than public market assets, and they may provide diversification benefits by hedging traditional asset performance during periods of market uncertainty.

b.reason: **Absolute claim.** B turns “potential” into “in every market environment”. The reading never promises higher returns. B would only be the right choice under a reversed qualifier, for example “which statement overstates the reading’s claim?”.

c.reason: **Polarity flip.** C reverses the timing of the diversification benefit: the reading places it during periods of market uncertainty, while C says it fades when uncertainty rises. C would be the right choice only if the stem asked which statement reverses the reading’s framing.

d.reason: **Sibling swap.** D attributes the diversification benefit to reaching regions without developed public markets, which is the wider geographic reach category. D’s second clause would be correct if the note were about the fifth category, wider geographic reach, rather than the first.

questions.question: A risk committee member at an Australian superannuation fund reviews two holdings. The fund owns 0.3% of the shares of an ASX-listed engineering firm (market value AUD 45 million) and 60% of a privately held engineering firm (AUD 210 million), where it appoints two directors and has placed an operating partner alongside management. She asks why the fund can shape strategy at the private firm but not at the listed one. Which of the following best explains the difference, as the reading describes the control and value creation motivation?

options.text: Investors in listed companies can never monitor or influence company performance, whatever the size of their ownership stake, so control is available only through private ownership.
At the private firm, it is the firm’s own management that supplies the capital, industry connections and operational expertise, while the fund’s role is limited to monitoring.
The difference illustrates the specialized investment structures motivation, because private ownership creates risk exposures that traditional investment channels cannot provide.
Private investors can monitor, guide and influence company performance, whereas comparable control in a listed company is generally available only with a very large ownership stake.

questions.solution:
Explain why an Australian fund can shape strategy at a 60%-owned private firm but not at a 0.3% listed holding.

**Concept and theory**

The control and value creation motivation has two halves.

- Control: private investors can monitor, guide and influence company performance. The reading adds a condition for the public market comparison: this level of control is generally not available in public markets unless the investor holds a very large ownership stake.
- Value creation: private investors can also contribute capital, industry connections and operational expertise, all of which can support and enhance the value creation process inside the private company.

The actor matters. It is the investor who brings capital, connections and expertise to the company. The condition matters too: the reading does not say public market control is impossible, only that it generally requires a very large stake.

**Applying it to this question**

At the listed firm the fund holds 0.3%, which is far from a very large stake, so the reading’s condition for public market control is not met. At the private firm the fund owns 60%, appoints directors (monitor, guide, influence) and has placed an operating partner (operational expertise contributed by the investor). The AUD market values are irrelevant to the explanation. The deciding fact is the reading’s statement that such control is generally unavailable in public markets without a very large ownership stake.

**Fragile fact.** Direction and actor: the investor contributes capital, connections and expertise; public market control is “generally not available unless” the stake is very large, not “never available”.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** “LO 93.a: Explain the motivations for investors to invest in private markets.”

**Schweser:** Book 5, Reading 93 (Private Markets Investing), Module 93.1, section “Private Market Investment Motivations”; item 2, Control and value creation; Key Concepts, LO 93.a.

**GARP:** GARP text in the project has no matching section; content from Schweser, a condensed source (Schweser cross-references Demaria et al., Chapter 3, not in the project’s GARP file). No GARP vs Schweser conflict arises.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-11 a, where it is Q3 of 10.

b.reason: **Role misassignment.** B gives the contribution of capital, industry connections and operational expertise to the company’s own management. The reading assigns these to the private investor, as the fund’s operating partner shows. B would be correct with the actors reversed: the fund supplies capital, connections and expertise, and management benefits.

C would fit a stem in which the fund chose a fund of funds or a co-investment to obtain a risk exposure unavailable through traditional channels.

I and III only

The reading’s six categories are distinct reasons, each with a hallmark phrase. Mapping questions are won by matching the hallmark, not by general impression.

|---|---|

| 3. Broader investment universe | More than 300 million private vs about 52,000 listed firms; more industries and business models; all lifecycle stages |

questions.question: A junior risk analyst at a Singapore life insurer is drafting a note for the investment committee, which is considering an SGD 300 million first allocation to private equity through a private fund. The analyst writes four candidate descriptions of the private fund structure. Which of the following descriptions is most accurate?

options.text: Investor capital is pooled, and each limited partner keeps a high degree of control over individual investment decisions in proportion to its commitment.
Investor capital is pooled, and the most common form is an open-end vehicle that lets investors redeem their interests periodically at net asset value.
Investor capital is pooled, specialized general partners make the investment and oversight decisions, and the most common form is a closed-end limited partnership.
Investor capital is pooled, and regulation in every jurisdiction restricts participation to institutional and large private investors such as pension funds.

questions.solution:
Singapore insurer’s analyst chooses the most accurate description of the private fund structure.

**Concept and theory**

An investment structure is the legal and economic wrapper through which an investor reaches a private asset. Schweser opens the LO by saying a structure “determines how capital is pooled, managed, and governed” and “defines the rights and obligations of managers and investors”. So every structure can be read along the same axes: who pools the money, who makes decisions, how diversified the result is, how easily the investor can get out, what it costs and how much say the investor keeps.

A private fund is the default institutional answer to these questions. Many investors (limited partners) pool capital; a specialized manager (the general partner) makes the investment and oversight decisions. Pooling buys diversification and professional management; the price is that each investor gives up control. Schweser calls funds “the most common type of institutional investment structure”, lists institutional and large private investors and pension funds as typical users, notes that retail investors may be permitted in some jurisdictions, and states that the most common fund structure is a closed-end limited partnership. A closed-end vehicle has a fixed life and no redemption right, which is why Figure 93.1 rates private fund liquidity as very low.

| Feature | Private fund (Schweser) |
|---|---|
| Who decides | General partner (specialized manager) |
| Investor control | Limited |
| Diversification | Moderate to high |
| Liquidity | Very low (closed-end limited partnership) |
| Cost | Management fees plus performance-based fees |
| Users | Institutions, large private investors, pensions; retail in some jurisdictions |

**Applying it to this question**

All four options start with the true fact that capital is pooled. The discrimination lies in the second half: who decides (A), what legal form is most common and what that implies for redemption (B), and who may invest (D). The SGD 300 million size is context only. The deciding facts are “specialized managers (i.e., general partners) make investment and oversight decisions” and “the most common fund structure is a closed-end limited partnership”.

**Fragile fact.** Closed-end limited partnership is the most common private fund form; decisions sit with the general partner, not the limited partners.

**Reference**

LO 93.b (verbatim): “Describe different investment structures that can be used to invest in private assets and compare their characteristics.” Source: Schweser Reading 93, Module 93.1, section “Private Market Investment Structures”, item 2 “Private funds” (Schweser lines 5254 to 5260) and Key Concepts LO 93.b. An open-end vehicle with periodic redemption describes a different, liquid fund type that is not one of the structures in this LO. questions.question:

- Mandate X: the manager makes all investment decisions.
- Mandate Y: the plan retains veto authority over each proposed investment.

Which of the following best describes the two mandates?

Mandate Y typically involves carried interest while Mandate X often does not, and only under Mandate Y can the plan block an individual investment.

**Concept and theory**

A managed account is a separate account tailored to one investor’s mandate, rather than a share of a pool. Because the account belongs to a single investor, the investor and manager can negotiate how decision rights are split. Schweser distinguishes two types of mandate:

|  | Discretionary mandate | Advisory mandate |
|---|---|---|
| Who makes decisions | Manager makes all investment decisions | Investor retains veto authority |
| Carried interest | Typically involved | Often not involved |

The logic is that performance-based pay (carried interest) rewards the person who takes the decisions. When the manager has full discretion, the manager earns carry; when the investor can veto, the manager is closer to an adviser and is often paid without carry.

**Applying it to this question**

Mandate X, where the manager makes all decisions, is discretionary. Mandate Y, where the plan keeps a veto, is advisory. Applying the source: X typically involves carried interest; Y often does not; only Y gives the plan the right to block an investment. The CAD 750 million size, buyout strategy and eight-year period are context and do not change the classification.

**Fragile fact.** Discretionary: manager decides, carry typical. Advisory: investor holds the veto, carry often absent. Say the actor aloud before reading the fee.

GARP: no matching section in the project’s GARP text; content from Schweser, a condensed source (no GARP vs Schweser comparison possible).

c.reason: **Role misassignment.** The fee half is right, but the veto is given to the investor under the discretionary mandate, where the manager makes all decisions. It would be correct if the question asked which mandate leaves the manager with no veto from the plan, that is, if the actor were the manager rather than the plan.

d.reason: **Scope error.** It ignores the condition that drives carry, the mandate type, and treats all managed accounts alike. Schweser ties carried interest to the type of mandate. It would be correct only if both proposals were discretionary.

questions.question: A senior risk analyst at a Brazilian single-family office is presenting to newly hired analysts on direct investment, which the office uses to buy ownership stakes in private Brazilian companies (current direct book: BRL 420 million). Which of the following statements in the presentation is least likely to be accurate?

options.text: Direct investment gives the investor a high degree of control, but it requires significant expertise and active involvement from the investor’s own team.
Successful direct investing typically depends on strong networks to source deals, because private market investing often relies on local presence and relationships.
Crowdfunding is another form of direct investment, and entrepreneurs and family offices are frequent users of the direct approach as well.
Information asymmetry is rarely a concern in direct investment, because the investor holds its ownership interest in the company without an intermediary.

questions.solution:
Brazilian family office analyst identifies the least accurate statement about direct investment.

**Concept and theory**

In a direct investment the investor acquires an ownership interest in a private company or asset itself, with no fund in between. Removing the intermediary has clear consequences, all listed by Schweser:

- Control is high, because the investor is the owner.
- Expertise and active involvement are significant, because the investor must source, diligence and monitor the deal itself.
- Concentration risk is high and diversification limited unless many positions are held.
- Sourcing depends on strong networks, and private investing often relies on local presence and relationships.
- Information asymmetry between the investor and the private firm “can also be a challenge”.
- Typical users are entrepreneurs, family offices and buyout investors; crowdfunding is another form of direct investment.
- In Figure 93.1 terms: high involvement, low diversification, very low liquidity, generally low cost.

The key insight is that owning the asset directly does not remove the information gap. Private firms are not subject to public-company disclosure, so the owner still knows less than the entrepreneur running the business, which is why expertise and due diligence matter so much.

**Applying it to this question**

Test each statement against the list above. A, B and C are each close restatements of source sentences. D claims information asymmetry is rarely a concern, which contradicts the source sentence that it can be a challenge. The BRL figure is context only.

**Fragile fact.** Direct ownership raises control but does not remove information asymmetry; Schweser lists it as a challenge of direct investing.

**Reference**

LO 93.b (verbatim): “Describe different investment structures that can be used to invest in private assets and compare their characteristics.” Source: Schweser Reading 93, Module 93.1, section “Private Market Investment Structures”, item 1 “Direct investment” (Schweser lines 5244 to 5253). Note: the same paragraph also states that strategies such as leveraged buyouts and distressed debt are generally not accessible through direct investment, while listing buyout investors as frequent users; because these two sentences sit in tension, neither appears in any question in this paper. GARP: no matching section in the project’s GARP text; content from Schweser, a condensed source (no GARP vs Schweser comparison possible).

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-11 b, where it is Q3 of 12.

a.reason: **Accurate statement.** Matches “offers a high degree of control but requires significant expertise and active involvement”. It would be inaccurate only if it had attached high control to a private fund or fund of funds (sibling swap).

b.reason: **Accurate statement.** Matches “Successful direct investing typically requires strong networks to source opportunities” and the reliance on “local presence and relationships”. It would be inaccurate if it claimed networks are unnecessary because deals are publicly marketed.

c.reason:
**Accurate statement.** Matches “Entrepreneurs, family offices, and buyout investors frequently use this approach. Crowdfunding is another form of direct investment.” (Buyout investors are deliberately left out of the option; see the note in the reference.) It would be inaccurate if crowdfunding were described as a fund of funds or a securitization (sibling swap).

The trap in D is a polarity flip: “can be a challenge” is turned into “rarely a concern”. Under the alternate stem “Which statement is most accurate?” A, B and C would all be defensible, which is why the qualifier here is “least likely”.

d.reason: D is the least accurate statement: Schweser states that “information asymmetry between investors and private firms can also be a challenge” in direct investment. Holding the interest directly does not close the information gap between owner and company.

questions.question:
A member of a university endowment’s investment committee is given the following profiles of four private market investment structures, with the structure names removed.

| Profile | Involvement | Diversification | Liquidity | Cost |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Very low | Very high | Very low | Higher fees than private funds |
| 2 | None after purchase | High | Higher than private funds | Tranche-based |
| 3 | High | Low | Very low | Generally low |
| 4 | Varies | Low | Very low | Setup and maintenance costs |

Which of the following correctly identifies the four structures?

options.text: 1: fund of funds; 2: managed account; 3: direct investment; 4: special purpose vehicle
1: fund of funds; 2: securitization; 3: direct investment; 4: special purpose vehicle
1: private fund; 2: securitization; 3: direct investment; 4: special purpose vehicle
1: fund of funds; 2: securitization; 3: special purpose vehicle; 4: direct investment

questions.solution:
Endowment committee member matches four unlabelled structure profiles to their names.

**Concept and theory**

Figure 93.1 compares the structures on the same dimensions, so each structure has a “fingerprint”. The quickest way to identify a profile is to look for the one attribute that is unique to a single structure:

- “Very high” diversification and “very low” involvement: only funds of funds, because they hold many funds and are the closest to passive.
- “None after purchase” involvement, liquidity “higher than private funds” and “tranche-based” fees: only securitization, because the securities can trade publicly.
- “High” involvement with “generally low” cost: only direct investment.
- “Varies” for involvement and “setup and maintenance” costs: only SPVs.

See the reference grid at the start of Part 3 for all six structures.

**Applying it to this question**

Profile 1: very low involvement, very high diversification, fees above private funds, so fund of funds.

Profile 2: no involvement after purchase, liquidity above private funds, tranche-based cost, so securitization.

Profile 3: high involvement, low diversification, generally low cost, so direct investment.

Profile 4: involvement varies, low diversification, setup and maintenance cost, so SPV.

**Fragile fact.** Direct investment and SPVs share low diversification and very low liquidity; separate them by involvement (high vs varies) and cost (generally low vs setup and maintenance).

**Reference**

LO 93.b (verbatim): “Describe different investment structures that can be used to invest in private assets and compare their characteristics.” Source: Schweser Reading 93, Module 93.1, section “Private Market Investment Structures”, Figure 93.1 as summarized in Key Concepts LO 93.b (Schweser lines 5648 to 5663). GARP: no matching section in the project’s GARP text; content from Schweser, a condensed source (no GARP vs Schweser comparison possible).

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-11 b, where it is Q4 of 12.

a.reason: A managed account has moderate involvement, very low liquidity and negotiated fees, not “none after purchase”, above-fund liquidity and tranche-based fees. A would be correct only if Profile 2 read “moderate, high, very low, negotiated”.

b.reason: B is the only option whose four labels match the Key Concepts profiles of funds of funds, securitization, direct investment and SPVs respectively.

c.reason: A private fund has low to moderate involvement, moderate to high diversification and management plus performance fees; “higher fees than private funds” cannot describe a private fund itself. C would be correct if Profile 1 read “low to moderate, moderate to high, very low, management and performance fees”.

d.reason: Both direct investment and SPVs have low diversification and very low liquidity, which is the trap; the discriminators are involvement (high for direct, varies for SPVs) and cost (generally low for direct, setup and maintenance for SPVs). D would be correct if the involvement and cost cells of rows 3 and 4 were exchanged.

questions.question: The treasurer of a Japanese corporate foundation is choosing how to make the foundation’s first private markets allocation of JPY 6 billion. The foundation has no in-house private markets staff, ranks diversification as its top priority and wants an approach that is as close to passive as possible. Its consultant compares a commitment to a single private fund with a commitment to a private fund of funds (FoF). Which of the following comparisons is most accurate?

options.text: The FoF diversifies more broadly than a single fund and is the closest approximation to a passive approach, but it adds a second layer of management fees.
The FoF diversifies more broadly than a single fund, and because the underlying funds share their costs, its total fees are lower than those of a single fund.
The FoF diversifies more broadly than a single fund and offers materially better liquidity, because it can redeem its underlying fund interests on demand.
The FoF diversifies more broadly than a single fund, but it needs more investor involvement, because the foundation must approve each underlying company.

questions.solution:
Japanese foundation’s treasurer compares a single private fund with a fund of funds.

**Concept and theory**

A private fund of funds (FoF) is a fund whose assets are interests in other private market funds. It adds a second layer of pooling on top of the first, and every feature follows from that layering:

- Diversification is enhanced compared with a single fund (Figure 93.1: very high), because the investor is spread across several managers and their portfolios.
- Involvement is very low; Schweser calls the FoF the closest approximation to a passive investment approach among private market options.
- Cost is higher: the FoF “introduces an additional layer of management fees”, so fees are higher than for private funds.
- Liquidity stays very low, the same as for private funds, because the underlying funds are themselves locked up.
- Typical users: investors with limited experience using it as an entry point, and investors who place a high priority on diversification.

|  | Single private fund | Fund of funds |
|---|---|---|
| Involvement | Low to moderate | Very low |
| Diversification | Moderate to high | Very high |
| Liquidity | Very low | Very low |
| Fees | Management and performance fees | Higher (extra management fee layer) |

**Applying it to this question**

The foundation has no in-house staff, ranks diversification first and wants a near-passive approach: the exact user profile of an FoF. The question asks for the most accurate comparison, so the deciding facts are the extra fee layer and the unchanged, very low liquidity. The JPY 6 billion size is context.

**Fragile fact.** More diversification in an FoF comes with higher fees, not lower, and no improvement in liquidity.

**Reference**

LO 93.b (verbatim): “Describe different investment structures that can be used to invest in private assets and compare their characteristics.” Source: Schweser Reading 93, Module 93.1, section “Private Market Investment Structures”, item 3 “Private funds of funds (FoFs)” (Schweser lines 5261 to 5268) and Key Concepts LO 93.b. GARP: no matching section in the project’s GARP text; content from Schweser, a condensed source (no GARP vs Schweser comparison possible).

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-11 b, where it is Q5 of 12.

a.reason: A states all three source facts: diversification enhanced compared with a single fund, the closest approximation to a passive approach, and an additional layer of management fees.

b.reason: **Polarity flip.** It reverses the fee direction. Schweser says the FoF adds a fee layer and costs more than a private fund. B would be correct only if the stem compared an FoF with building the same portfolio from many separate commitments while ignoring the FoF’s own fees, which the source does not do.

c.reason: **Scope error.** It extends the FoF’s diversification advantage to liquidity. Figure 93.1 rates both private funds and FoFs as very low liquidity; an FoF cannot redeem locked-up fund interests on demand. Among the six structures, only securitization has liquidity higher than private funds, so C would be correct if “FoF” were replaced by “securitization”.

d.reason: **Role misassignment.** It moves decision-making from the managers to the investor. In an FoF the FoF manager picks funds and the underlying general partners pick companies, which is why involvement is very low. D would describe a direct investor, who does make each company decision.

questions.question: An internal auditor at a UK insurer is reviewing the section of a risk report that describes the insurer’s GBP 180 million holding of securitized private credit. Which of the following statements in the report is NOT correct?

options.text: In a securitization, assets, typically debt, are pooled together and divided into tranches with different risk and return characteristics.
The resulting securities can trade publicly, so the liquidity of securitization is higher than that of a private fund interest.
Securitization increases transparency relative to other private structures, because tranching makes each slice’s risk explicit to investors.
The structure suits investors who want exposure to a specific risk profile or want to transfer certain risks, and it gives no control after purchase.

questions.solution:
UK insurer’s internal auditor finds the incorrect statement about securitization.

**Concept and theory**

Securitization pools a set of assets, typically debt, and issues securities in tranches. Each tranche has a different claim on the pool’s cash flows, so tranches carry different risk and return characteristics. Schweser lists these features:

- The securities can trade publicly, which is why its liquidity is higher than that of private funds.
- The structure introduces additional complexity and reduces transparency.
- Typical users want exposure to a specific risk profile or want to transfer certain risks.
- In Figure 93.1: no involvement after purchase, high diversification, tranche-based fees, no control.

The tension worth understanding: tranching creates a cleaner choice of risk level, but the investor is now further from the underlying loans. The pooling and the tranche terms add layers, so the investor sees the assets less clearly. Choice of risk profile and transparency move in opposite directions.

**Applying it to this question**

Check each statement against the source. A, B and D restate source sentences. C says tranching increases transparency, which is the opposite of “introduces additional complexity and reduces transparency”. The GBP size is context.

**Fragile fact.** Securitization: liquidity goes up (relative to private funds), transparency goes down, control is none.

**Reference**

LO 93.b (verbatim): “Describe different investment structures that can be used to invest in private assets and compare their characteristics.” Source: Schweser Reading 93, Module 93.1, section “Private Market Investment Structures”, item 6 “Securitization” (Schweser lines 5281 to 5285) and Key Concepts LO 93.b. GARP: no matching section in the project’s GARP text; content from Schweser, a condensed source (no GARP vs Schweser comparison possible).

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-11 b, where it is Q6 of 12.

a.reason: **Correct statement.** Matches “assets (typically debt) are pooled together and divided into tranches with different risk and return characteristics”. It would be incorrect if it said the assets are typically equity.

b.reason: **Correct statement.** Matches “these securities can trade publicly” and the Key Concepts line “liquidity higher than that of private funds”. It would be incorrect if it claimed liquidity equal to listed equities, an overextension the source does not make.

c.reason: C is the incorrect statement, so it is the answer. Schweser states that securitization “introduces additional complexity and reduces transparency”. Tranching lets the investor choose a risk profile; it does not make the underlying assets more visible.

d.reason:
**Correct statement.** Matches the typical users (“exposure to a specific risk profile or . . . transfer certain risks”) and the Key Concepts entry “no control”. It would be incorrect if it claimed a moderate level of control, which belongs to managed accounts (sibling swap).

The corruption in C is a polarity flip: “reduces transparency” turned into “increases transparency”.

questions.question: A portfolio manager at an Australian superannuation fund with an experienced in-house infrastructure team wants targeted exposure to a single operating toll road, a private real asset, worth about AUD 900 million. The team proposes to hold the investment through a special purpose vehicle (SPV). Which of the following statements about the proposed SPV is most accurate?

options.text: It must be financed entirely with equity, because any SPV that issues debt to fund the asset becomes a securitization structure instead.
It is created to hold a specific asset or group of assets, it offers low diversification, and its costs relate mainly to setup and maintenance.
It offers high diversification for the fund, because an SPV can be structured with either equity or debt and can therefore hold many assets.
It is best suited to investors with limited private markets experience who want a near-passive and broadly diversified entry point.

questions.solution:
Australian superannuation PM assesses an SPV holding one toll road.

**Concept and theory**

A special purpose vehicle (SPV) is an entity created to hold a specific asset or group of assets. Its purpose is to ring-fence one deal or asset so an investor can get precise exposure to it. Schweser’s features:

- Can be structured with either equity or debt.
- Often used to facilitate investment in private real assets (PRAs), such as infrastructure.
- Typical users: more sophisticated investors seeking targeted exposure to a particular deal or asset.
- Figure 93.1: involvement and control vary, diversification low, liquidity very low, costs tied to setup and maintenance.

Low diversification follows from the purpose: a vehicle built to hold one asset is concentrated by design.

**Applying it to this question**

The fund is sophisticated (experienced in-house team), wants targeted exposure to one asset, and the asset is a PRA. This is the textbook SPV use. The question asks which statement about the SPV is most accurate: the deciding facts are “specific asset or group of assets”, low diversification and setup and maintenance costs. The AUD value is context.

**Fragile fact.** SPV users are the sophisticated end of the spectrum (targeted exposure); the inexperienced, diversification-first investor belongs to funds of funds.

**Reference**

LO 93.b (verbatim): “Describe different investment structures that can be used to invest in private assets and compare their characteristics.” Source: Schweser Reading 93, Module 93.1, section “Private Market Investment Structures”, item 5 “Special purpose vehicles (SPVs)” (Schweser lines 5277 to 5280) and Key Concepts LO 93.b. GARP: no matching section in the project’s GARP text; content from Schweser, a condensed source (no GARP vs Schweser comparison possible).

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-11 b, where it is Q7 of 12.

a.reason: **Absolute-claim trap, scope error.** Schweser says SPVs “may be structured with either equity or debt”. Adding debt does not turn an SPV into a securitization; securitization requires pooling assets and dividing them into tranches. A would be correct only if the source restricted SPVs to equity, which it does not.

b.reason: B combines the definition (“an entity created to hold a specific asset or group of assets”) with the Figure 93.1 entries for diversification (low) and cost (tied to setup and maintenance).

c.reason: **Sibling swap.** It gives the SPV the high diversification of securitization or managed accounts, using the true fact that SPVs can use equity or debt as a false reason. Financing choice says nothing about the number of assets held. C would be correct if the structure were a securitization of a diversified loan pool.

d.reason: **Sibling swap on users.** The limited-experience, near-passive, diversification-first user is the typical fund of funds investor. SPVs are considered by more sophisticated investors seeking targeted exposure. D would be correct if “SPV” were replaced by “private fund of funds”.

questions.question:
A credit analyst on the private credit desk of a Chinese commercial bank is preparing training notes, for a CNY 2 billion private markets program, on how private equity and private debt investments can be structured. The notes contain four statements.

I. Preferred shares in a private company can be negotiated to include specific rights and protections, so their features differ from deal to deal.

II. Convertible private debt provides downside protection through its debt component and upside potential through the option to convert into equity.

III. Private debt can be arranged with senior, subordinate or junior rights, each giving a different level of priority over other creditors.

IV. Preferred shares in private companies all confer the same standard level of influence, and this uniformity is what distinguishes them from common shares.

Which of the statements are correct?

options.text: I and II only
I and III only
II, III and IV only
I, II and III only

questions.solution:
Chinese bank’s credit analyst identifies correct statements on private equity and private debt security forms.

**Concept and theory**

Beyond choosing a structure, the investor chooses the security inside it. Schweser closes the LO section with two short paragraphs:

- Private equity can be common shares or preferred shares. Preferred shares “can be negotiated to include specific rights and protections”; as a result, “not all preferred shares offer the same features or level of influence”. In private markets, terms are bargained deal by deal rather than standardized.
- Private debt can be convertible or nonconvertible, with varying seniority. Convertible debt gives downside protection through its debt component and upside potential through the option to convert into equity. Debt can be organized with senior, subordinate or junior rights, each giving a different priority over other creditors.

The idea that unifies both paragraphs is customization: because the securities are privately negotiated, their rights depend on the bargain struck, which is the same theme as the structures themselves.

**Applying it to this question**

I restates the preferred share paragraph: true. II restates the convertible debt sentence: true. III restates the seniority sentence: true. IV says all preferred shares carry the same standard influence, the opposite of “not all preferred shares offer the same features or level of influence”: false. The correct set is I, II and III. The CNY program size is context.

**Fragile fact.** Preferred shares in private companies are negotiated, so they are not uniform; convertible debt gives downside protection and upside, both.

**Reference**

LO 93.b (verbatim): “Describe different investment structures that can be used to invest in private assets and compare their characteristics.” Source: Schweser Reading 93, Module 93.1, section “Private Market Investment Structures”, paragraphs following Figure 93.1 on equity and debt structuring (Schweser lines 5287 to 5296). Boundary call: these paragraphs sit inside the LO 93.b section in Schweser and are treated as in scope. GARP: no matching section in the project’s GARP text; content from Schweser, a condensed source (no GARP vs Schweser comparison possible).

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-11 b, where it is Q8 of 12.

a.reason: **Scope error, omission.** It drops III, treating the seniority statement as false, although Schweser explicitly lists senior, subordinate and junior rights. A would be correct if III had wrongly claimed that all private debt has the same priority.

b.reason: **Scope error, omission.** It drops II, perhaps from believing convertible debt offers only upside. Schweser states it offers both downside protection (debt component) and upside (conversion option). B would be correct if II had said convertible debt offers upside potential with no downside protection.

c.reason: **Absolute-claim trap accepted.** It accepts IV, whose “all . . . the same” is a classic absolute claim, and rejects the true statement I. C would be correct only if preferred share terms were standardized, which the source denies.

d.reason: D selects exactly the three statements supported by the source and excludes IV, which contradicts it.

questions.question: A supervisor at a European securities regulator is reviewing a fund distributor’s marketing brochure, which compares private market structures for clients with EUR 5 million or more to invest. Which of the following comparisons in the brochure is most accurate?

options.text: Direct investment is generally a low-cost structure and offers higher liquidity than private funds, because the owner can sell its stake whenever it wishes.
Securitization offers higher liquidity than private funds, but the investor has no involvement in, and no control over, the assets after purchase.
Direct investment carries higher costs than private funds, because a direct investor pays both management fees and performance-based fees.
Private funds give each investor more control than a managed account, because the general partner acts on behalf of all the limited partners.

questions.solution:
European regulator’s supervisor checks the most accurate structure comparison in a brochure.

**Concept and theory**

The “compare” verb in the LO is tested by asking how two structures differ on one dimension. Three dimensions trap candidates most often:

- Liquidity: five of the six structures are rated very low. Only securitization is higher than private funds, because its securities can trade publicly.
- Cost: direct investment is generally low cost (no manager to pay); private funds charge management and performance-based fees; FoFs add another fee layer; managed account fees are negotiated; SPVs carry setup and maintenance costs; securitization fees are tranche-based.
- Control: direct investment high; managed accounts moderate; private funds limited, because pooling “limits the level of control available to individual investors”; securitization none.

See the reference grid at the start of Part 3.

**Applying it to this question**

Check each comparison on its stated dimension. A: liquidity of direct investment (very low, not higher than funds). B: liquidity of securitization (higher than funds) and its involvement and control (none). C: cost of direct investment (generally low, not higher). D: control in private funds (limited) versus managed accounts (moderate). Only B survives. The EUR 5 million threshold is irrelevant.

**Fragile fact.** Only securitization beats private funds on liquidity; it pays for that with no control and reduced transparency.

**Reference**

LO 93.b (verbatim): “Describe different investment structures that can be used to invest in private assets and compare their characteristics.” Source: Schweser Reading 93, Module 93.1, section “Private Market Investment Structures”, items 1, 2, 4 and 6 (Schweser lines 5244 to 5285) and Key Concepts LO 93.b (lines 5648 to 5663). GARP: no matching section in the project’s GARP text; content from Schweser, a condensed source (no GARP vs Schweser comparison possible).

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-11 b, where it is Q9 of 12.

a.reason: **Scope error.** The cost half is right, but it extends ownership into liquidity. Direct investment liquidity is very low, the same as private funds; owning a private stake does not create a buyer. A would be correct if it compared securitization, not direct investment, with private funds.

b.reason: B matches the Key Concepts entry for securitization: “No involvement after purchase, . . . liquidity higher than that of private funds, . . . and no control.”

c.reason: **Sibling swap.** It gives direct investment the fee structure of private funds (management and performance-based fees). Direct investment is generally low cost. C would be correct if it said private funds cost more than direct investment.

d.reason: **Polarity flip.** It reverses the control ranking. A private fund limits individual investor control; a managed account offers moderate control and, under an advisory mandate, even a veto. D would be correct if “more” were changed to “less”.
