**Concept and theory**

The history in LO 96.a runs in two phases, and the order matters. Phase one is a genuine, and for its time innovative, brokerage business. BMIS was founded in 1960 as a brokerage that quoted bid and ask prices and executed over-the-counter (OTC) trades for clients. It was an early adopter of technology and focused quickly on electronic trading. Its key structural insight was NYSE Rule 390: Schweser describes the rule as allowing NYSE-listed stocks to be traded away from the exchange floor and its specialists. Because NYSE members were prohibited from making markets in exchange-listed stocks, a firm positioned to make those markets off the floor had a competitive advantage. To exploit this, Madoff became a member of the struggling Cincinnati Stock Exchange (CSE) and invested in upgrading its computer systems, which turned the CSE into the first fully electronic trading exchange in the United States. Phase two, the investment advisory business, came only in the late 1980s.

|---|---|
| 1960 | BMIS founded as a brokerage: bid and ask quotes, OTC execution |
| Early on | Early adopter of electronic trading |
| Later | Identifies Rule 390; joins the struggling CSE as a member, funds its computer upgrade; CSE becomes first fully electronic US exchange |
| Separately | Board of governors of NASDAQ, later chairman of its board of directors |
| Late 1980s | Separate investment advisory firm set up as brokerage margins shrink |

| Option | Source of trading profit | Order-routing payment | Industry view of the payment |
|---|---|---|---|
| A | Bid-ask spread quoted in fractions | BMIS paid brokers USD 0.01 per share | Controversial |
| B | Bid-ask spread quoted in fractions | Brokers paid BMIS USD 0.01 per share | Controversial |
| C | Bid-ask spread quoted in pennies | BMIS paid brokers USD 0.01 per share | Controversial |

questions.solution:

**Concept and theory**

A market maker earns the bid-ask spread: it buys at the bid and sells at the ask, keeping the difference on each round trip. In the era Schweser describes, US equity spreads were quoted in fractions (one-eighth or one-fourth of a dollar) rather than in pennies, so the spread per share was large by modern standards. A market maker with wide spreads wants as many orders as possible flowing through it, which motivates payment for order flow: the market maker pays the routing broker a small amount per share to send its customers’ orders. BMIS paid brokers USD 0.01 per share to route orders through the firm. The practice helped BMIS capture more than 5% of trading volume by 1989 and approximately 10% by 2008, but Schweser calls the model “controversial within the industry.”

| Element | BMIS (Schweser) | Common confusion |
|---|---|---|
| Profit source | Bid-ask spread, quoted in fractions | Pennies (modern quoting) |
| Who pays whom | BMIS pays the routing broker | Broker pays BMIS (a commission) |
| Price | USD 0.01 per share |  |
| Industry view | Controversial | Widely accepted |

Each row has three cells. The correct row needs all three: fractions, BMIS paying the broker, and controversy. The volume shares in the stem (5% by 1989, about 10% by 2008) are true context and do not discriminate between rows.

A senior risk analyst at a Brazilian pension fund is writing a training note that replicates Madoff’s reported split-strike conversion strategy. She drafts the following statements.

I. The equity leg is a long position in a portfolio of stocks highly correlated with the S&P 100.

II. The calls are written out of the money on the S&P 100, with a notional value approximately equal to the equity portfolio.

III. The puts are bought at the money on the S&P 100, so that the floor sits exactly at the starting value of the equity portfolio.

IV. The option notional is set at about half the value of the equity portfolio, so that only half of the portfolio’s upside is capped.

Which of the statements accurately describe the reported strategy?

options.text: I, II and III only
I, II and IV only
I only
I and II only

questions.solution:
Pension fund analyst drafting a training note on the legs of the split-strike conversion; which of statements I to IV are accurate.

**Concept and theory**

Madoff described a three-leg position that option traders know as a collar:

1. Long a portfolio of stocks highly correlated with the S&P 100.
2. Write (sell) out-of-the-money (OTM) calls on the S&P 100, notional approximately equal to the equity portfolio.
3. Buy OTM puts on the S&P 100, notional approximately equal to the equity portfolio.

Why each design choice matters. Moneyness: OTM options mean the cap sits above, and the floor below, the starting level, so there is a band in which the position moves with the market. Notional: because each option’s notional approximately equals the equity portfolio, the whole portfolio is capped and floored, not a fraction of it. Underlying: the options are on the S&P 100 so that the hedges match the stock basket. The short call’s premium partly finances the long put.

| Leg | Position | Moneyness | Notional |
|---|---|---|---|
| Stocks (S&P 100-correlated) | Long | n/a | Portfolio value |
| S&P 100 calls | Written (short) | OTM | About equal to portfolio |
| S&P 100 puts | Bought (long) | OTM | About equal to portfolio |

**Applying it to this question**

Check each statement against the three steps. I matches Step 1. II matches Step 2. III changes the puts to at the money: Step 3 says OTM. IV halves the notional: Steps 2 and 3 say approximately equal to the equity portfolio. So I and II only.

**Fragile fact.** Direction and moneyness: calls written, puts bought, both OTM, both on the S&P 100, both with notional approximately equal to the equity portfolio.

**Reference**

LO 96.a (verbatim): “Explain the history of Bernie Madoff’s hedge fund and describe the fund’s reported strategy and its reported performance.” Schweser Book 5, Reading 96, Module 96.1, section “Reported Investment Strategy and Performance”. GARP: the GARP text in the project has no matching section for this reading; content from Schweser, a condensed source whose wording may compress the original framing.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-14 a, where it is Q6 of 13.

a.reason: III moves the puts from out of the money to at the money. With ATM puts the floor would be at the starting value, which is not what was described. A would be correct only if the strategy had been described with ATM puts.

b.reason: IV halves the option notional. Schweser states the notional of both the calls and the puts is “approximately equal to the equity portfolio,” so the entire portfolio is collared. B would be correct only for a partial collar.

c.reason: Rejecting II implies the analyst thinks the call leg was not written OTM with matching notional, typically because she believes the calls were bought. The calls were written (sold). C would be correct only if the strategy held long calls, which it did not.

options.text: In a strong rally, gains on the stocks are eventually offset by the rising liability on the short calls, creating a ceiling; in a sharp fall, declines below a certain point are offset by gains on the long puts, creating a floor.

In a strong rally, gains on the stocks are eventually offset by losses on the long puts, creating a ceiling; in a sharp fall, declines below a certain point are offset by gains on the short calls, creating a floor.

In a strong rally, the return keeps rising one for one with the index because the calls were written out of the money; in a sharp fall, declines below a certain point are offset by the long puts, creating a floor.

In a strong rally, gains on the stocks are eventually offset by the short calls, creating a ceiling; in a sharp fall, the long puts prevent any loss at all, so the position cannot finish a period below its starting value.

questions.solution:
CRO asks how the reported position behaves at expiry in a rally and in a fall; which description is right.

**Concept and theory**

At expiry, with index level $\text{S}_{\text{T}}$, call strike $\text{K}_{\text{c}}$ above the starting level $\text{S}_{0}$ and put strike $\text{K}_{\text{p}}$ below it, the value per index unit of the collared position is

$\underbrace{\text{S}_{\text{T}}}_{\text{stocks}} - \underbrace{\max(\text{S}_{\text{T}} - \text{K}_{\text{c}}, 0)}_{\text{short call}} + \underbrace{\max(\text{K}_{\text{p}} - \text{S}_{\text{T}}, 0)}_{\text{long put}} = \begin{cases} \text{K}_{\text{p}} & \text{S}_{\text{T}} \le \text{K}_{\text{p}} \\ \text{S}_{\text{T}} & \text{K}_{\text{p}} < \text{S}_{\text{T}} < \text{K}_{\text{c}} \\ \text{K}_{\text{c}} & \text{S}_{\text{T}} \ge \text{K}_{\text{c}} \end{cases}$

(ignoring premiums). Schweser in words: “As stock prices rise, gains in the equity portfolio are eventually offset by the increasing liability of the short call position, creating a ceiling on potential returns. Conversely, the long put position establishes a floor, because declines in the equity portfolio are offset by gains in the put options once prices fall below a certain point.” Two features matter: the actor (short call makes the ceiling, long put makes the floor) and the word eventually or “below a certain point” (because both options are OTM, there is a band between $\text{K}_{\text{p}}$ and $\text{K}_{\text{c}}$ where the position simply tracks the index, including losses down to $\text{K}_{\text{p}}$).

**Applying it to this question**

A correct answer must assign the ceiling to the short calls, the floor to the long puts, and keep the floor below the starting level. Only A does all three.

**Fragile fact.** Actor: short call creates the ceiling, long put creates the floor; and the OTM floor sits below the starting value, so small losses are still possible.

**Reference**

LO 96.a (verbatim): “Explain the history of Bernie Madoff’s hedge fund and describe the fund’s reported strategy and its reported performance.” Schweser Book 5, Reading 96, Module 96.1, section “Reported Investment Strategy and Performance”. GARP: the GARP text in the project has no matching section for this reading; content from Schweser, a condensed source whose wording may compress the original framing.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-14 a, where it is Q7 of 13.

a.reason: A is a faithful restatement of Schweser’s two sentences on how the ceiling and floor arise.

b.reason: **Role misassignment: legs swapped.** B gives the ceiling to the long puts and the floor to the short calls. A long put gains when prices fall and expires worthless in a rally, so it cannot cap gains; a short call loses in a rally, so it cannot cushion a fall. B would be correct only for a position that was short puts and long calls, which is not a collar at all.

c.reason: **Scope or condition error: OTM taken to mean no cap.** Writing the calls OTM means the cap starts above the current level, not that it never binds. Once $\text{S}_{\text{T}} > \text{K}_{\text{c}}$, every extra index point gained on the stocks is lost on the calls. C would be correct only for an index move that stays below $\text{K}_{\text{c}}$.

d.reason: **Absolute-claim trap: floor said to prevent any loss.** The puts are OTM, so the position absorbs losses from $\text{S}_{0}$ down to $\text{K}_{\text{p}}$ before the puts pay off. The floor limits losses; it does not eliminate them. D would be correct only with puts struck at or above $\text{S}_{0}$ and net premium no worse than zero.

questions.question:
A portfolio manager at a US family office models one cycle of the reported split-strike conversion strategy. The equity basket tracks the S&P 100 exactly, and the option notional equals the portfolio value. Ignore dividends, interest and transaction costs.

| Input | Value |
|---|---|
| Equity basket value | USD 400 million |
| S&P 100 level at inception | 800 |
| Strike of calls written | 832 |
| Premium per call (index points) | 12 |
| Strike of puts bought | 776 |
| Premium per put (index points) | 8 |
| Implied volatility of the options | 16% |
| Days to expiry | 28 |

What are the maximum and minimum returns on the hedged position over the option life, measured against the initial basket value?

options.text: Maximum +4.0%; minimum −3.0%
Maximum +4.5%; minimum −2.5%
Maximum +3.5%; minimum −3.5%
Maximum +6.5%; minimum −0.5%

questions.solution:
Family-office PM computes the maximum and minimum return of one collar cycle from strikes and premiums, with two irrelevant inputs.

**Concept and theory**

For a collar on a basket that tracks the index exactly, with option notional equal to the basket, the return over one cycle is the index return, truncated at the strikes, plus the net option premium (premium received on the written call minus premium paid on the bought put), all scaled by the starting level $\text{S}_{0}$:

$\text{R}_{\text{max}} = \frac{(\text{K}_{\text{c}} - \text{S}_{0}) + (\text{c} - \text{p})}{\text{S}_{0}}$ , $\text{R}_{\text{min}} = \frac{(\text{K}_{\text{p}} - \text{S}_{0}) + (\text{c} - \text{p})}{\text{S}_{0}}$

where $\text{K}_{\text{c}}$ is the call strike, $\text{K}_{\text{p}}$ the put strike, c the call premium received and p the put premium paid (all in index points). The ceiling comes from the short call, the floor from the long put (Schweser, “Reported Investment Strategy and Performance”). Implied volatility and days to expiry affect what premiums are, but once premiums are given they do not change the payoff range.

**Applying it to this question**

Step 1, net premium:

c $- \text{p} =$ 12 − 8 = 4 index points = 4/800 = 0.5% of $\text{S}_{0}$

Step 2, distance to each strike:

$(\text{K}_{\text{c}} - \text{S}_{0})$/S$_{0} = ($832 − 800)/800 = +4.0%, $(\text{K}_{\text{p}} - \text{S}_{0})$/S$_{0} = ($776 − 800)/800 = −3.0%

Step 3, add the net premium:

$\text{R}_{\text{max}} =$ 4.0% + 0.5% = +4.5%, $\text{R}_{\text{min}} = -$3.0% + 0.5% = −2.5%

In USD on the USD 400 million basket: best case +USD 18 million, worst case −USD 10 million. Meaning: whatever the index does over the 28 days, the hedged position ends between −2.5% and +4.5%. The 16% implied volatility and the 28 days are irrelevant inputs.

**Fragile fact.** Net premium is call premium received minus put premium paid, and it shifts both the ceiling and the floor by the same amount.

**Reference**

LO 96.a (verbatim): “Explain the history of Bernie Madoff’s hedge fund and describe the fund’s reported strategy and its reported performance.” Schweser Book 5, Reading 96, Module 96.1, section “Reported Investment Strategy and Performance”. GARP: the GARP text in the project has no matching section for this reading; content from Schweser, a condensed source whose wording may compress the original framing. The arithmetic applies the standard expiry payoffs of the long put and short call described there; no figures in this question come from the source.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-14 a, where it is Q8 of 13.

a.reason: +4.0% **and** −3.0% **(dropped term: net premium omitted).** These are the Step 2 strike distances with the 0.5% net credit left out. A would be correct if the call and put premiums were equal (a zero-cost collar).

b.reason: B is the only option that both truncates at the two strikes and adds the 0.5% net premium received.

c.reason: +3.5% **and** −3.5% **(sign error on the net premium).** Here the 0.5% is subtracted: 4.0% − 0.5% and −3.0% − 0.5%. That treats the position as paying the net premium. C would be correct if the put premium were 12 and the call premium 8, i.e., a net debit of 4 points.

d.reason: +6.5% **and** −0.5% **(sign error on the put leg: both premiums treated as received).** Adding c $+ \text{p} =$ 20 points = 2.5% gives 4.0% + 2.5% and −3.0% + 2.5%. That is what a seller of both options would collect, but the puts are bought, not written. D would be correct only if the put premium were a credit rather than a cost, which no bought put provides; if the puts were genuinely written, there would be no floor at all.

questions.question:
A treasury analyst at a UK building society reconstructs what a single reported split-strike conversion cycle would have produced in a falling market. The basket tracks the S&P 100 exactly, the option notional equals the basket value, and dividends, interest and transaction costs are ignored. All figures are in USD.

| Input | Value |
|---|---|
| Equity basket value at inception | USD 300 million |
| S&P 100 level at inception | 600 |
| Strike of calls written | 612 |
| Premium per call (index points) | 2.40 |
| Strike of puts bought | 576 |
| Premium per put (index points) | 1.80 |
| S&P 100 level at expiry | 552 |
| Days to expiry at inception | 24 |

What is the profit or loss on the combined position over the cycle?

options.text: A loss of USD 12.0 million
A loss of USD 23.7 million
A profit of USD 6.3 million
A loss of USD 11.7 million

questions.solution:
Building society analyst computes the USD profit or loss of one collar cycle when the index falls through the put strike.

**Concept and theory**

The profit or loss of the collared basket at expiry is the sum of three legs plus the net premium. With N index units of exposure (N $= \text{V}_{0}$/S$_{0}$ when the option notional equals the basket value $\text{V}_{0}$):

$\left[ \right]$

P&L $= \text{N} (\text{S}_{\text{T}} - \text{S}_{0}) - \text{max}(\text{S}_{\text{T}} - \text{K}_{\text{c}}$, 0$) + \text{max}(\text{K}_{\text{p}} - \text{S}_{\text{T}}$, 0$) + (\text{c} - \text{p})$

where $\text{S}_{\text{T}}$ is the index at expiry, $\text{K}_{\text{c}} \text{and K}_{\text{p}}$ the call and put strikes, c the call premium received and p the put premium paid. Below $\text{K}_{\text{p}}$, the stock loss beyond the put strike is offset one for one by the put, so the loss is locked at $(\text{K}_{\text{p}} - \text{S}_{0})$ plus net premium (Schweser: the long put “establishes a floor”).

**Applying it to this question**

Step 1, index units:

N = 300,000,000/600 = 500,000

Step 2, equity leg:

(552 − 600) × 500,000 = −USD 24.0 million

Step 3, long put (in the money, $\text{K}_{\text{p}} =$ 576 > 552):

(576 − 552) × 500,000 = +USD 12.0 million

Step 4, short call $\text{(K}_{\text{c}} =$ 612 > 552, expires worthless): 0. Step 5, net premium:

(2.40 − 1.80) × 500,000 = +USD 0.3 million

Step 6, total:

−24.0 + 12.0 + 0 + 0.3 = −USD 11.7 million (= −3.9% of USD 300 million)

Meaning: an 8% fall in the index costs the collared basket only 3.9%, which is the floor (−4.0%) improved by the 0.1% net credit. The 24 days to expiry is an irrelevant input; the call strike matters only to confirm the call expires worthless.

**Fragile fact.** Below the put strike the loss is fixed at $(\text{K}_{\text{p}} - \text{S}_{0})$ plus net premium; check which strike is the put’s before computing.

**Reference**

LO 96.a (verbatim): “Explain the history of Bernie Madoff’s hedge fund and describe the fund’s reported strategy and its reported performance.” Schweser Book 5, Reading 96, Module 96.1, section “Reported Investment Strategy and Performance”. GARP: the GARP text in the project has no matching section for this reading; content from Schweser, a condensed source whose wording may compress the original framing. The payoff arithmetic applies the long put and short call described there; no figures come from the source.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-14 a, where it is Q9 of 13.

a.reason: −24.0 + 12.0 = −12.0: the net premium of +0.3 million is omitted. It is also the floor loss (576 − 600) × 500,000 on its own. A would be correct for a zero-cost collar.

b.reason: −24.0 + 0.3 = −23.7: the put is treated as expiring worthless, as if the analyst forgot it is in the money at 552. B would be correct only for a basket that had written the calls but bought no puts.

c.reason: (612 − 552) × 500,000 = +30.0 million, then −24.0 + 30.0 + 0.3 = +6.3. Using 612 instead of 576 creates a “put” struck above the starting level, which would make the position profit in a fall. C would be correct only if the puts were struck at 612, i.e., deep in the money at inception.

d.reason: D is the only option that includes all four components (stocks, put payoff, zero call payoff, net credit).

questions.question: An investment consultant at a Canadian pension plan is reviewing an old feeder-fund document that summarised Madoff’s split-strike conversion strategy and how he said he implemented it. Which of the following statements about the strategy as reported is least accurate?

options.text: Once established, the position typically needed little attention until the options neared expiration, which is why it is sometimes called a vacation trade.
The strategy was implemented over short time horizons, typically less than 30 days.
The equity basket stayed fully invested in S&P 100 stocks at all times, with the options rolled each month so that the hedge never lapsed.
The firm actively traded a portfolio of stocks and options designed to closely mirror the S&P 100 Index.

questions.solution:
Pension consultant reviews a feeder-fund summary of the reported strategy and its implementation; which statement is least accurate.

**Concept and theory**

LO 96.a asks you to describe the reported strategy, which includes not just the three legs but how Madoff said he ran them:

- The firm “actively traded a portfolio of stocks and options designed to closely mirror the S&P 100 Index.”
- The collar is “sometimes described as a vacation trade because, once established, the position typically required little attention until the options neared expiration.”
- “Madoff claimed that the portfolio was held in cash most of the time and that the split-strike conversion strategy was implemented over short time horizons, typically less than 30 days.”

The cash claim is the distinctive one: the strategy was supposedly switched on for short windows and the rest of the time the money sat in cash.

**Applying it to this question**

Three of the four options match the source. The deciding fact is the cash claim: a basket that “stayed fully invested in S&P 100 stocks at all times” contradicts “held in cash most of the time.”

**Fragile fact.** Claimed state of the money most of the time: cash, not invested; active periods typically under 30 days.

**Reference**

LO 96.a (verbatim): “Explain the history of Bernie Madoff’s hedge fund and describe the fund’s reported strategy and its reported performance.” Schweser Book 5, Reading 96, Module 96.1, section “Reported Investment Strategy and Performance”. GARP: the GARP text in the project has no matching section for this reading; content from Schweser, a condensed source whose wording may compress the original framing.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-14 a, where it is Q10 of 13.

a.reason: **Consistent with the source.** The vacation-trade description is in Schweser. A false version would say the position needed constant intraday rebalancing.

b.reason: **Consistent with the source.** “Short time horizons, typically less than 30 days” is stated. A false version would give a multi-month or annual horizon (scope error on the horizon).

c.reason: C reverses the stated cash position. Even its plausible detail (monthly rolling, consistent with horizons under 30 days) does not rescue it, because the claim of permanent full investment is the opposite of what Madoff said.

d.reason: **Consistent with the source.** Active trading of stocks and options to closely mirror the S&P 100 is stated. A false version would substitute another index such as the S&P 500 (sibling swap).

questions.question:
A risk consultant at a Chinese fund of hedge funds (reporting in CNY) is training staff to recognise the return profile that Madoff’s feeder funds reported over their 17-year history. She shows four anonymised profiles alongside the S&P 100.

| Profile | Average annual return (%) | Annual volatility (%) | Positive months (%) | Worst calendar year (%) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| S&P 100 (reference) | 10.8 | 14.5 | 61 | −21.4 |
| Profile W | 10.3 | 2.6 | 96 | +5.9 |
| Profile X | 10.6 | 13.9 | 63 | −18.7 |
| Profile Y | 19.4 | 2.8 | 97 | +11.2 |
| Profile Z | 10.1 | 2.4 | 97 | −1.3 |

Which profile is most consistent with the reported performance of Madoff’s feeder funds?

options.text: Profile W
Profile X
Profile Y
Profile Z

questions.solution:
Fund-of-funds consultant compares four anonymised return profiles with the S&P 100; which matches Madoff’s reported record.

**Concept and theory**

The “reported performance” half of LO 96.a has four checkable facts:

| Dimension | Reported record (Schweser) |
|---|---|
| Level | Steady annual returns of 8% to 12%, comparable to the S&P 100 |
| Volatility | Dramatically lower than the S&P 100 |
| Monthly hit rate | More than 95% of months positive (negative in fewer than 5%) |
| Annual record | Never a single down year, over a 17-year period |

The combination, index-like return with a small fraction of index volatility, is what makes the record remarkable. (Why that combination signals fraud is LO 96.b and is not tested here.)

**Applying it to this question**

Screen each profile against the four facts:

| Profile | 8% to 12%, near index? | Vol far below 14.5%? | > 95% positive? | No down year? |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| W | Yes (10.3) | Yes (2.6) | Yes (96) | Yes (+5.9) |
| X | Yes (10.6) | No (13.9) | No (63) | No (−18.7) |
| Y | No (19.4) | Yes (2.8) | Yes (97) | Yes (+11.2) |
| Z | Yes (10.1) | Yes (2.4) | Yes (97) | No (−1.3) |

Only W passes all four.

**Fragile fact.** Return comparable to the index, volatility dramatically lower; more than 95% positive months and zero down years, both conditions required.

**Reference**

LO 96.a (verbatim): “Explain the history of Bernie Madoff’s hedge fund and describe the fund’s reported strategy and its reported performance.” Schweser Book 5, Reading 96, Module 96.1, section “Reported Investment Strategy and Performance”, plus the LO 96.a key concepts. GARP: the GARP text in the project has no matching section for this reading; content from Schweser, a condensed source whose wording may compress the original framing. Key concepts wording: “negative results in fewer than 5% of months.” The profile figures are illustrative; the source gives no volatility number.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-14 a, where it is Q11 of 13.

a.reason: Profile W shows a return comparable to the index (10.3% against 10.8%), volatility far below it (2.6% against 14.5%), 96% positive months and a worst year that is still positive: every element of Schweser’s description.

b.reason: X has the right return level but index-like volatility, hit rate and drawdown. Madoff’s reported volatility was “dramatically lower” than the S&P 100, not similar. X would be correct for an unhedged index tracker.

c.reason: Y has the smoothness but a 19.4% average return, outside the 8% to 12% range and far above the index. Schweser says returns were “comparable to those of the S&P 100.” Y would be correct only if the record had been described as significantly beating the index.

d.reason: Z matches return, volatility and hit rate, but its worst calendar year is −1.3%. A high share of positive months does not guarantee no losing year. Schweser: the advisory business “never recorded a single down year.” Z would be correct only if the record had included one small losing year.

questions.question:
An examiner at a securities regulator is writing a case study on how BMIS collapsed in December 2008. She lists the following events.

I. Madoff tries to raise additional capital but cannot do so quickly enough.

II. Madoff’s sons report him to US authorities.

III. Amid market turmoil, redemption requests arrive faster than BMIS can meet them.

IV. Madoff tells his sons, wife and brother that the advisory business is “a giant Ponzi scheme.”

V. Madoff is arrested and charged with securities fraud; his family’s assets are frozen and a receiver is appointed for BMIS.

Which sequence correctly orders these events from first to last?

options.text: III, IV, I, II, V
III, I, IV, II, V
I, III, IV, II, V
III, I, II, IV, V

questions.solution:
Regulator’s case study orders five events in the December 2008 collapse.

**Concept and theory**

A Ponzi scheme pays withdrawals with other investors’ money rather than with investment returns, so it survives only while inflows cover outflows. Schweser’s account of the end is a causal chain, not just a list of dates:

1. By late 2008 markets were in turmoil and redemption requests flooded in faster than BMIS could meet them.
2. Madoff tried to raise additional capital but could not do so quickly enough.
3. “At that point,” on December 10, 2008, he admitted to his sons, wife and brother that it was “all a big lie,” a “giant Ponzi scheme.”
4. That evening his sons reported him to US authorities.
5. He was arrested the following day, charged with securities fraud; his family’s assets were frozen and a receiver was appointed to oversee BMIS.

Schweser stresses that Madoff “was not discovered through an investigation”; the trigger was his own confession under liquidity pressure.

**Applying it to this question**

Map the statements: III (redemptions) → I (failed capital raise) → IV (confession) → II (sons report) → V (arrest, charges, freeze, receiver). The sequence is III, I, IV, II, V.

**Fragile fact.** Confession on December 10, 2008 to sons, wife and brother; sons report that evening; arrest the following day. GARP’s “Predicting Fraud” reading dates the SEC charge to December 11, 2008, consistent with this.

**Reference**

LO 96.a (verbatim): “Explain the history of Bernie Madoff’s hedge fund and describe the fund’s reported strategy and its reported performance.” Schweser Book 5, Reading 96, Module 96.1, section “Fund Collapse and Confession”. GARP: the GARP text in the project has no matching section for this reading; content from Schweser, a condensed source whose wording may compress the original framing. GARP cross-check: “Predicting Fraud,” Section 11.1 Introduction (“On December 11, 2008, the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) charged Bernard Madoff with securities fraud”); consistent with Schweser.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-14 a, where it is Q12 of 13.

a.reason: Schweser places the failed attempt first and the confession “at that point.” A would be correct only if Madoff had confessed and then sought money to repay investors.

b.reason: B is the only option that keeps cause before response (redemptions before the capital raise), response before confession (“At that point, he admitted”), and confession before the sons’ report.

c.reason: The capital raise was a response to redemptions he could not meet. C would be correct only if the scheme had sought new money before the redemption wave, which is not how the source tells it.

d.reason: **confession).** Placing II before IV means the sons reported him before he confessed, i.e., that they uncovered the fraud themselves. They reported him the evening of his confession to them. D would be correct only if the family had found the fraud independently.

questions.question: The chief compliance officer of a Swiss private bank is preparing a report for the board on why the Madoff scheme collapsed when it did and what followed. Which statement should she include as the most accurate?

options.text: Madoff confessed out of remorse, choosing to end the scheme at a time when BMIS could still have met all pending redemption requests.
The 2008 fall in equity prices pushed the S&P 100 through the strikes of the puts, inflicting genuine trading losses that the strategy could not absorb.
Much like the subprime mortgage episode, the structure could persist only while asset prices were rising; had the 2008 downturn not intensified, the scheme might have continued for some time.
The losses fell mainly on BMIS’s own USD 700 million of equity capital, so the final investors in the feeder funds were largely protected.

questions.solution:
CCO’s board report on why the scheme collapsed when it did and what followed; which statement is most accurate.

**Concept and theory**

Schweser makes three points about the collapse and aftermath.

- Motive: “Madoff did not confess out of remorse or honesty.” Redemptions arrived faster than BMIS could meet them and he could not raise capital quickly enough.
- Mechanism: “Had the market downturn not intensified, the scheme might have continued for some time.” Schweser compares it with the subprime mortgage crisis: “it could persist only while asset prices were rising, but once prices began to fall, the entire structure collapsed.” What failed was funding, not a trading strategy, because the business was “all a big lie.”
- Aftermath: a 150-year prison sentence; total investor losses estimated at up to USD 50 billion; losses extended beyond individuals to charities, pension funds, hedge funds, funds of hedge funds, banks and celebrities, and investors lost their life savings.

**Applying it to this question**

The deciding facts are the motive (not remorse), the mechanism (a funding run in a falling market, not trading losses) and who bore the losses (the investors). Only C states the mechanism as the source does.

**Fragile fact.** Motive: liquidity pressure, not remorse; the run on the fund happened because prices were falling, in the same way as the subprime analogy.

**Reference**

LO 96.a (verbatim): “Explain the history of Bernie Madoff’s hedge fund and describe the fund’s reported strategy and its reported performance.” Schweser Book 5, Reading 96, Module 96.1, section “Fund Collapse and Confession”, plus the reading’s opening paragraphs (sentence and losses). GARP: the GARP text in the project has no matching section for this reading; content from Schweser, a condensed source whose wording may compress the original framing.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-14 a, where it is Q13 of 13.

a.reason: **Polarity flip on motive and solvency.** Schweser states he “did not confess out of remorse or honesty” and confessed because redemptions could no longer be met. A would be correct only for a voluntary wind-down by a solvent manager.

b.reason: **Sibling swap: a real hedging-strategy failure substituted for a Ponzi funding failure.** B explains the collapse with genuine option-strategy losses. There was no genuine strategy, and in any case a collar’s long puts limit losses in a fall. The collapse came from redemptions outrunning inflows. B would be correct only for a legitimate fund hit by a market move.

c.reason: C reproduces Schweser’s subprime analogy and its counterfactual: the structure persisted only while prices rose, and absent the intensifying downturn it “might have continued for some time.”

d.reason: **Role misassignment: losses placed on the firm instead of the investors.** USD 700 million was BMIS’s equity capital, but losses were estimated at up to USD 50 billion and fell on investors, including charities, pension funds and banks. questions.question:
A senior risk analyst at a Canadian public pension plan is reviewing an equity options manager that runs about CAD 2.4 billion. The manager’s operational due diligence questionnaire shows the following service-provider map.

| Function | Provider |
|---|---|
| Investment management | The manager |
| Trade execution | Broker-dealer owned by the manager |
| Custody of assets | Broker-dealer owned by the manager |
| Fund administration and NAV | In-house team of the manager |
| Year of first launch | 1994 |

Which of the following best explains why this arrangement is a potential fraud-risk indicator?

options.text: The arrangement establishes that reported performance has been fabricated, so the plan should treat the manager as a confirmed fraud rather than as a risk to investigate.
The arrangement is a concern only where the fund’s own auditor is small; once a large audit firm signs the fund’s accounts, keeping these functions in-house removes the fraud risk.

With no separate executing broker, custodian or administrator, no independent party confirms that trades occurred or that assets exist, which makes performance easier to manipulate and assets easier to misappropriate.
The main concern is that an in-house administrator may lack the systems to price positions correctly, so the risk is honest valuation error in NAV rather than deliberate misstatement.

questions.solution:
Senior risk analyst at a Canadian pension plan: manager whose execution, custody and administration are all in-house.

**Concept and theory**

In a normally structured fund, the functions that create and record value are split among separate entities: the investment manager decides what to buy, an executing broker carries out the trades, a custodian holds the assets, and a fund administrator values the portfolio and calculates NAV. The point of the split is not efficiency; it is verification. Each independent party produces records that the others cannot alter: the custodian can confirm that the securities exist, the broker that the trades happened, the administrator that the NAV reflects real prices. Schweser lists “lack of independent service providers” as the first operational red flag: BMIS performed all of these roles in-house, which “made it far easier to manipulate performance results and potentially misappropriate assets.”

| Function | Typical fund | BMIS |
|---|---|---|
| Investment management | Manager | BMIS |
| Trade execution | Independent broker | BMIS |
| Custody | Independent custodian | BMIS |
| Administration and NAV | Independent administrator | BMIS |

Context only (neighbouring GARP chapter, not the assigned reading): GARP’s “Predicting Fraud by Investment Managers” notes that custody “facilitates fraud by removing external oversight” (GARP text lines 17668 to 17669), which is the same mechanism.

**Applying it to this question**

The table shows that every function that could verify the manager’s claims is performed by the manager or an entity it owns. The question asks how this indicates fraud risk, so the answer must name the mechanism (no independent verification, therefore easier manipulation and misappropriation) without overclaiming. The year of first launch is irrelevant data.

**Fragile fact.** The red flag is the absence of independent verification across execution, custody, administration and management, and it signals fraud risk, not proof.

**Reference**

Schweser Reading 96, Module 96.2, Operational Red Flags, “Lack of independent service providers”; Key Concepts “Lack of independent oversight”. GARP: no matching section in the project’s GARP text; content from Schweser, a condensed source.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-14 b, where it is Q1 of 14.

a.reason: **Absolute claim.** A red flag indicates potential fraud risk; it does not prove fraud. The source’s wording is “easier to manipulate” and “potentially misappropriate”. A would be right only if the stem added evidence that assets were missing, for example a failed custody confirmation.

b.reason: **Condition error.** B adds a condition that removes the risk when a large firm audits the fund. Madoff’s feeder funds were audited by large firms such as KPMG, yet those firms relied on the work of BMIS’s tiny auditor without verifying it, so the large-firm name did not restore independent verification. B would be closer to right only if the large auditor itself independently confirmed custody and trades at the manager.

c.reason: C names exactly the mechanism in the source: with no separate parties, no one independently confirms trades or assets, so performance is easier to manipulate and assets easier to misappropriate.

d.reason: **Scope error.** D recasts the risk as honest valuation error. The red flag is about the opportunity for deliberate manipulation and misappropriation created by the absence of independent checks, not about system quality. The chief compliance officer of a private bank in Singapore is preparing an SGD-denominated training pack on governance red flags at Bernard L. Madoff Investment Securities (BMIS). A junior colleague has drafted four statements.

I. BMIS acted as both broker-dealer and market maker for some of its own strategies, which created opportunities for self-dealing and removed a layer of independent oversight.

II. Because family members held senior positions, BMIS was legally unable to register with the SEC as an investment adviser until 2006.

III. Regulatory filings reported only one to five individuals running the investment advisory business, an implausibly small number for a firm with about \$17 billion under management.

IV. The dual broker-dealer and market-maker role was a red flag chiefly because it allowed BMIS to charge investors both a management fee and a performance fee.

Which of the statements should be kept in the training pack as accurate?

options.text: I and III only
I, III and IV only
III only
I, II and III only

questions.solution:
CCO at a Singapore private bank auditing four statements on BMIS’s governance red flags.

**Concept and theory**

Two operational red flags concern governance. First, the conflict of interest: BMIS acted as both broker-dealer and market maker for some of its own strategies. When the same firm sets prices, executes and records trades for its own clients, there is room for self-dealing and one layer of independent oversight disappears. Second, family members in key roles: Madoff’s brother, sons, niece and nephew held senior positions, which raised concerns about independence and internal oversight, and regulatory filings reported only one to five individuals managing the investment advisory business, implausibly few for about \$17 billion under management. Both flags matter for the same underlying reason: they weaken the internal and external checks that would expose fabricated results.

**Applying it to this question**

Test each statement against the source. I matches the conflict-of-interest flag word for word in substance. II links family control to the 2006 registration date; the source attributes late registration to a loophole that let BMIS count feeder funds as its clients, not to family roles. III matches the family-control flag and its staffing detail. IV attaches fees to the dual role, but BMIS charged no management or performance fees. Only I and III survive.

**Fragile fact.** The conflict is the broker-dealer plus market-maker dual role; the staffing number is one to five people for about \$17 billion.

GARP: no matching section in the project’s GARP text; content from Schweser, a condensed source.

a.reason: I and III restate the source: the dual role “created opportunities for self-dealing and removed an important layer of independent oversight”, and filings reported “only one to five individuals” running a \$17 billion advisory business.

b.reason: **Accepts IV, a polarity flip on fees.** IV says BMIS charged management and performance fees; the source says it charged neither and collected only brokerage commissions. B would be right if the stem described a manager whose dual role let it extract layered fees.

c.reason: **Rejects I, polarity flip on the dual role.** C keeps III but drops I, treating BMIS’s broker-dealer and market-maker dual role as if it were not a red flag. The actual cause was the loophole of counting feeder funds as “clients”. D would be right if II read “BMIS avoided registration until 2006 by counting feeder funds as its clients”.

Internal auditor at a Japanese insurer: why a large audit firm’s sign-off on the feeder fund gave false comfort.

|---|---|---|
| Feeder funds | Major firms (e.g. KPMG) | Relied on the BMIS auditor’s work |
| BMIS | Friehling & Horowitz (3 people) | No credible audit of BMIS |

The approval memo took comfort from the large auditor of the feeder fund. The deciding fact is the role split: the large firm audited the feeder, not BMIS, and it relied on the tiny BMIS auditor. The JPY amount is irrelevant.

The underlying manager, which has reported steady positive returns for many years, charges the feeder no management fee and no performance fee and collects only brokerage commissions on trades. Which of the following best explains how this fee structure can indicate potential fraud risk?

options.text: A manager with apparently superior, consistent results would be expected to capture fees on that success; forgoing millions in fees was economically illogical, and leaving the fee margin to the feeders encouraged them to overlook other red flags.

**Concept and theory**

Fees are a manager’s reward for producing returns. A manager with a long record of steady, positive results has strong bargaining power and would normally charge management and performance fees. Read together, the fee structure both signalled that the returns might not be what they seemed and weakened the incentive of the feeders, the only parties positioned to do due diligence, to look closely.

The stem gives exactly the BMIS pattern: manager charges no management or performance fee, collects commissions; feeder charges 1.5% and 20%. The question asks how this indicates fraud risk, so the answer must contain both the illogic and the feeder incentive, without the overstatement that BMIS charged nothing at all.

**Fragile fact.** BMIS charged commissions only (not zero fees); the feeders charged the high fees, which gave them a reason to look away.

b.reason: **Absolute claim.** B says the manager charged no fees of any kind and that this alone establishes fabrication. The unusual fee structure red flag rests on a split of economics: BMIS charged no management or performance fees, only brokerage commissions, while the feeders charged high fees to their investors. $\text{F}_{\text{total}} = \text{m} \times\text{A}_{0} + \text{p} \times(\text{R}_{\text{g}} \times\text{A}_{0})$,

Gross reported gain = 0.10 × 200 = BRL 20.0 million

Performance fee = 0.20 × 20.0 = BRL 4.0 million

$\text{F}_{\text{total}} =$ 3.0 + 4.0 = BRL 7.0 million

Meaning: the feeder earned BRL 7.0 million (35% of the BRL 20.0 million gross gain) while the manager earned no management or performance fee: the gap the source calls illogical, and the feeders’ incentive to overlook red flags.

A trade confirmation is evidence that a trade happened at a stated price. Its value as evidence depends on who produces it and whether anyone else can check it. Combined with the lack of third-party verification, this “made it possible for the firm to fabricate trade confirmations after the fact to match reported performance results.” The mechanism is timing plus control: if the firm alone creates the record and the record can be produced days later, the firm can choose prices after seeing how the market moved, producing a confirmation consistent with whatever return it wants to report. Electronic access to an independent account would remove that freedom.

questions.question: A senior risk analyst at an AUD fund of hedge funds is presenting the Madoff case to newly hired analysts. She explains that, before 2008, investors offered several explanations for the manager’s near-perfect record: superior stock selection, use of market-making profits to smooth results, leverage, and front running. Which of the following statements is most accurate?

options.text: A genuine split-strike strategy would inevitably produce some negative months; none of the explanations was legitimate, and Markopolos argued the returns were impossible without front running or a Ponzi structure.
The long put in a split-strike strategy eliminates all losing months, so the absence of negative months was consistent with the strategy, and the red flag lay only in the level of returns.
Using market-making profits to smooth results would have been a legitimate explanation, so the record was a red flag only to the extent that it also relied on leverage.
The SEC concluded in 2005 that the returns were impossible without front running or a Ponzi structure, but Markopolos dismissed these warnings when he reviewed the fund.

questions.solution:
FoHF analyst presenting the Madoff case: evaluating the explanations offered for near-perfect returns.

**Concept and theory**

A split-strike conversion holds a stock portfolio, sells out-of-the-money calls and buys out-of-the-money puts. Because the puts are out of the money, the portfolio can still lose value between the current price and the put strike, and the calls cap the upside. Such a strategy “can be profitable over time but will inevitably produce some negative months”. Madoff’s reported record had essentially none, which is why Schweser calls it a black box strategy red flag. Investors rationalised the record in four ways: superior stock selection, using market-making profits to smooth results, leverage, and front running (an illegal practice in the United States). The source’s conclusion is that “no legitimate explanation could account for his results”. Harry Markopolos, a former portfolio manager, repeatedly warned the SEC, including in his 2005 report The World’s Largest Hedge Fund Is a Fraud, arguing that the returns were impossible without either front running or a Ponzi structure; regulators dismissed his warnings.

| Rationalisation | Why it fails as a legitimate explanation |
|---|---|
| Stock selection, leverage | Cannot remove the losing months a collar produces |
| Smoothing with market-making profits | Misstates the strategy’s real results |
| Front running | Illegal in the United States |

**Applying it to this question**

Deciding facts: a genuine split-strike strategy must produce some negative months, none of the four explanations was legitimate, and Markopolos warned while the SEC dismissed.

**Fragile fact.** Markopolos warned, the SEC dismissed; front running is illegal, so it is not a legitimate explanation.

**Reference**

LO 96.b: Identify characteristics of Bernie Madoff’s hedge fund that can serve as warning signs or potential “red flags” and explain how they can indicate potential fraud risk. Schweser Reading 96, Module 96.2, Investment Red Flags, “Black box strategy”; closing paragraph on Markopolos. Collar mechanics belong to LO 96.a and serve only as the frame. GARP: no matching section in the project’s GARP text; content from Schweser, a condensed source.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-14 b, where it is Q10 of 14.

a.reason: A combines the three sourced facts: inevitable negative months, no legitimate explanation, and Markopolos’s argument that the returns required front running or a Ponzi structure.

b.reason: **Absolute claim.** The long put sets a floor below the put strike; it does not eliminate losing months, and the source says the strategy “will inevitably produce some negative months”. B would be right only for a hedge that removed all downside, which a collar with out-of-the-money puts does not.

c.reason: **Scope error.** C treats smoothing with market-making profits as legitimate. The source lists it among the rationalisations and concludes that no legitimate explanation could account for the results. C would be right only if the source had accepted smoothing as a valid explanation.

d.reason: **Role misassignment.** D swaps the actors: Markopolos made the argument and warned the SEC; the regulators dismissed the warnings. D would be right with the names reversed.

A treasury analyst at a Hong Kong insurer is checking a manager’s quarter-end Form 13F filings against its stated strategy. The data are summarised below.

| Item | Observation |
|---|---|
| Stated strategy | Split-strike conversion on S&P 100 stocks |
| Assets under management | About USD 17 billion |
| Holdings shown on Form 13F | Small positions in minor, non-S&P 100 companies |
| Manager’s explanation | Portfolio converted to cash at each quarter end |
| Insurer’s proposed allocation | HKD 400 million |

Form 13F is a required quarterly filing of equity holdings. It gives an outside view of what a manager actually held at quarter end. BMIS’s filings showed small holdings in minor, non-S&P 100 companies, inconsistent with a strategy built on S&P 100 stocks. Madoff’s explanation was that he converted the portfolio to cash at the end of each quarter to avoid public scrutiny of his positions. Schweser rejects this: moving such enormous sums each quarter “would have been impractical and implausible, given the scale of AUM.” The red flag thus has two layers: the holdings contradict the strategy, and the excuse for the contradiction is itself implausible at the manager’s size.

**Applying it to this question**

The table gives both layers: non-S&P 100 holdings and a quarter-end cash explanation for a manager with about USD 17 billion. The HKD allocation is irrelevant.

**Fragile fact.** 13F showed small, non-S&P 100 holdings; the quarter-end cash excuse fails on scale.

Madoff did claim to hold cash most of the time, but the source’s point is that converting such enormous sums at every quarter end was implausible given the AUM. No counterparties were confirmed, suggesting the trades were never executed.

II. The use of paper trade confirmations is classified as an investment red flag, because it reveals an inconsistency with the stated strategy.

UK insurer board member: classifying red flags and judging whether they were detectable from public information.

**Concept and theory**

Schweser groups the red flags in two families. Operational red flags concern how the firm was run and verified: lack of independent service providers, conflict of interest, questionable auditing firm, family members in key roles, unusual fee structure, lack of transparency, late SEC registration and paper trade confirmations. Investment red flags are those that “pointed to inconsistencies in Madoff’s strategy and performance”: black box strategy, questionable style exposure, illogical Form 13F filings and impossible use of S&P 100 options.

| Operational (how the firm was run) | Investment (strategy and performance) |
|---|---|
| Independent service providers; conflict of interest; auditor; family roles; fees; transparency; late registration; paper confirmations | Black box strategy; style exposure; Form 13F filings; S&P 100 options |

The closing paragraph adds that the flags were detectable: Markopolos warned the SEC repeatedly (regulators dismissed the warnings), a few banks declined to do business with BMIS, and even using only public Form ADV information, a methodology developed by Brown, Goetzmann, Liang and Schwarz (2008) would have identified the firm as problematic. The fraud did not come to light through these warnings; Madoff confessed to family members in December 2008 when he could not meet redemptions (LO 96.a content, used here only to judge statement IV).

Context only (neighbouring GARP chapter, not the assigned reading): GARP’s “Predicting Fraud by Investment Managers” reports that the predicted fraud risk of BMIS from Form ADV data is above the 95th percentile (GARP text line 17273, footnote 2), which supports the same point using a different study.

**Fragile fact.** Paper confirmations are operational; Form 13F is investment; Markopolos’s warnings were dismissed.
